#3201. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3199. Prediction: AbbVie's Next Blockbuster Is Hiding in a Two-Drug Crohn's Combo

AbbVie (ABBV -2.39%) has already pulled off one of the great commercial pivot stories in pharmaceutical history. When Humira -- once pharma's top-selling drug -- lost patent exclusivity, the Chicago-based company leaned on Skyrizi and Rinvoq, which generated $17.5 billion and $8.3 billion respectively in 2025. Skyrizi alone exceeded $10 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026.

Most investors consider that reinvention story complete. It isn't. AbbVie may be building its next blockbuster -- and this one could eventually outperform its predecessor.

AbbVie's ABBV-466 pairs its blockbuster Skyrizi with a second antibody called trosunilimab, each targeting a different driver of Crohn's inflammation. In a Phase 2 clinical study, the combination put more patients into remission than either drug delivered on its own -- meeting the study's primary endpoint.

The numbers are striking. At week 12, 30.2% of patients treated with the combination reached endoscopic remission -- defined as the absence of visible inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract -- compared to 21.3% of those on Skyrizi and 18% of patients on trosunilimab. More importantly, the advantage widened as the trial progressed. At week 24, 40.5% in the ABBV-466 group reached endoscopic remission, compared to 22.4% of patients treated only with Skyrizi and 20% of those on trosunilimab monotherapy.

That's not a modest improvement over Skyrizi -- already the standard of care in Crohn's disease. It's nearly double the remission rate, and the gap widened over time, a pattern that typically signals a durable biological effect rather than a transient one.

The science behind the result makes intuitive sense. Skyrizi targets one key driver of Crohn's inflammation, but AbbVie's research showed that some patients were still experiencing flare-ups through a second, separate pathway that Skyrizi leaves untouched. Trosunilimab was added specifically to block that second pathway. The result is a combination that closes both doors simultaneously, applying the same logic that has made combination therapy the standard of care in cancer treatment.

Rates of serious adverse events were slightly higher for ABBV-466 at 10.4%, compared to 9.6% on Skyrizi monotherapy and 9% on trosunilimab alone. However, that's a modest difference that isn't unusual for a combination regimen and one that the clinical benefit appears to justify.

Wall Street took notice immediately. The result led BMO (BMO +1.18%) Capital Markets to ask: "Sky is the limit?" BMO analysts said the early data for ABBV-466 "could chart a path for a more efficacious dual-targeting version of Skyrizi" and called the results "a positive for ABBV shares, potentially positioning the company with an efficacious follow-up molecule to Skyrizi in Crohn's."

BMO wasn't alone in its enthusiasm. RBC (RY +0.77%) Capital Markets analysts wrote that they see it "as a win for ABBV's lifecycle management with Skyrizi and for its next-gen agents in development, and reinforces our thesis that ABBV is building a durable moat in IBD through next-gen combo strategies."

ABBV-466 holds the potential to add to AbbVie's success story. The pharma stock is up almost 30% year-to-date. It has more than doubled over the past three years, handily beating the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%). AbbVie's stock is also a favorite for income investors. The company is a member of the Dividend Kings, an elite group with dividend increase streaks of at least 50 consecutive years.

I predict that ABBV-466 is the beginning of AbbVie's next blockbuster story. I also think that this story is one that the market is not yet pricing into the stock.

There's a caveat to my prediction, though. ABBV-466 has only had Phase 2 results so far. A Phase 3 program and a multi-year path to potential approval still lie ahead. Investors buying AbbVie today on ABBV-466 are doing so well before the confirmatory evidence arrives.

That caveat aside, AbbVie has earned the benefit of the doubt on lifecycle management. When Humira's exclusivity ended, most analysts underestimated how completely Skyrizi and Rinvoq would fill the commercial gap. My prediction is that ABBV-466 tells that same story a second time.

Keith Speights has positions in AbbVie. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends AbbVie. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3197. This tool can recover deleted AI chats from your phone – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This new tool proves it's still best to limit the info you share with chatbots.

Researchers at Georgia Tech have created a tool that can recover deleted conversations with AI assistants from Android phones. That has potentially promising implications for getting other types of erased information off phones during investigations, for example. But it also means your on-device AI chats, which are supposed to be private, may have a longer shelf life than intended.

But, as it turns out, some information from those sessions can stick around in your phone’s working memory even if you’ve deleted the chats themselves. Georgia Tech researchers created ORISA, a tool that searches that memory for clues to deleted conversations. They designed a fake note-keeping AI assistant for their experiment using the ChatterUI Android app, gave it a set of 100 fictional pieces of information about a project, and then deleted that information.

Also: You can run local AI on your Android or iOS device

Using ORISA, the researchers then searched the device memory for remnants of that information that could be used as context to restart the session. ORISA found enough usable information to create a new working session with 26 fictional facts from the original set of 100. That’s more than the 14 the original assistant session had access to, “because the rest had fallen outside its active memory,” the researchers explained.

“It can help establish what information someone shared with an AI assistant and what assistance they received,” Ph.D. student Ken Xu, and lead author of the study, said of the experiment.

ORISA was developed to fill a cybersecurity gap. The researchers noted that a downside of local AI is its lack of “centralized logging and enforcement.” That means bad actors can fine-tune models for crimes, for example, and then make the evidence untraceable by deleting them after they’ve used them.

Until now, that reality has made it difficult for investigators using forensic memory techniques to recover useful evidence of that activity.

Also: Lenovo’s RTX Spark laptop passed my completely bonkers AI coding test

“ORISA leverages the batch tokens and key-value (KV) caches preserved in process memory to reconstruct token sequences and restore session-level attention states,” the researchers wrote.

That means a tool like this is most relevant to those trying to stop cybercrime rather than to those digging into your personal data. That said, if hackers recreate a technology like this or get their hands on a tool like ORISA itself, they could theoretically use it to gather deleted information from your chats and recreate your queries using that information as context. But ORISA’s efficacy also depends on time — the researchers noted that it’s harder to recover deleted information as time goes on, because your phone’s memory gets overwritten by newer activity.

Either way, our long-standing advice remains: Don’t share sensitive information with chatbots, even in a local session.

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3195. Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

Available to Windows Insiders, the built-in tool measures your upload and download speeds over Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

Does the internet performance on your Windows PC ever feel sluggish? Testing the actual speed can tell you if it matches what you expect or what’s promised from your internet provider. To run a speed test in the past, you typically had to go to a dedicated website or install a special app. Now Microsoft is rolling out an integrated speed test tool designed to save your time.

Also: The right way to run an internet speed test

Currently available to Windows Insiders using the Experimental channel, the new built-in internet speed tester measures your download and upload speeds over Ethernet or Wi-Fi. The tool first tests your download performance and then segues to uploads. The final results show you the average speeds for both.

To try the new tool, you need to be part of Microsoft’s Windows Insider Program if you haven’t already joined. When setting this up, make sure you choose the Experimental channel. Since these Insider builds can be unstable, don’t do this on your primary PC. Instead, use a spare computer, a dual-boot setup, or a virtual machine. I run the Insider builds in a VM through VMware Workstation Pro.

Even with the Experimental channel, I had to enable a special flag for the test. To do this, go to Settings, select Windows Update, and then click Windows Insider Program. Select the option for Feature Flags and scroll down the screen to the entry for Quick Settings Speed Test. Click the drop-down button next to it and change the setting to Enabled if it’s not already set that way. Then restart your PC.

Also: Slow Wi-Fi? I found 10 proven ways to fix your internet

After you log back in, you can access the new speed test one of two ways. Left-click on the System tray and choose Speed test from the Quick Settings menu. Otherwise, right-click on the Network icon and select “Test internet speed” from the pop-up menu. With the tool open, just click the Test button to kick it off. The graph will show the download and upload speeds as they’re being tested, with the results giving you the numbers for both.

If this sounds familiar, that’s because Windows 11 already includes an internet speed test tool. In your current version of Windows 11, right-click on the Network icon in the System tray and choose “Perform speed test” from the menu. But as you’ll see, this test isn’t integrated into Windows. Instead, it takes you to a Bing search page where you then have to run the test and see the results on the page. In contrast, the new tool is built into Windows, making it a vast improvement over the existing one.

Also: Ookla’s Wi-Fi diagnostic tool offers one-tap troubleshooting

“Because the test runs against your active internet connection, you can quickly understand how your current connection is performing without leaving your workflow,” Microsoft said in its blog post. “This updated experience builds on the internet speed test we previously introduced for Windows Insiders, bringing the test and its results directly into Windows.”

Microsoft didn’t reveal the source behind the speed test. But the Info icon for the tool says “Powered by SpeedTest,” an indication that this is from internet speed tester Ookla. To gauge the results, I ran both the built-in speed test and the one at Ookla’s website several times, and the performance for both downloads and uploads were similar between the two.

Since the new speed test is only now hitting the Insider Experimental channel, we might have to wait a while before it officially rolls out to all Windows 11 users. But the tool is convenient to use, runs smoothly, and appears to be accurate. So, hopefully we won’t have to wait too long.

#3193. Netflix now, Hulu later? T-Mobile’s T-Mix plans let you switch perks – what you need to know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Networking > Mobile Carriers

T-Mobile's new T-Mix plans deliver tons of extras ranging from streaming to mobile discounts, but there are some caveats to know.

T-Mobile’s phone plans just got a facelift, and now it’s easier than ever to pick and choose the benefits you want. Announced on October 26, T-Mobile’s T-Mix is replacing the old Mobile Experience plans. The three new T-Mix plans are postpaid phone contracts with a core set of features and multiple “Picks” options that can be interchanged to add benefits, streaming services, gaming subscriptions, and device financing.

Also: I switched to Mint from T-Mobile to save money

These new plans aren’t available yet (they launch in early November, though T-Mobile hasn’t confirmed a specific date). Existing T-Mobile Experience 2.0 plans will not be available to new customers, but current customers on those plans will be allowed to maintain them.

T-Mobile’s new offerings let customers pick and choose which perks they want, rather than having specific benefits tied to certain plan tiers. T-Mobile’s previous Experience plan options provided fixed benefits, much like plans from Verizon and other carriers. This means that some customers had to level up (and pay more) to get exactly the perks they wanted, like Hulu or Netflix access, while other customers didn’t have an option to select a benefit that best fit them if they didn’t want the entire tier of services.

To compete in today’s market, carriers must be more adaptable than ever to retain their customer base. It’s not just about phone discounts, preorders, or the flashiest family plans anymore. Customers want to tailor carrier services in ways that save them the most, and T-Mobile is delivering.

T-Mobile says T-Mix offers no fixed bundles or wasted benefits, and offers customers the freedom to choose how the value built into a wireless plan works for them.

Also: How to unlock your Verizon, T-Mobile, or AT&T phone

The new T-Mix plans include a base set of high-speed data, hotspot data, video streaming speeds, and international options. There’s also a selection of picks that allows customers to choose perks like streaming services, game passes, or services like DoorDash or T-Satellite. Picks can also go toward financing your new phone.

T-Mobile’s plans will maintain a one-plan-fits-all policy for accounts with numerous lines. Individual family members won’t be able to maintain their own plan; rather, everyone must agree on a T-Mix base plan to begin with. Customers can select from Standard, More, and Loaded plans.

The Standard plan offers 50GB of high-speed 5G data, unlimited hotspot data at 3G speeds, unlimited international data while traveling in Canada and Mexico at 2G speeds, unlimited texting in more than 215 countries, and up to 480p streaming resolution.

The More plan offers unlimited data, 60GB of high-speed hotspot data, 15GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico, up to 5GB of high-speed data when traveling internationally, and up to 4K streaming resolution.

The Loaded plan includes data, up to 250GB of hotspot data, 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico, up to 15GB high-speed data when traveling, and up to 4K streaming resolution. The Loaded plan also allows customers to connect a cellular-enabled device (add a smartwatch or tablet) for only $5 per item.

Also: I speed-tested T-Mobile’s international plan vs. two eSIMs in Berlin

Generally, all plans include unlimited texting in more than 215 countries, long-distance calling at $0.50 per minute, and T-Mobile’s Basic Scam Shield service. Financing is also comparable across plans. You can choose to finance a new phone using T-Mobile’s Classic 24-month term or the recently introduced Flex 36-month commitment.

Pricing for the Standard plan, with no fees or taxes, starts at $55 for a single line or $85 for two lines. Three lines cost $100, and each additional line costs $15. There is a 12-line maximum for each T-Mobile account. The More and Loaded plans will cost more per line, which you can compare in the chart above.

T-Mobile’s new Picks option gives you the ability to activate perks you’ll actually use, but there are a few things to note. There’s a certain number of picks you get on your account, and a strict timeline for changing them.

Picks operate like a form of currency, with different perks being assigned a pick value. Two picks can get you an Apple Music subscription or Google AI Pro, while one pick can nab you Netflix with ads. The most premium benefits cost three or four picks and are for services like ESPN Unlimited and Netflix without ads.

It’s important to note that you’re at the mercy of T-Mobile’s business partners, and these perks can change over time.

Thankfully, you can choose internal T-Mobile picks too. T-Satellite can be activated with one pick, for example. You can also skip your perks to get discounts on a new device, which could cost between one and three picks, though this option automatically sets yo up with the Flex 36-month financing terms.

Also: I cloned my voice with free AI tools – and tested a scam call

Here’s how I’d use my one pick if I enrolled in the $55 one-line standard plan. According to T-Mobile, I can use one pick every 90 days as a benefit. Through June 2027, Apple TV is only worth one pick. That’s what I’d spend it on first, so I could enjoy shows like The Servant, Ted Lasso, The Morning Show, and more, without paying more than $55 for my one line.

The number of picks you get depends on the plan and how many lines it includes, though picks can be pooled for everyone’s benefit. Not using your picks won’t lower the sticker price of your plan, and you can’t pay to add benefits, either. Your picks still remain separate from other T-Mobile promotions.

On its first quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Oct. 30, 2026, Unifi (UFI -2.54%) announced a gross profit surge to $12.5 million as operational efficiency efforts took hold. For long-term shareholders, a lower cost structure and aggressive debt elimination create a cleaner foundation to weather macro demand swings. Three things management said stand out.

Management sold two nonstrategic real estate assets, which are facilities outside its core manufacturing operations, and used the proceeds to pay off debt without reducing production capacity. Clearing the $55.5 million term loan, a fixed debt obligation, removes balance sheet leverage and restores financial flexibility for future growth.

To combat illegal foreign imports that bypass regional trade rules, management co-founded YarnProof. The industrywide program embeds physical markers directly into synthetic yarn, and scanners can verify product origin at any point in the supply chain. That gives brand partners a turnkey solution for trade compliance.

Net sales fell nearly 6% year over year due to soft apparel ordering. But cost reduction and footprint consolidation pushed gross margin, the share of revenue remaining after direct production costs, up to nearly 10%. Cutting unprofitable product lines also allowed the business to generate $2.5 million in free cash flow, showing that structural cuts can defend earnings during cyclical downswings.

Order volumes across North America remain muted as retail brands keep inventories lean, but management isn't changing its full-year expectations. A leaner manufacturing footprint and expanding non-apparel product lines give the business structural cost protection. In the meantime, executive leaders are watching raw material pricing discipline and Central American demand recovery.

With term debt eliminated and cost structures permanently lowered, executive focus is shifting toward expanding value-added product lines in military, automotive, and packaging markets. Management intends to maintain strict capital allocation while leveraging its proprietary recycled fiber technologies for long-term growth.

#3191. Why this new Fitbit feature takes us one step closer to non-invasive glucose tracking

Insulin resistance and blood pressure trends are now available on two new Fitbit devices.

Google just added insulin resistance and blood pressure trends to the Fitbit Air and Edge, taking these devices beyond basic fitness monitoring and sleep tracking and into deeper health insights. The new features are part of Google’s “Health Guardian” suite of proactive safety tools for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit.

Also: Are AI health coach subscriptions a scam? My verdict after testing Fitbit’s for a month

They’re available solely for Google Health Premium users, a $100 annual subscription that grants users access to Google’s AI health coach, advanced sleep tracking, and a more expansive selection of health-tracking features.

While it doesn’t measure your insulin or glucose outright, its algorithm analyzes heart rate, activity level, sleep, and other metrics to show changes in metabolic health. The Fitbit will also track your blood pressure patterns without a cuff, monitor your pulse while you’re asleep or awake, and, at the end of the month, provide you with insights. Eligible Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge users who have worn their device for five days or more will see this insight in the Health tab of the app.

Similar to blood pressure trends, the insulin resistance feature uses Fitbit sensors to monitor shifts in metabolic health. Insulin resistance is a precursor to type 2 diabetes, potentially giving users insight into changes in their insulin levels in a less invasive way, but pointing more toward overall trends than a direct diagnosis.

Unlike a continuous glucose monitor, which penetrates the skin and uses blood to gather metabolic data, the insulin resistance feature was built to assess biometric and metabolic patterns through its multimodal model. Google trained its insulin resistance model on data gathered by other wearables as well as compiled demographic data, according to its paper in Nature.

Also: I tested Google’s Fitbit Edge – its standout feature also left me wanting more

Once the feature detects elevated insulin resistance patterns, it notifies the user to take additional action. Fitbit users can even connect their Abbott CGM to the Google Health app for additional glucose monitoring. By offering these Health Guardian features to more devices than just its flagship Pixel Watches, Google is giving more users — specifically budget-conscious users who own a $100 and $180 Fitbit Air or Edge — the ability to track and stay ahead of some common and serious health conditions.

While the insulin resistance feature is nowhere near the capabilities of a non-invasive CGM, Google’s development of a multimodal model for tracking biometric responses to insulin activity suggests the company is getting closer to that non-invasive reality.

Also: The 5 most popular Garmin watches of 2026: What readers are buying most, and last chance Prime Day prices

Non-invasive glucose monitoring is like the foldable phone of wearable technology. It’s a product idea that’s been around for years now, and every tech company is racing to deploy its own, with varying degrees of success and adoption. Even Steve Jobs had dreams of an Apple glucose monitor that people could use — no finger prick necessary. Rumors suggest that Apple has also been working on this for years now.

But Google might be a few steps ahead of Apple on this one. Its deployment of insulin resistance trends to new Fitbit devices is one way it is advancing toward a CGM that uses algorithmic AI instead of needles and blood.

#3189. iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some displays are failing within hours of unboxing. Apple is offering replacements, but is the issue really that widespread?

Some iPhone Duo owners began reporting screen damage shortly after their new phones arrived last Friday, with bright white lines appearing on the inner display within hours of unboxing. It’s a problem for affected owners, but the reports alone don’t establish how widespread it is or common.

Apple has acknowledged a display issue now and said it will offer replacements: “We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.”

Also: Live now! Watch CNET fold the iPhone Duo thousands of times

The cause and failure rate remains unconfirmed, but teardown experts have identified several ways the hinge could damage the screen. Here’s what we know about the reports, how concerned you should be, and what to do if your display fails — including how to decide between a refund or a replacement.

If this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, it’s ultimately not down to you. However, based on the reports I’ve read from users in this situation, the customer service and support messaging around this issue seems to be a little muddled at present.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases in 2026: Expert recommended

One affected user reports that an Apple Genius they spoke to at an Apple Store in Jacksonville, Fla., told them that they must have damaged or dropped the Duo before going on to say “it’s a new device and it’s fragile and these things should be expected with new technology,” and then suggested the owner insure it and make a claim. But don’t let this put you off.

Supplies of the Duo are low, which means you’re highly unlikely to walk out of a retailer with a replacement in hand (even if that retailer is Apple). I’ve only come across one report in which an affected owner received an immediate replacement. Most are being told they’ll have to wait until January for a replacement. This might change, as Apple could choose to divert more stock to replacement channels to address this issue.

Of course, this assumes the issue isn’t particularly widespread (more on this in a second) and Apple can figure it out and resolve it quickly.

If you can wait, then my advice is to wait. But if you were planning to sell or trade in your existing handset, that would leave you in a bit of a bind. Grabbing a refund and waiting for all this to blow over before buying another one will be the best option for you.

Tricky question. What if your Duo is fine right now but falls victim to “Crackgate” down the line?

ZDNET sibling site CNET built a custom machine to open and close the iPhone Duo 20,000 times a day. It’s well past 80,000 cycles now with no crack yet, so I wouldn’t assume your Duo will meet the same fate as those above. You can check in on CNET’s most current results via its livestream on YouTube.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

That said, I’m assuming most people dropping $1,999 to $3,199 on a handset will have AppleCare or some third-party insurance. That’ll give you peace of mind moving forward, no matter what Apple’s policy on this ends up being in the long term.

Also, if you bought the handset directly from Apple, you have 14 days to return it if this issue has made you lose confidence in the robustness of a folding iPhone. If you bought it from a carrier or third party, you’ll have to check its returns policy (and be aware of any fees).

Not very. It’s safe to say that any new iPhone launch will see hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of devices land in the hands of new owners on day one. Despite the hype around “Crackgate,” I’ve read fewer than a dozen firsthand reports of the issue.

This, combined with the fact that the damage all seems to be exactly the same, suggests it’s likely a batch of defective hinges that made it into the wild, and it’s an issue that’ll be sorted out going forward. But whether that causes more shortages in the short term remains to be seen.

Bottom line: We don’t know, but there are some well-informed guesses out there.

Another pattern I’ve noticed in reports from affected users is that their Duos initially opened and closed smoothly, but then they began to encounter resistance when opening and closing the handset. After this, the display would break within a few open/close cycles.

Also: Want an iPhone Duo before 2027? Don’t preorder from Apple – try this instead

The speed with which these damage reports began to appear — some within a few hours — suggests this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, not wear. It’s a complicated hinge made up of more than 100 components, so there’s a lot of scope for things to go wrong.

There was a flurry of activity over the weekend related to what is, rather predictably, being called “Crackgate.” The teardown experts at iFixit have been busy — they completely disassembled a Duo, built a 3D model of the hinge, and identified several ways the hinge mechanism could be damaging the inner display.

It could be that the flexible display is coming into contact with a support bar that doesn’t retract properly, or that a rail that moves during folding is brushing against the screen, causing a pressure hotspot. Finally, the damage appears to start where a lot of edges, components, and moving parts converge, and that convergence could be stressing the display more than expected.

South Korean YouTuber CuriousHagi 궁금하기 also took apart an iPhone Duo to examine the hinge and posted a very informative video.

I’ve reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if and when we hear back.

#3186. Robinhood Markets vs. Nu: Two Fintech Growth Stocks, but One Looks Like a Better Bargain

The fintech landscape is evolving as mobile-first platforms challenge traditional institutions. Deciding between Robinhood Markets (HOOD +1.65%) and Nu (NU +1.77%) depends on whether you prefer domestic diversification or international banking scale.

Robinhood transformed trading for a new generation of American investors by making stocks and cryptocurrencies accessible. Meanwhile, Nu disrupted the Brazilian banking market and is now expanding its digital-first model throughout Mexico and Colombia. Both companies are aggressively pursuing growth, but they operate in different regulatory environments and geographic markets.

Robinhood operates a diverse financial services platform that serves approximately 27 million funded customers. Originally focused on U.S. stock trading, the company has expanded into cryptocurrency, options, retirement accounts, and subscription-based financial services through Robinhood Gold. It is also expanding internationally, with operations and new offerings across Europe and other markets.

In FY 2025, Robinhood generated $4.47 billion in revenue, an increase of 51.6% year over year, supported by stronger trading activity, higher net interest income, and growth in subscription services. Net income reached approximately $1.9 billion, resulting in a 42.1% profit margin. These results demonstrate the company's ability to generate substantial profits as it expands its customer base and financial product offerings.

Robinhood ended 2025 with approximately $4.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Its current ratio stood at 1.3x, while free cash flow reached approximately $1.6 billion for the year, including the effects of brokerage-related working capital movements. This financial position provides flexibility to invest in new products, expand internationally, and support continued business growth.

Nu operates a digital-first banking platform serving approximately 131 million customers across Latin America. The company focuses on providing accessible, low-cost financial services to consumers and businesses, with operations in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. Its technology-driven model allows it to expand its customer base and lending operations without the extensive branch networks required by traditional banks.

In FY 2025, Nu generated approximately $15.8 billion in revenue, an increase of 37% year over year, driven by growth in credit card activity, personal lending, and interest income. Net income reached nearly $2.9 billion, up 45.6%, resulting in a profit margin of approximately 18.2%. These results reflect the company's ability to expand its lending business while maintaining profitability.

Nu ended 2025 with approximately $15 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $11.3 billion in total equity. Its debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.5x, excluding customer deposits, while operating cash flow reached $3.5 billion for the year. The company's growing earnings and deposit base provide a foundation for continued expansion, although managing credit losses and maintaining sufficient capital remain important considerations as its loan portfolio grows.

Robinhood faces regulatory and legal risks related to its payment for order flow model, cryptocurrency trading, and rapidly expanding event contracts business. Its revenue also depends heavily on trading activity, making earnings vulnerable to periods of reduced market participation.

Nu faces a different set of challenges. Operating primarily across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, the company is exposed to regional economic conditions, currency fluctuations, and changing banking regulations. Competition from established banks and other digital financial platforms could also pressure profitability. As Nu expands its lending operations, managing credit defaults and maintaining sufficient capital will be essential, particularly if economic conditions weaken or borrowing costs remain elevated.

Nu appears cheaper than its peer based on the Forward P/E and the P/S ratio, which measures market cap against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Both Robinhood and Nu have demonstrated impressive growth, but at their current valuations, I would favor Nu as the better long-term investment.

Robinhood has successfully expanded beyond its roots as a stock trading platform, building a profitable business across brokerage services, cryptocurrency trading, and financial products. However, much of that success appears reflected in its valuation. At 47.3 times forward earnings, investors are paying a substantial premium for continued growth, leaving the stock vulnerable if trading activity slows or earnings fall short of expectations.

Nu offers a different opportunity. Its digital banking model continues to attract customers across Latin America, where opportunities for expanding access to credit and financial services remain substantial. Revenue grew 37% in 2025, while net income increased nearly 46%, demonstrating its ability to scale profitably. Despite that performance, the stock trades at just 16.9 times forward earnings, a considerably more attractive valuation than Robinhood.

Nu isn't without risks. Its lending business remains sensitive to credit losses, interest rates, and economic conditions across Latin America. However, the valuation provides a greater margin for potential setbacks.

For investors looking beyond 2026, Nu looks like the better buy. Robinhood remains a compelling growth company, but Nu combines strong earnings growth, substantial room for expansion, and a much more reasonable price.

#3184. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

Samsung’s new Galaxy Buds On may be about to take open-ear earbuds beyond a music-playing vessel for the hyper-aware listener. With smart features like summoning Gemini Live chats and accepting or declining calls via Head Gestures, Samsung’s clip-style buds are actually smart, and competitors will need to take note.

Also: We put 8 pairs of earbuds to the test in our lab – this pair won best ANC

The Galaxy Buds On are built for the Galaxy ecosystem, with features like Head Gestures, Quick Voice Memo, and Auto Volume reserved for Samsung phones running up-to-date One UI and compatible with Galaxy AI. Samsung released the Galaxy Buds On in Korea earlier this month and announced their US availability on Wednesday for $229, beginning in early November.

The Galaxy Buds On feature two of Samsung’s proprietary Bluetooth codecs: SSC and SSC UHQ, which deliver audio quality up to 24-bit/48kHz and 24-bit/96kHz, respectively, when connected to compatible Galaxy devices.

Samsung’s new clip-style earbuds promise up to nine-and-a-half hours of continuous playtime, and their charging case promises an additional 38 hours. Samsung also fitted the Galaxy Buds On with Bluetooth 6.2, which may set them up for future Channel Sounding support via a firmware update.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade

Finally, the Galaxy Buds On sport an IP54 durability rating, making them dust and water protected, not waterproof. So, you can take the Galaxy Buds On with you on a brisk walk in light rain or wear them during a particularly sweaty workout, but they’re not fit for water submersion.

Samsung’s clip-style earbuds’ durability rating is stronger than Bose’s Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen), which sport an IPX4 rating, meaning Bose’s buds weren’t tested for dust ingress but offer as much water protection as Samsung’s.

However, Shokz’s clip-style Open Dots 2 have an IP57 rating, offering the same level of dust protection as the Galaxy Buds On, but their stronger water protection makes them waterproof.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Still, one thing Samsung has over all of its competitors is access to an ecosystem, which allows the Galaxy Buds On to be smarter than their counterparts from Sony, Shokz, or Bose. Given that Samsung controls its hardware and software ecosystem, it can grant the Galaxy Buds On unique access to AI-powered features, making the earbuds a stronger asset to one’s device ecosystem.

You’ll find features similar to Samsung’s Audio Leakage Reduction, Intelligent Clear Call, and Voice Pickup Unit in many premium open-ear earbuds, but these earbuds’ real strength is that they operate like the flagship Galaxy Buds 4 Pro without the intrusive in-ear design.

Samsung releasing the Galaxy Buds On in Korea before the US isn’t surprising; not only is Korea its home country, but Asian consumers took to open-ear earbuds — especially the clip-on variety — long before American consumers. Many open-ear earbuds made by Asian manufacturers for domestic markets already have smart features, such as AI-powered live translation and note-taking.

Also: How I share audio from my Android phone to multiple earbuds

There are two reasons why American consumers seem so far behind in this tech category: the heavy hitters are banned or scaling back in US markets, and use cases vary across cultures. Asian tech giants like Xiaomi, Huawei, and Oppo face bans and market troubles in the US and often focus on high-value local markets instead. Plus, Asian consumers exhibit greater demand for fashion-forward clip-style earbuds, such as the Moto Buds Loop, which are available in the US, while Americans seem more interested in earbuds for exercise features.

However, there’s a market in the US for clip-style earbuds suited for exercise that offer advanced, everyday, useful features, and Samsung is taking advantage of the opportunity.

#3180. Opera will run AI locally in your browser now – why that’s a gamechanger and how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Thanks to the newly proposed WebAI web standard, the company will start shipping local AI models with its flagship browser.

Opera just made a bold choice: Thanks to the newly proposed WebAI web standard, the company will soon be shipping local AI models with its browser. By doing so, Opera’s AI ensures that your queries and/or data remain on your machine.

Also: How Opera’s new Air browser helped me to keep calm and surf on

According to Opera, because this new feature uses open-weight AI models, anyone can build on top of those models without running expensive AI infrastructure or paying for every request. That equates to more innovation for the Opera browser.

This is a bigger deal than you might think.

Most browsers include AI that depends on the cloud for responses; a user’s data is not limited to the local machine and could be used by third-party organizations to train LLMs or even build profiles.

Opera aims to resist that trend by leaning into local AI, made possible by open-weight models that have become smaller and more capable, while hardware continues to become more powerful.

“A lot of what people want from AI doesn’t need a data center. Your laptop can already do it, without sending your data anywhere,” said Krystian Kolondra, EVP Browsers and AI at Opera. “We first shipped local models to developers in 2024. Now we’re bringing them to everyone. More models and tools are coming, and you’ll always decide what runs on your machine.”

Opera also plans on bringing more open models optimized for specific devices, as well as more tools to make it easier to build browser experiences on local AI.

WebAI is a newly proposed web standard (backed by companies like Google and Microsoft) that allows websites and extensions to use browser-hosted AI. Opera’s implementation of WebAI is model-agnostic and built around open-weight models, so users can select models from the likes of Google and Apple.

Also: Opera now detects and blocks malicious clipboard content

WebAI is also opt-in; nothing is downloaded until the user does so. Developers can check out example extensions that use WebUI from WebAI: Local AI for the web, now in Opera.

I’ve been a fan of the Opera browser for a long time — it has served as my default for the past five years on Linux, MacOS, and Android.

I’ve seen Opera features come and go, but the good ones always stick around. Opera was one of the first browsers to integrate AI into the UI, making it very easy (and free) to use. The longer I use AI, the more one particular issue has become my calling card — local AI.

I’m a champion of local AI, and that’s the hill I will die on.

The problem thus far is that using local AI with browsers isn’t always easy. Firefox made it possible with Smart Window, but it’s not set up to use local AI by default. (You have to choose a custom provider and have Ollama installed and running on your machine.)

Also: Firefox is the browser to beat right now if you use AI

Opera is ready to make this reality even easier.

To try the local-first version of Opera, do the following:

According to Opera, WebAI is an early preview, available on Windows PC (64-bit, Intel/AMD) and Macs with Apple silicon. It isn’t available on Intel-based Macs, Linux or Windows on Arm.

#3179. Alphabet Plummets After Earnings. I Think the Stock Looks Like a Genius Buy Now.

Alphabet (GOOG +1.80%) (GOOGL +2.16%) just reported third-quarter earnings, and I thought the results were pretty good. However, the market did not. The stock sold off around 10% following earnings for a variety of reasons, but I think there's far more to the sell-off.

The market is being extremely shortsighted here, and that may be a perfect opportunity for investors to swoop in and scoop up shares at a sizable discount.

One of the biggest reasons the market cited for selling off Alphabet stock following earnings was its free cash flow dipping into negative territory. The analyst community expects Alphabet's free cash flow to remain positive, but it reported a $9 billion free cash outflow for the quarter. The market wasn't thrilled with that, and the stock sold off.

However, I think that's ignoring the broader picture. Alphabet is spending whatever it can to invest in its AI computing infrastructure. Why? Just look at its Google Cloud growth rate.

Google Cloud is Alphabet's cloud computing platform, and it's where many AI start-ups are moving to run AI workloads. One of Alphabet's biggest clients is Anthropic, and that's because it can use Alphabet's impressive TPUs, or tensor processing units, custom AI chips with better cost-performance than GPUs when the workload is properly configured. TPUs are so popular that Alphabet is starting to sell them to external clients, helping boost their business.

Overall, Google Cloud's revenue rose a jaw-dropping 103% year over year to $30.7 billion. Its operating margin was also very healthy at 36%, up from 24% last year. In fact, Google Cloud is about half the size of its Google Search business, which grew at a 12% pace to $63.4 billis in Q3.

During its earnings call, Alphabet highlighted that it was struggling to monetize its results in AI mode, which contributed to lower revenue. The market didn't like that language, so it sold off the stock. However, this is completely missing the obvious.

Alphabet knows that growth in search is limited and the landscape is shifting with the rise of AI. However, it's spending as much money as it can to build out its AI infrastructure to continue its cloud computing growth. That's the real business unit investors should be focusing on here, and because the market isn't, it's time to take advantage of a major opportunity.

Alphabet has had its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio affected by various investments, so using a different metric, like its operating P/E ratio, makes more sense. This year, Alphabet has seen its premium rise as the market has recognized it as an AI leader delivering strong growth. However, with the latest sell-off, that's no longer the case. After the sell-off, Alphabet is now trading in its normal valuation range.

I think that pretty clearly points to Alphabet stock now being back in the buy zone, and with the stock now 30% down from its all-time high, it's time to take advantage of the sale price.

The market is worried about AI monetization, but Alphabet has already shown investors a path forward: cloud computing. This should be the primary focus of investors and the market, but it's not right now. Eventually it will be, and when that time comes, Alphabet will be one of the top stocks to own. In the meantime, I think it's a perfect stock to buy on the dip, as it's well positioned to thrive over the next few years.

#3176. Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

"Captain Picard stood for the best of us," wrote William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk.

Patrick Stewart, the British actor whose calm demeanor and steely strength led the Star Trek television franchise into its next generation, died Wednesday at age 86. The actor suffered from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his beloved wife Sunny,” a Thursday post on Stewart’s Instagram account read in part. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Through a long career, Stewart starred in everything from Shakespeare productions to superhero films, but his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation is firmly cemented in entertainment culture. Show creator Gene Roddenberry didn’t at first think Stewart, who was bald, could play the virile captain he had envisioned for the new Star Trek series. Stewart even had his wife ship his toupee over from London, and he wore it for an audition scene, but executives saw him with both styles and chose the bald look.

Stewart was stepping into big boots. While the original Star Trek only ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969, it soon became a pop culture fixture, and the success of the first Star Wars film in 1977 finally allowed Roddenberry to make feature films using his original cast. The success of those movies led to a new series, Star Trek: The Next Generation, which launched in 1987 and took place about a century after the original show.

With his resonant voice and complete command of the crew, Stewart’s Picard came off as a trained diplomat compared with the more swashbuckling Capt. James T. Kirk, as played by William Shatner on the original Star Trek. But there was no question who was in charge on his bridge, and his crew followed him unhesitatingly. That made later episodes, including the third-season plot where Picard was assimilated by the alien Borg, even more meaningful, as a very human Picard struggled to recover from what had been done to him.

Stewart’s iconic lines, including “Engage!” and “Make it so!” — and his favorite beverage order, “Tea. Earl Grey. Hot.” — have passed into pop culture immortality. He re-created the character in Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 to 2023, in which the retired leader was drawn into new adventures.

Star Trek: The Next Generation ran from 1987 to 1994, but Stewart wasn’t done playing leaders. He took on the role of Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men superhero franchise, playing a telepathic, wheelchair-using mutant who founded the X-Men superhero team. He portrayed Xavier in multiple films over the span of 17 years, acting alongside his longtime friend, Ian McKellen.

Ironically, McKellen originally advised Stewart not to accept the Star Trek role as Picard, reportedly telling him, “You have too much important theater work to do. You can’t throw that away to do TV.”

Stewart began his acting career on the British stage, working with the Royal Shakespeare Company and winning numerous acting awards.

He was bluntly open about his childhood with an abusive father, writing in the Guardian newspaper in 2009 that the experience never left him.

“As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him,” Stewart wrote. “If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down.”

Shatner remembered his successor with tenderness and also referenced the death days earlier of Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek.

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on X. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

George Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu on the original Star Trek, also remembered Stewart.

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before.”

You can ask Amazon's voice assistant to show you your favorite photos.

Amazon’s new Alexa Photo Frame is available now, with a 10-inch HD screen, Alexa+ built in, and prices starting at $200. I’ve been looking for a new photo frame to set up in my dining room or kitchen and display some of the photos my wife and I have snapped over the years. So far, the frames I’ve seen and tested haven’t quite done the trick for me. Amazon’s newly launched frame could be the one.

Released as part of the company’s latest product blitz, the Alexa Photo Frame has a semi-matte, anti-glare finish that Amazon said makes your images look more like actual prints and lets you view them from any angle. Plus, the frame’s brightness automatically changes based on the surrounding lighting conditions. I’d definitely like to see all that in action.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

The Alexa Photo Frame comes in three varieties and two price tags. The one with a simple black frame runs $200, while a walnut or birch frame costs $230. For me, the wooden frame would be worth the extra $30 for the added style and pizzazz.

Apparently, you don’t have to fiddle with SD cards or local storage, as the frame picks up your photos directly from Amazon Photos. The only drawback is that I don’t actively use Amazon Photos. But I have the app on my iPhone, so it would be easy enough to turn on automatic photo syncing with Amazon’s cloud service.

With my photos syncing to Amazon Photos, any new shots I take would automatically upload, so I wouldn’t have to manually add the latest ones. The frame will even skip certain images like screenshots and receipts, which is handy as I do take a lot of screenshots on my phone. And since I’m an Amazon Prime member, I get unlimited space to store my photos.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

But the real appeal for me is that this frame comes with Alexa+ built in. We’re an Alexa house with Echo speakers in several different rooms.

Using AI, Alexa+ chooses the best photos to display at any given time, according to Amazon. That could be based on certain people or seasons of the year, or whether you’re smiling and how nice the lighting is. My wife always tells me that I look like the Joker when I smile for a photo. Maybe Alexa can find ones where my smile is a bit less maniacal.

You can also ask Alexa to display your favorite photos. As Amazon suggests, you could tell Alexa to “show photos from the trip to the beach with mom” or “show photos of the kids.” In my case, I might tell it to display photos from all our travels to New York Comic Con or photos from our trip to Paris in 2025.

Also: Amazon’s Echo Show 16 makes Apple’s 7-inch HomeView look puny – is it worth $100+ extra?

According to Amazon, Alexa+ knows when to display two photos together. For example, the company said it might display one photo of you eating an ice cream cone when you’re a kid next to another of you as an adult also eating a cone.

Another feature I like: Often a photo may appear on your frame’s screen, but you may not quite remember where or why you took it. With the Alexa Photo Frame, you can add voice notes to any photo. The frame will play your note to remind you of any special meaning behind that photo.

The Alexa Photo Frame is now for sale at Amazon. If you pick one up, check the return policy in case you don’t like it. As for me, I think I’m going to order one as soon as I’m done here. I just need to decide whether I want the walnut or birch frame.

#3174. Medallion Financial: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 30, 2026, Medallion Financial (MFIN -0.99%) announced third-quarter results driven by expansion in consumer lending. Management is trading higher net interest margin (the difference between interest earned on loans and interest paid on deposits) for lower credit risk. That creates a safer balance sheet and positions the business for durable compounding over the long run. Three things management said stand out.

Management is intentionally growing its home improvement lending segment faster than its recreational loan segment to target higher-credit borrowers. That strategic pivot reduces net interest margin (the spread between loan yields and borrowing costs) but protects portfolio quality over the economic cycle.

Medallion Financial relies heavily on brokered deposits (certificates of deposit acquired through third-party brokers) to fund consumer loans with predictable maturities. By expanding into non-brokered time deposits and high-yield savings accounts, the company is working to reduce funding costs while preserving solid asset-liability matching.

Over the past six months, the company raised $130 million in debt and preferred stock to maintain capital flexibility. And because shares trade below tangible book value (net worth excluding goodwill and intangible assets), management launched a fresh share repurchase program.

Asset expansion is accelerating toward a target of $5 billion over the next few years. Marketing efforts and new partnership programs are supporting market share gains, while disciplined loan pricing protects credit quality. And to preserve net interest income, management is raising loan rates across the board.

On the capital allocation side, the focus remains on consumer loan growth, dividend increases, and stock repurchases. Retiring $15 million in debt at a discount further bolsters balance sheet strength.

The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.
