#3173. The Massive DHS Breach Is Hacktivist Payback for Government Surveillance

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The personal information of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees was exposed by a hacker group.

A Department of Homeland Security breach by an activist group has exposed the personal information of more than 41,000 employees, including Customs and Border Protection workers, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and others who work in government cybersecurity.

Information collected from the breach was published online in a searchable repository called Icepick on the Distributed Denial of Secrets website. According to the news leaks site, a hacktivist group called the Department of Peace breached an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS, stealing employees’ names, contact information and assignments. The group then distributed copies of the database through the leak-hosting group DDoSecrets and to a self-described investigative journalist and cybersecurity researcher from Switzerland known as maia arson crimew, who created an online tool to search the data.

The hacktivist crimew described the leak as an “unprecedented” and “massive” exposure of the DHS’s internal structure. By detailing exact roles, chains of command and agent identities across agencies like ICE, the dataset is a “complete game changer” that leaves the department highly vulnerable to outside investigation for years to come.

The breach appears to be the latest retaliation against government-led surveillance, including ICE’s increasingly tech-driven enforcement tactics and private partnerships with companies such as Flock Security. The Department of Peace directly cited DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s July statement about “turning up the heat on the streets” — a reference to ramping up the immigration crackdown and arrests — and responded, “This is what happens to ICE when you do that.” The hackers also attached a note to the files reading, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

A DHS spokesperson told CNET that the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The statement went on to say: “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”

Since the leak, the DHS has been working to take down sites hosting the information, including Icepick’s searchable archive domain. The social network Bluesky opted to block links to DDoSecrets, telling TechCrunch that the platform’s community guidelines prohibit “the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks.”

Much of the attention on the Icepick leak has focused on its size. While the 41,000 affected employees represent only a fraction of the nearly quarter-million people at the DHS, the data goes far beyond basic contact information. Reports indicate the leak exposes office addresses and phone numbers, as well as details on internal work systems and the department’s inner workings.

Because the hackers gained access through Okta, a secure portal for employee login, they also saw the master list of apps connected to that dashboard. That revealed an inventory of surveillance applications used by ICE, including specialized wiretapping and surveillance software, such as Penlink, and popular AI applications like ChatGPT and Gemini, raising questions about how federal agencies feed case files or border data into commercial AI models.

While cross-referencing Icepick data could expose undercover operations, it also risks including unrelated personnel, such as airport security workers. However, DDoSecrets cofounder and journalist Emma Best argued the release is strategic rather than an indiscriminate dump. “Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” Best wrote.

The public response to the breach also points to a crisis of institutional legitimacy, with many viewing the exposure not as a crime but as forced transparency against a federal department that has acted with impunity. In a Facebook comment thread accompanying an NPR story about the incident, many responded with support for the hacktivists: “Not all heroes wear capes,” one commenter wrote, while another said, “Law enforcement identities must be public. Otherwise, it’s just a gang.”

When an agency known for aggressive enforcement and widespread surveillance gets breached, a segment of the population sees it as poetic justice.

There’s also been an escalating operational crisis for any tech company that signs a contract with ICE or DHS agencies. From the outside, hacktivists are targeting their infrastructure (like this recent breach) to unmask federal agents and leak their surveillance toolkits. And from the inside, employees are sounding the alarm, demanding that leadership cancel contracts on moral grounds.

That was the case recently with the robot company Boston Dynamics, after it was reported that ICE planned to spend up to $2 million on Spot robots made by the company. Hundreds of employees signed a petition saying that they can’t be proud working for Boston Dynamics “when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians.” The employee noted that friends and family are asking them “in disbelief and horror” how they can work on ICE robots, an indication of broader distrust.

The recent massive DHS breach isn’t a random, isolated cyberattack. Earlier this year, the Electronic Frontier Foundation detailed the spread of “enterprising hackers [that] have started projects to do counter surveillance against ICE,” including applications and web tools geared toward tracking officers’ movements and countering Flock surveillance cameras that can read license plates.

“It’s important to remember that we are not powerless,” wrote EFF’s Senior Staff Technologist Cooper Quintin. “Even in the face of a domestic law enforcement presence with massive surveillance capabilities and military-esque technologies, there are still ways to engage in surveillance self-defense.”

#3172. Your public Discord messages may soon appear in Google search results – how to opt out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Discord announced a new feature that can make your server messages discoverable on Google. Here's how to opt out.

Also: My 5 favorite Discord alternatives – no ID verification required

Normally, in order to join a Discord server, you need an invitation link that has been generated by a current admin or member. These links usually have a very short lifespan, expiring after just a few minutes to help protect private groups from bad actors looking to cause trouble. However, for very large Discoverable Servers, Discord has an internal search function called Server Discovery that allows users to join communities without an invite link. The new policy will create a Server Web Page for each of these very large servers, discoverable in search engines like Google or DuckDuckGo, that will show a short description of the server and a summary of conversations in its public channels. New members can join servers directly from their Server Web Pages.

As for what exactly is shared on Server Web Pages, Discord’s related support page says, “From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words.”

Server Web Pages will begin to go live on Nov. 16, 2026, but server admins have already been given access to tools for opting out entire channels from the program:

Once you’ve accessed the controls, you can either pick which channels will be shown in your community’s Server Web Page (something like a general chat for a content creator’s community server, or a hobby community’s rules page) or opt out of all channels so that only a server description will be visible. And even the server description can be disabled if you’re trying to keep your community as private as possible.

Discord plans to start adding chat summaries and individual example messages in mid-December, and regular users will be able to opt out of having their part of conversations shown.

Along with toggles to opt out of personalized ads and data collection (which I strongly suggest you turn off as well), you’ll see a button to block your message text and data from being used in Server Web Pages. And one toggle will cover permissions in every Discoverable Server that you belong to, so you won’t have to waste time updating your preferences for every community.

Also: Strangers can find your info with a 5-minute search – delete it ASAP

Don’t worry, the private server you have set up for playing games and chatting with friends, and even larger communities not designated as Discoverable Servers, aren’t affected by this announcement. Only official Discoverable Servers with at least 1,000 members, that are at least eight weeks old, and meet Discord’s activity and safety standards will have the new web pages and message summary features.

The move seems to position Discord as an alternative to Reddit in the market of obscure tech questions with answers that were previously only available on now-defunct Q&A forums market. Discoverable Servers will be analogous to sub-Reddit communities, offering vital information to hobbyists and pros alike that might otherwise be locked behind paywalls or “walled garden” private servers.

#3171. Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Streaming Services

Celebrate the life of Patrick Stewart through his iconic roles in TV and movies.

Patrick Stewart, the legendary actor known to many as Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the Star Trek universe and Professor Charles Xavier from the X-Men movie franchise, died on Wednesday at age 86. An Instagram post announcing the news says Stewart passed after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

When looking back at the slate of work Stewart put out into the world, you’ll find over six decades worth of performances. The actor cut his teeth in the world of Shakespearean stage productions and smaller TV projects, mostly in the UK, before he broke out into mainstream popularity in 1987, leading the crew of the Enterprise in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

Along with Picard, he’s most known for the role of Professor Charles Xavier, the wheelchair-using leader of the X-Men. His final performance as Professor X will be seen in Avengers: Doomsday later this year.

To remember Stewart, you can tune in to many of his projects on various streaming services. Since I’ve stuck to roles that can be streamed, his memorable performances as Ebenezer Scrooge in 1999’s A Christmas Carol, John Thornton in 1975’s North & South and the ghost of Hamlet’s father in 2009’s Hamlet, for instance, aren’t listed.

Read more: ‘Star Trek: Picard’ Season 3 Review: The ‘Next Generation’ Reunion We’ve Been Waiting For

Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Stewart made Star Trek an obsession for me growing up, and his performance as Captain Jean-Luc Picard is simply iconic. He starred as Picard in seven seasons of Star Trek: The Next Generation before taking the character to the big screen in four movies in the grander franchise. Stewart reprised his role as Picard in the aptly titled sequel series Star Trek: Picard, which lasted three seasons, with the final one acting as a must-see TNG reunion.

After he made a name for himself, boldly going wherever the Enterprise took him, Stewart stepped into an even more legendary role: Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 X-Men movie. He reprised his role as leader of the X-Men in six installments in the franchise, including the stand-alone Wolverine movie, Logan. In December, audiences will see him one final time in the role in Avengers: Doomsday.

It wasn’t common to see Stewart in a villainous role, so his performance as Darcy Banker in Green Room is a riveting turn for the actor. The movie takes place mostly inside a bar that caters to a white supremacist crowd, and Darcy is not just the bar owner, he’s their soft-spoken, violent leader.

Stewart starred as Captain Ahab in the 1998 miniseries adaptation of Herman Melville’s epic Moby Dick. The series follows the quintessential story of Ahab’s hunt for the white whale and delves into his backstory and relationships, introducing his wife, Elizabeth. Costarring in the series are Gregory Peck, Piripi Waretini and Henry Thomas.

David Lynch’s take on Dune may have been a box office failure, but in the years since it hit theaters, the movie has achieved cult status. Stewart takes on the supporting role of Gurney Halleck, who Josh Brolin played in the new Dune franchise.

Stewart had a recognizable, resonant voice, and his voice-acting work appeared in a slew of animated films. The Prince of Egypt featured the actor as Pharaoh Seti I, the film’s antagonist. He was joined by a stacked slate of talent, including Val Kilmer, Ralph Fiennes, Steve Martin and Sandra Bullock.

Sometimes, the best Stewart was the one who poked fun at Stewart. In the first season of the Ricky Gervais comedy series Extras, Stewart appeared as a heightened version of himself. He may have just appeared in one episode (Episode 6, to be exact), but he definitely left an impact.

Jeffrey is a comedy that came out at a time when gay-themed movies were few and far between. The movie stars Steven Weber as the titular character, who decides to become celibate out of fear of contracting AIDS. It should be noted that this is a comedy and Stewart and Weber, along with the likes of Michael T. Weiss, Bryan Bratt, Nathan Lane and Sigourney Weaver, deliver on that front.

One of Stewart’s final roles is that of Sir Ritchfield, the elder sheep featured in The Sheep Detectives, from Amazon MGM Studios. The movie follows a group of sheep who take it upon themselves to investigate the untimely death of their shepherd, George Hardy, played by Hugh Jackman.

#3170. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

Byrne ranks No. 303 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 18.5%. See EOG Resources Statistics on TipRanks.

#3169. Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pros may be late, but they have one big advantage

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple finally revealed its new MacBook M5 Pro and Max with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing the best features from the iPhone to its laptops.

Steve Jobs might be rolling over in his grave, but at long last, Apple announced a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen display. The new MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max features a tandem OLED display Apple is calling “ProLED XDR”, scaling up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 120Hz refresh rate. For the first time, the MacBook Pro will feature touchscreen capabilities and the Dynamic Island — a feature first introduced on the iPhone.

Also: Forget the touchscreen MacBook – Apple’s new M6 is the laptop I recommend for most people

The display and controversial form factor aren’t its only draws: it features a thinner, lighter design and brings back the illuminated Apple logo on the back — some of the most significant changes to the MacBook chassis in years. The new MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips will come in both 14- and 16-inch sizes, with up to 128GB of unified memory, and weigh less than ever: the smaller model at three pounds and the 16-inch at four pounds.

The company, under new CEO John Ternus, is on a spree with new products, with its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, earlier this month (another product that’s been in development for years), and an all-new lineup of smart home products aimed at challenging Amazon’s dominance in that market.

The MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max feature new ProLED XDR displays that control color and pixel luminance at the sub-millisecond level, while monitoring and adapting usage over time, Apple says. The panels feature a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and cover both the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts, high-end specs indeed for a laptop display.

To reduce glare, Apple says it etched the nano-texture directly into the glass, since the touch sensor is built directly into the panel rather than layered on top of it.

The displays work with Apple’s ProMotion technology, which adjusts refresh rates based on what the device is actively doing: scaling down to 10Hz while idle for better power efficiency and ramping up to 120Hz during gaming or graphics-heavy tasks.

In terms of software and usability, Apple says apps should be ready to go on the new MacBook Pros, since they’re set to register touches as clicks.

Touchscreen laptops are nothing new, having been standard fare on laptops of all kinds for years now. Apple’s entrance into the market is notable because the company took such a hard-line stance against them for years (Jobs famously called them “ergonomically terrible“), but honestly, the everyday consumer in 2026 may struggle to see the big deal.

Either you like using your finger or a stylus on a screen, or you don’t. Can Apple really deliver a touchscreen experience that is worlds better than what’s available on Windows PCs or Chromebooks (or Googlebooks)? It’s debatable.

However, there are a few things Apple has up its sleeve that set it apart from the competition, and they have to do with its most successful product of all time (which also happens to have a touchscreen): the iPhone.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: The $2,000 foldable has some magical touches

Apple smartly made the iPhone’s usability wins core to its approach to the new MacBook. For example, it features a Dynamic Island cutout, doing away with the notch in favor of a dynamic multitasking hub. This allows it to adapt through unique touch-based interactions that were previously impossible on a MacBook.

The Dynamic Island serves as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri, changing how you interact with these features by putting them front and center. The design intent here appears to be to keep dynamic, time-sensitive events and apps in close view for quick reference, an interesting merge of how we use both our iPhones and laptops.

Also: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook is days away – with another OLED surprise

Plus, with Apple’s vast App Store library, there is already a host of touch-optimized programs for Apple’s ecosystem. It doesn’t look like Apple is interested in bringing these directly to MacOS — this is still very much a MacBook Pro — instead, folding in the touch functionality as part of the feature set of these laptops’ premium displays.

In that sense, this is already well-trodden ground for Apple. Bringing the best features of the iPhone to the MacBook Pro isn’t even that revolutionary when you think about it; it’s a smart way to improve its product line.

You already know these new MacBooks aren’t going to be cheap. The base model with the lowest configuration starts at $2,899: the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB of local storage. The prices only scale up from there to seriously astronomical figures, particularly for the ultra-high-end storage options. 16TB of storage will start at $14 grand.

We haven’t seen these laptops in person yet, but I have no doubt the new ProLED XDR screens look fantastic. However, it’s a lot of money for a touchscreen laptop. These devices come hot on the heels of Microsoft and Nvidia’s recent RTX Spark devices, which also target the high end of the market, with AI enthusiasts looking for local AI performance to be front and center.

These laptops are niche, to be sure, but they also don’t speak to such a specific subset of users; instead, they focus on their impressive hardware and implications for creators, artists, and power users.

Also: Apple’s touchscreen Mac event: 3 things I’m excited for – and my one concern

Apple isn’t showcasing a reinvention of the MacBook Pro, but rather a bonus feature for its most powerful ultra-premium laptops. With the recent announcement of the M6 MacBook Pro, consumers looking for an accessible workhorse MacBook already have that option. This is for someone else entirely.

The new MacBook Pros with M5 Pro and M5 Max are now available for preorder, with general availability beginning Friday, Nov. 6.

#3168. Here’s Why You’re About to See More Ads in Google’s AI Overviews

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With Google now injecting "sponsored" links directly into AI follow-up queries, traffic to online publishers will suffer even more.

If you happened to listen to Alphabet’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday, you might have heard that searches are up, but ad revenue is down. According to Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because user queries are migrating to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which suffer from “lower monetization.”

You actually know how this works. When you type a question into Google, a summarized AI response often appears immediately, reducing the classic ad-clicking behavior further down on the page, which generates Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

#3167. The Stock Market Has Done This Just Twice in 156 Years. Now It's Happening Again.

For four years now, the stock market has been on a massive bull run. Since bottoming out in October 2022, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%) has soared, fueled in no small part by enormous gains in stocks connected to artificial intelligence (AI). But with stock valuations approaching very extreme levels, investors have good reason to pause and ask: How much longer can this rally last?

It turns out history has something to say about that.

Throughout the history of the stock market, periods of unusually high stock valuations have been followed by significant market downturns. To see why that matters today, just consider how expensive stocks have become by one of Wall Street's most widely followed valuation metrics: the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio.

The CAPE ratio compares the S&P 500's current price with its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the past 10 years. Put simply, it shows us how expensive the stock market is relative to what companies have earned over the last decade.

Looking at the chart above, we can see that the CAPE is hovering at 40.71, one of the highest readings in 156 years. The last time the CAPE ratio was this high was the dot-com bubble, when the stock market was in the midst of an extraordinary bull run. Of course, a market downturn followed that rally, leading to one of the worst downturns in recent history.

Notably, the dot-com rally wasn't the first time investors paid such high prices for stocks, only to watch the market collapse later. Something similar happened in 1929, when the CAPE reached what was then a record high, shortly before the stock market famously crashed.

Nearly a century after the Great Depression, valuations have spiked in a similar fashion for the third time. That doesn't, of course, mean a crash is inevitable. But it would be unwise, I think, to ignore what happened the last two times, especially with obvious parallels between this bull market and its predecessor in the late 90s.

There are, of course, very important differences between today's AI-driven bull market and the internet boom of the 90s. Unlike many of the speculative internet companies that dominated in the late 1990s, today's AI boom is driven by enormously profitable companies, like Nvidia (NVDA +1.60%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%), and Alphabet (GOOG +1.80%) (GOOGL +2.16%). That gives today's bull market a much more solid foundation than the fuzzy promises of future profits that fueled the dot-com bubble.

The dot-com boom, then, isn't an exact synonym for today's AI rally. But if there's one lesson we can take from it, it's that even a promising technological revolution doesn't guarantee a bull market will last forever. The internet did, after all, revolutionize the world (just consider the screen in front of you). That didn't spare investors from incurring enormous losses when the dot-com bubble burst.

Right now, the stock market could be approaching a similar reckoning. That's not a reason to sell everything, but it is a good reason to look over your portfolio and ensure it is prepared for a potential downturn. Today's bull market might be different, but that doesn't mean it's immune to the same risks that brought previous rallies to an end.

For the exterior of your home, enter your address, and the app will generate an Alexa Home Map of your residence using existing map data.

#3164. Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding, ranking alongside Codex GPT-6.1 Terra

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Mistral has released the weights for Large 4, along with some impressive Artificial Analysis scores.

French AI lab Mistral shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, in preview on Oct. 6. As promised, the lab has released the model’s weights, alongside some new benchmark scores that show Western open models gaining ground over their Chinese peers.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

After three weeks of testing with a select group of partners, Mistral’s model sets a new standard for Western-made open models, ranking at the top of Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index among open models globally. The model also comes with three reasoning modes now (low, medium, and high), as is common for heftier models to give users more options based on their level of task complexity.

ML4’s score on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped to 41% from its preview version’s 28% to 41%, beating Opencode’s GLM-5.3 by one small but important point. On the overall Index, however, which shows a model’s composite score across three relevant benchmarks, ML4 is a point behind GLM-5.3, scoring a 48 to GLM-5.3’s 49. Codex GPT-6.1 Terra also scores a 48 overall.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Still, that improvement in performance is meaningful for just a few weeks of extra training. As proprietary AI remains expensive to use, economical models that don’t sacrifice performance are eye-catching. ML4 “rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% less tokens per task on average,” Mistral said.

When Mistral released ML4 in preview earlier this month, it touted how the model prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty. The company has spent the last few weeks working with developers and leaders to assess the model’s cybersecurity capabilities, a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model security mounts.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, Mistral’s initial testing partners got access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

At least by some measure, ML4’s promises seem to have come true: Le Chonk scored just above DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the CyberGym benchmark for defensive cybersecurity, which measures how well models find “real memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ open-source projects, reproducing them with proof-of-concept inputs, and patching them without breaking the projects’ tests.”

Recent AI security incidents have somewhat pitted open and proprietary models against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4 is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said during a briefing for the Oct. 6 preview release.

Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argues open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs.

#3163. Using AI to Vibe Code Your TV Is Stupid

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

No one likes clunky TV interfaces or their activity being tracked, but using AI isn’t how to avoid it. There’s an easier way.

Recently, some posts on X/Twitter and discussed elsewhere have claimed that AI has helped people “vibe code” their way to a better TV interface. Less clutter, no ads, less tracking and more are all ascribed to AI’s magical powers. Not only is this nonsense, but it’s also stupid.

First, let me say up front that I understand the frustration. TV interfaces have gotten bloated; they often have ads, and their creepy and invasive tracking properties have long been discussed and warned about by me and others.

That said, AI is not doing anything unique here. Not only can you do this without AI, but it’s also probably better if you don’t. Using AI risks potentially TV-ruining issues or worse.

“Vibe coding” is the colloquial term for using AI to assist or fully write programming code for apps, websites and so on. Instead of learning a programming language, people tell AI agents in plain English (or their language of choice) what they want, and the AI does it, or at least something close to it.

In this case, people are claiming they’re using an AI agent, usually Claude, to write a new operating system for TVs. This “new” OS is, they claim, faster, easier to use, has no ads and so on.

As with all claims about AI, you should be suspicious. First, TV operating systems are far more complex than they appear. Messing around “under the hood,” especially with no programming knowledge, can easily cause serious problems.

One TV engineer I spoke to for this article, who asked to remain anonymous, literally laughed out loud when I asked him about this. He explained that his engineers will often fix one bug in their software, and it will cause 10 other bugs in random, seemingly unrelated parts of the TV. That’s pretty typical with software development, by the way. There are reports already that people have “bricked” their TVs trying this. As in, they turned their TV into an expensive and unusable brick.

There are also a lot of potential issues down the road, even if you have initial success. For instance, will the new vibe-coded OS actually run Netflix and other apps? They might seem to load and then not be able to play anything. What happens if one of the apps needs an update? Will you still be able to? What if that update requires a specific Android version? Maybe you won’t have any issues, but there’s no guarantee of that, and if you don’t have any background in software or coding, can you be sure that more AI vibe coding will fix the issue? Will you be able to perform a factory reset and restore it to the way it was when you bought it? Hopefully yes, but not necessarily.

If you’re not a programmer, how sure are you that the code you’re using is secure? How sure are you that it’s only doing what you want and not exposing your TV to external access? This isn’t as likely as just breaking your TV, but if you don’t know or understand what’s going on “under the hood,” can you really be sure?

And what’s the end goal here? If it’s a faster interface with fewer ads, you can do that already without AI, as I’ll discuss in the next section. If it’s to minimize tracking, maybe changing the OS or interface will help, but not entirely.

AI can’t invent anything, and you can already change your TV’s interface with just an app install. Android TV launchers, as in the user interface, can be swapped out. So if your TV runs on Android, you can change the interface without any AI vibe coding. These launchers are often far simpler than the stock Google TV interface and are highly customizable.

Launchers like Projectivity, Monet and TV Launcher Premium Smart UI are some of the top-rated and most popular ones. The AT4K Launcher even makes your Android TV interface look like the Apple TV interface. There are many more options.

If you have a TV with a company-specific operating system, like LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, Hisense’s VIDAA and so on, the AI vibe coding trick isn’t likely to work anyway. Companies do their best to lock down their operating systems to prevent exactly the kind of thing we’re talking about here.

It’s entirely arguable that AI wasn’t doing anything clever in the first place. It was just regurgitating what human programmers had already figured out.

I think there’s a hilarious irony in not wanting your personal data to be out there, so in order to block your TV from tracking you, you give your personal data to AI. If you don’t understand why that’s ironic, you definitely shouldn’t give your data to AI. As I’ve talked about before, there is no easy way to prevent your TV from tracking you and selling your data. You can minimize it, or go to more extreme measures like Pi-holes and not connecting it to the internet at all, but then you’ll just be switching which device is tracking you. Still want streaming? All the streaming devices track you to some extent (the Apple TV 4K less so).

Using AI to vibe code your way into a better TV experience, however, is a dumb idea. Try a launcher app first and see if that gets you most or all the way to what you’re looking for. Will it be a magical fix to speed up a slow TV? No, but it could be much closer to what you’re looking for, and it’s far less likely to nuke your TV. If you want to go even further, there are apps that give you even more control, but with more potential for issues. Or hey, if you have a TV you don’t mind ruining, and you want to see what you can come up with using an AI that is just stealing from other people’s work, go for it.

#3160. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. #3159. Strategy's Michael Saylor Blames These 3 Factors for Bitcoin's Recent Sluggish Performance. The Most Important Is Treasury Yields.

Strategy (MSTR +2.38%) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor says trade policy, rising Treasury yields, and a roughly $1 trillion artificial intelligence (AI) build-out are making it harder for Bitcoin (BTC -0.28%) to recover from its recent bear market as vigorously as expected. As of Oct. 30, the coin is near $77,000, which means it's still 39% below its all-time high set in October 2025, despite climbing about 22% since late July.

Let's weigh each of the factors Saylor identified and figure out which is the most important -- spoiler alert, it's the Treasury yields -- and why.

In remarks at ParaFi Capital's Investor Day on Oct. 17, Saylor argued that Bitcoin is "pure capital," meaning its price tends to fall harder than stocks when the market is in a risk-off mood.

In particular, Saylor said that restrictive trade and monetary policy, repeated trade-war declarations against Canada, and rising Treasury bond yields were to blame. The $1 trillion in AI build-out spending is also something he cited as preventing Bitcoin from receiving available capital as it normally would.

The common theme here is that each of those factors saps the pool of money that's willing to hold a volatile asset that doesn't offer a yield like a bond does. The Trump administration's tariffs damped growth forecasts, and it's happening right as investors are funneling their capital into AI stocks and data centers instead of crypto because they believe the returns there are higher.

On Oct. 22, Bitcoin fell as much as 2.9% after disappointing tech earnings reports revived the market's doubts about the sustainability of the current pace of AI spending. So an AI bust could sink Bitcoin before any freed-up money rotates its way.

The Treasury issue is more cut-and-dried than the others. The 10-year Treasury yield was close to 5% on Oct. 30, versus 4% a year earlier.

During the same stretch, the 10-year breakeven inflation rate, which is a gauge of the inflation bond investors expect to experience, barely moved at all between last year and this year, holding at about 2.3%. Inflation expectations do not explain the recent jump in yields, but the war with Iran (and its deleterious effect on the global energy markets) does.

That undercuts a popular bull case for Bitcoin.

If investors feared inflation or fiscal deficits, Bitcoin's fixed supply and its status as a scarce store of value might lure them into a purchase, whether it actually works as an inflation hedge, which is still unproven. Instead, buyers of safe Treasury bonds lock in a real yield of about 2.6% a year higher than expected inflation, making a coin with no yield (and no government backing its value) a much harder sell.

And the Federal Reserve is likely going to tighten again before the close of 2026 in an attempt to control inflation; it raised its benchmark rate on Sept. 16 and held steady on Oct. 28. Investors now expect a December hike. That would only make bonds look more appealing in comparison to Bitcoin.

Even Saylor's company has paused its buying.

Strategy holds 848,517 coins and it didn't make any new purchases from Oct. 19 to Oct. 28.

Still, a yield headwind getting a bit stronger for a while says nothing about Bitcoin's capped supply failing or the other elements of its investment thesis being undermined.

Strategy will probably return to buying Bitcoin soon, and, for those willing to hold it for at least five years, there's little reason to avoid making a purchase so long as your portfolio is adequately diversified already with safer investments.

#3156. Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Your JBL, Sony, or Bose Bluetooth headphones got a top-to-bottom wireless makeover -- not just Auracast.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Auracast, the Bluetooth protocol that enables one-to-many audio streams and is the most popular LE Audio feature, but several other LE Audio upgrades don’t get as much attention. These features improve wireless voice call quality, reduce battery drain in true wireless earbuds, and remove ecosystem barriers to low-latency mobile gaming. Here’s why they matter just as much as Auracast.

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

Also: Bluetooth’s latest could solve a common connectivity problem

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.

LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

Also: Frustrated with multipoint? How it works – and why it sometimes won’t

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.

LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.

Also: Your iPhone may support Bluetooth Channel Sounding – and it’s a big deal

LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.

So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.

#3155. Take These Precautions Before Using AI for Your Election Research

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

There are good reasons why you may not want to use a chatbot for your midterm election research.

There are hundreds of races happening during this year’s midterm elections, from every seat in the US House of Representatives to various state and local government roles. Many tech issues are on the ballot, including AI policies, but people are also reportedly turning to generative AI chatbots to help them prepare for Election Day.

One of the biggest uses for chatbots is searching for information, so it isn’t surprising to see people using ChatGPT, Claude or another AI tool to learn about their candidates and ballot measures. But we know that generative AI tech has some serious risks, such as bias, sycophancy, hallucinations and drawing incorrect conclusions using bad information.

But if you’re going to use chatbots for your election research, make sure you take these precautions. You can also check out CNET’s guide to spotting political scams and deepfakes.

This is good advice for any conversation you have with a chatbot, but it’s especially important for election research: Verify that AI is telling you the truth.

Chatbots have come a long way since the original ChatGPT launched in 2022, but they still mess up. They work by pulling information from the web (or its database, if it isn’t web-connected) and synthesizing it. But along the way, facts can be scrambled in the AI blender.

Because the big chatbots try to personalize results to you to keep you engaged, they can end up misleading you. AI’s overly people-pleasing tendency is called sycophancy, and it can lead it to give you false information.

Chatbots can also hallucinate, or make up information. This is less of a concern with national election campaigns, which have a big online footprint that you can easily check against. But if you’re looking for polling locations or what your ballot will look like, you’re better off going to your state or local government’s election website to find that information. You can find your state’s board of elections contact information here. Those official government channels will also have the most up-to-date information.

You should also check a chatbot’s sources. For example, if you ask about a candidate’s position on data centers, see if the chatbot is citing a video clip of the candidate speaking, a news interview or a random post on social media.

This is especially important for social media citations. While we as humans can understand Reddit sarcasm or spot a bot X account, chatbots struggle with nuance and tone. Remember in 2024 when Google’s AI Overviews told people to put glue on pizza to help the cheese stick? That was based on a facetious Reddit post, and at the time, the AI couldn’t spot the joke.

Political misinformation certainly existed before AI, but like many digital maladies, AI can make the problem worse by confidently presenting it as truth to people searching for answers.

“AI is making it easier to generate misinformation,” says Jonathan Nagler, professor of politics at New York University.

Even if misinformation doesn’t make up the majority of most people’s media diet, Nagler says, it can be weaponized to speed up bad actors’ misinformation campaigns and translate them for a wider online audience. “We would be foolish not to worry about AI influencing this.”

It’s not just tech being weaponized by malicious actors; it’s also influencing our ability to spot misinformation. A recent study from MIT Media Lab found that just as GPS can weaken our navigation skills, using AI systems to verify facts made people worse at identifying misinformation on their own.

Misinformation produced by AI “can sway voters’ political views, so the stakes are real,” says Isabel Linzer, policy and elections analyst at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

A study published in Science found that when AI systems are optimized to be persuasive, there is “a troubling trade-off” in which the AI then increasingly provides false information.

The other major consideration when using AI for election research is bias. Some AI companies like OpenAI say they have “politically neutral” answers. But chatbots are not neutral platforms — no technology made by humans is. The AI models that run chatbots are coded by humans and, therefore, they’re encoded with human biases and can further harmful stereotypes.

“It’s hard to imagine what perfect political neutrality about a candidate or political issue would even look like in a personalized conversation, so while neutrality is an admirable goal, I’m skeptical of what it means in practice,” Linzer says.

There are also a lot of outside efforts to influence what appears in AI answers. Marketing and search engine optimization teams are now trying to get their companies cited in AI results, such as Google’s AI Overviews, which appear at the top of most searches.

Political actors are doing the same, producing content that’s intentionally flattering to one candidate or misleading about another to get cited favorably in AI answers. This is sometimes called “poisoning” the search results, Linzer says.

“Sometimes political campaigns use these techniques to boost their candidate, as do foreign state actors trying to mislead American voters,” she says.

The people leading these AI companies can also influence how the AI tool works. Elon Musk has said for years that he wanted his chatbot, Grok, to be more “politically neutral” than what he saw as a field of too-liberal alternatives. But a 2023 analysis from The New York Times found that Musk’s tweaking made Grok’s answers more aligned with conservative views.

In more recent years, engineers and executives working on Grok have pushed updates that have repeated controversial falsehoods about the Holocaust and refused to answer questions about Donald Trump and Musk as sources of misinformation.

When I asked ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok who I should vote for in North Carolina’s senate race, only Claude explicitly told me that it wasn’t going to push me toward either candidate. Google displayed a pop-up message in my Gemini window telling me to verify election information with official sources. ChatGPT and Grok didn’t say anything out of the ordinary.

AI chatbots are popular tools for sifting through online information, but they’re unreliable. They can accidentally give you false or outdated information, and both developers and outside forces can sway or bias the answers you get.

If you’re absolutely sure you want to use a chatbot for election research, you need to verify the information it provides against official sources.

But because chatbots are such an imperfect research tool, particularly for sensitive topics, it may actually save you time and energy to just do your own searching, reading and thinking. Chatbots can help lay out information — and misinformation — but you’re ultimately the only person responsible for your vote.

#3153. Smart Glasses Detector Apps Are Here. How Well Do They Work?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Bluetooth-scanning apps like Zuckoff can tell you when a pair of smart glasses is nearby. Whether the glasses are recording is another question.

Google Glass drew so much hostility after its 2013 debut that some bars and restaurants banned it. Meta’s Ray-Bans have sold far better, partly because they look like ordinary sunglasses — the same quality that troubles people who don’t want to be filmed.

A new crop of phone apps, led by Zuckoff, offers a workaround. They scan for the Bluetooth signals smart glasses give off while powered on and alert you when a pair turns up nearby. The alert tells you the glasses are present, not that they’re recording, but it’s more notice than most people get today.

Apps such as Zuckoff take a different approach to the problem, scanning for the Bluetooth signal that smart glasses emit while powered on and alerting nearby app users before anyone in range of the built-in LED indicator realizes recording might be happening.

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

One of those developers has already gained traction with a free Apple iOS app called Zuckoff, a digital detection tool to spot nearby Ray-Ban Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles or similar hardware.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

Space is vast, with trillions of objects in it, so it’s not necessarily a surprise when scientists find new objects there, even if it’s sometimes entirely by accident. Some objects are scarcer than others, and dwarf planets in our solar system are among the rarest, with only five recognized examples. A group of researchers from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory may have just found a sixth.

Meet ED138, a dwarf planet candidate. It was found earlier in October when Rubin Operations team member Matthew Holman noted an unusually large object uncovered by a program he’d written with colleague Kevin Napier to scan Rubin Observatory data for moving objects.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said in a statement. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

Holman ran the search a second time through archived data and found the same object 20 more times dating back to March 2026. He checked even more data from the Dark Energy Camera at the US National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory and the Asteroid Institute’s Asteroid Discovery Analysis and Mapping Precovery service, and found the object in observations going all the way back to 2016.

This presented enough evidence to submit the object to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center, which will conduct additional research to determine whether it is, in fact, a dwarf planet.

Researchers at the Rubin Observatory are hopeful, since ED138 seems to have all the properties of a dwarf planet. It’s further away from the sun than Neptune, which classifies it as a trans-Neptunian object. Not all TNOs are dwarf planet candidates, but ED138 is also the right size and shape. Based on preliminary estimates, the icy body is between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, which should be large enough for its shape to be round due to the pull of its own gravity.

The discovery of a new dwarf planet is a bigger deal than it seems. Tens of thousands of new celestial objects are discovered each year, and the Rubin Observatory alone has submitted 11,000 new asteroid discoveries since it started scanning the skies in June 2025.

If ED138 becomes a dwarf planet, it’ll join just five other such celestial objects with that distinction. They include Eris, Ceres, Haumea, Makemake and Pluto, which was downgraded to a dwarf planet 20 years ago.

Part of the reason for that is the strict definition of a dwarf planet. It has to be big enough to shape itself into a sphere with the force of its own gravity, orbit the sun and not be a moon. Another important distinction is that dwarf planets have not cleared their orbits of debris, which means they share their orbits with untold numbers of asteroids, comets and other space debris.

That last distinction is important because regular planets are considered to have cleared their orbits, either by absorbing the debris, sending it away through gravitational interactions or pulling it into stable orbits, as Earth did with the moon.

In short, a regular planet has enough gravitational pull to clear out the space around it, whereas dwarf planets do not.

The other reason why this would only be the sixth dwarf planet ever discovered is that there’s a lot of stuff in space and researchers often simply don’t know where to look. ED138 orbits in such a spot where it’s backdropped by the Milky Way, a region of space crowded with millions of stars. Thus, it’s very likely that ED138 had been observed by a telescope before but simply got lost in all the background noise.

Holman says that if Rubin can find this one, it can find others as well, so ED138 may not be the observatory’s last such discovery.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Mario Jurić, Rubin Solar System Operations team member, said in a statement. “And the discovery is just the beginning: once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look.”
