#3127. You Can End Spammy Election Phone Calls Now With This iPhone Trick

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The election is almost over, and you can end spam calls now.

Election day is a few days away, and that means political campaigns are mounting one last push to advocate for their candidate and issue. So you might be getting more election-related phone calls than usual. While those calls are well-meaning, they can be annoying if you’ve already voted early or have made up your mind about who to vote for. Luckily, if you keep your iPhone updated to the most recent iOS version, you can enable call screening on your device.

Apple introduced call screening in iOS 26. It isn’t an Apple Intelligence feature, so any iOS 27-compatible iPhone, such as the iPhone 14 Pro, can use it. I enabled the feature over a year ago and my iPhone has diligently held back spam calls, like the Hoover Dam, ever since. But you have to enable it first.

Here’s how to enable call screening in a few easy steps and what to know about the new feature.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps near the bottom of the menu.3. Tap Phone.

Under the section Screen Unknown Callers, you’ll see three options: Never, Ask Reason for Calling and Silence. Here’s what you should know about each of these options and which one is right for most people.

Choosing Never is the default option and lets calls from unsaved numbers come through and ring on your phone. It also documents missed calls in your Recents list in your Phone app, just like before call screening was available.

If you tap Ask Reason for Calling, your iPhone will ask anyone who calls you from an unsaved number why they are calling you without ringing your iPhone. After the caller answers a few questions, your iPhone will notify you with a transcript of the caller’s answers. Then you can decide whether you want to answer the call.

You can also pick Silence, which is the nuclear option for phone calls. Any unsaved numbers that call you will be silenced and sent to voicemail, no questions asked.

Ask Reason for Calling is the best option for most people who want to screen calls. I chose it, and while it notified me when scam callers answered some questions, which they rarely did, it also notified me when my doctor’s office called to go over some test results. If I had chosen Silence, I would have missed my doctor’s office (and choosing Never would mean checking every call if I was expecting something important).

If you choose Ask Reason for Calling and dislike it, you can always follow the steps above again and choose one of the other options. And remember, you can always silence your iPhone and not be bothered by any phone calls at all. My wife has not taken her phone off silent in months, and she remains blissfully unbothered by spam calls.

#3126. Prediction: Netflix Will Begin Paying a Dividend in 2027 and Beat the S&P 500 During the Next Decade

Since its initial public offering in May 2002, Netflix (NFLX -0.02%) has delivered a mind numbing 52,150% return -- making it a generational wealth builder for long-term investors. But during the past five years, it may surprise you to learn that Netflix has produced a negative 7% return while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.84%) has jumped 75% and the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%) has popped 66%.

Netflix is at its lowest level in more than two years. Here's why Netflix has gone from a market darling to the bargain barrel, why I predict it will begin paying a dividend, and why it's a buying opportunity for long-term investors.

In its first quarter 2024 shareholder letter, Netflix said it would stop reporting quarterly membership numbers and average revenue per membership in 2025, preferring instead to focus on revenue, operating margins, and engagement (time spent) on its platform.

Netflix partially backed up that decision, as its revenue and earnings are at all-time highs, and operating margins have expanded nicely. But those figures are inflated by a one-time $2.8 billion termination fee from Skydance -- which outbid Netflix for Warner Bros. Discovery.

Engagement has been solid, but Netflix isn't exactly taking market share either. According to Nielsen's August data, Netflix accounted for 7.7% of U.S. monthly TV viewing, well ahead of its streaming peers but lagging significantly behind Alphabet-owned YouTube's 15.8%.

Netflix's lower-cost ad-supported tier has been a key driver of higher engagement and TV time. But Netflix is now projecting $2.7 billion in full-year 2026 advertising revenue, down from an earlier forecast of $3 billion. Based on company estimates for $51.1 billion in full-year revenue, advertising accounts for just 5.3% of total revenue -- underscoring how Netflix relies heavily on its ad-free standard and premium subscriptions. However, that isn't necessarily a bad thing.

Still, investors may be concerned that Netflix's future growth will be far slower because its pricing tiers are already relatively high, and customers face no shortage of lower-cost streaming alternatives, as well as ad-based free options from YouTube and on mobile platforms like Meta Platforms' Instagram and TikTok.

Analyst average estimates have Netflix generating $3.77 in 2027 earnings per share, which is just 5.3% growth from the projected $3.58 in 2026 earnings per share. Because Netflix's stock price has been falling while its earnings have been rising, Netflix now trades at just 16.4 times 2026 projected earnings, while the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500 is 18.7.

Netflix's transition from a high-flying growth stock to a high-margin cash-generating value stock provides the ingredients necessary for a sustainable dividend program. As a company matures, it tends to return excess cash to shareholders through share buybacks before implementing a formal quarterly dividend policy. Although buyback and dividend distributions are not equally flexible. Investors tend to expect a predictable or regularly increased dividend because it's a payment that directly hits their brokerage accounts. Buybacks, in contrast, are better suited for market fluctuations and the business's underlying performance.

The best signal that a Netflix dividend could be on the horizon is the size of its buybacks. In the third quarter of 2026, Netflix bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion, which was its largest quarterly stock buyback ever. And it still has $22.3 billion of authorized spending left for additional buybacks. For context, Netflix exited its latest quarter with almost 4.2 billion shares -- having reduced its share count by 1.6% quarter-over-quarter and 3.3% year-over-year. That's a rapid repurchase rate, which is encouraging for investors who view the stock as undervalued.

Given its impeccable fundamentals, excellent balance sheet, recurring revenue stream, and high free cash flow -- I could see Netflix implementing a dividend in the coming years as a mechanism to directly pass along profits to shareholders rather than relying solely on buybacks. That recipe could turn the streaming service company into an excellent dividend growth stock, with high-single-digit percentage revenue and earnings growth that supports year-after-year dividend raises.

While no one knows what the S&P 500 will do at any given moment, it has historically returned about 10% per year, including dividends, over the long term. Since Netflix's valuation is so cheap, a combination of solid earnings growth and valuation expansion could allow it to outpace the S&P 500's return during the next decade.

#3125. iPhone Duo Just Passed 185,000 Folds in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. How Far Can It Go?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We're folding Apple's iPhone Duo over and over -- 900 times an hour -- to test the durability of its hinge.

Happy November! The air is getting chillier, retailers are shifting from Halloween to the holidays, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to test Apple’s first-ever folding phone, the $2,000 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than a week ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 9:30 a.m. ET on Monday Nov. 2, we’ve passed 200,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3123. Should You Invest $1,000 in BridgeBio Pharma Right Now?

BridgeBio Pharma (BBIO +1.65%) is a biotech on the verge of a breakout. The company focuses on rare genetic diseases. It has only two approved therapies right now: Attruby and Nulibry.

Attruby is the company's main earner right now. The drug treats transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), a rare type of heart disease. The drug was responsible for 71% of the company's revenue in the third quarter.

Nulibry is designed to treat infants with molybdenum cofactor deficiency, a rare disease that can lead to seizures and brain abnormalities.

BridgeBio has three other therapies that could launch in the coming months, which is one reason the stock has risen more than 6% over the past month. Here are three reasons to consider buying BridgeBio stock.

The company is positioned at a major inflection point with its pipeline heading into late 2026 and 2027. It has three key milestones coming up.

The first is BBP-418, which could become the first treatment for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2i, a rare genetic disorder that leads to muscle weakness and wasting. The company just announced positive phase 3 trial results, and the therapy has a target Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) date of Nov. 27 with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Oral infigratinib, which performed well in a phase 3 trial to treat achondroplasia, the most common cause of dwarfism, has a Feb. 4 PDUFA date and is under priority review. The drug is designed to promote bone growth by reducing the overactivity of the FGFR3 gene. The therapy is also being examined as a treatment for hypochondroplasia, another cause of dwarfism.

Encaleret, after positive phase 3 trials, has a PDUFA date of May 8 to treat autosomal dominant hypocalcemia type 1 (ADH1), a rare genetic hormonal disorder.

Securing these regulatory green lights will significantly diversify BridgeBio's commercial portfolio beyond its initial core market. The company, in its third-quarter report, said its field teams, including sales staff, were already in place for all three therapies.

BridgeBio's third-quarter 2026 financial report highlighted strong commercial execution, driven heavily by its primary revenue driver.

The company posted total third-quarter revenues of $353.2 million, up 193% year over year. That increase was led by $253.2 million in U.S. net product revenue for Attruby, its core therapy.

The company also improved its earnings per share (EPS) loss to $0.42, compared to an EPS loss of $0.95 in the same period a year ago.

Recent strategic financing moves, such as closing a $1 billion preferred equity financing partnership with backers that include Sixth Street and HealthCare Royalty, have provided the company with more financial resilience.

The company has more than $1.5 billion in cash, nearly 3 times as much as it had in the same quarter a year ago.

This means that BridgeBio is well capitalized to fund upcoming commercial rollouts and pipeline expansions without facing near-term liquidity pressure.

There are still many questions for BridgeBio, as it focuses on rare therapies with relatively low patient populations. However, with three drugs lined up for potential FDA approval, the odds don't look quite as long for a breakout.

Relatively small biotechs come with a degree of risk, but BridgeBio's scientific breakthroughs could easily lead to continued revenue growth, a good reason to buy the stock before it soars.

#3122. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3121. The world has a new plan to save nature, but it still needs the money

A new action plan aims to rescue 2030 nature targets as financing remains inadequate.

The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.

Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.

The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.

The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”

“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

Catherine Weller, global policy director at the campaign group Fauna & Flora, said the Yerevan agreement was welcome but also noted that funding fell far short of a pledge that had been a key part of the 2022 deal. “In a world of trillionaires, we can certainly afford to spend $200 billion a year on protecting and restoring the very thing keeping us all alive: nature,” she said.

Conference organizers said governments, philanthropists, and businesses had announced close to $2 billion in new financial commitments to coincide with the Armenian gathering.

This included a commitment by the Netherlands to contribute $500 million to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazilian initiative to pay countries to keep their forests standing. The pledge was announced in the Dutch parliament the day after Brazilian leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected as president, to the relief of many attending the biodiversity summit.

After the close of the conference, Carina Pimenta, Brazil’s national secretary for bioeconomy, highlighted Lula’s record of protecting the Amazon rainforest and spoke of hope. “At a time of growing global uncertainty, the Yerevan Declaration sends a powerful message: world leaders recognise that protecting biodiversity is essential to food security, livelihoods, and economic resilience,” she said.

A growing number of countries to have drawn up national diversity plans, and the new pledge to the Brazilian fund, were “reasons for cautious optimism,” said Brian O’Donnell, director at Campaign for Nature.

But international funding for protected and conserved areas has fallen in a number of countries over years of disruption from war and high energy prices, with a 27 percent decline in environmental funding for the 2026-30 period.

#3120. Growing Expectations for a Midterm Election "Blue Wave" Holds 2 Risks for the 2nd Priciest Stock Market in History

Tomorrow, people from across our great nation will head to the polls or mail in their ballots to chart America's course over the next two years. The Nov. 3 midterm elections can shake up Congress and directly impact the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +1.10%), benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%), and tech-driven Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.84%).

To be clear, the stock market can thrive regardless of which party is in power. According to online retirement planning site Retirement Researcher, the worst political scenario since 1926 -- a Republican president overseeing a divided Congress -- delivered an average annual return of 7.33%. That's still a more robust average annual return than bonds, commodities, and real estate.

The makeup of Congress under President Trump could soon look a lot different. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

Nevertheless, shifting from a unified Republican government (i.e., one in which the GOP controls the House, Senate, and White House) to a divided Congress can create problems for the second-priciest stock market in history.

According to prediction market Polymarket, as of Oct. 29, traders are pricing in just a 7% chance that Republicans sweep and retain both houses of Congress. By comparison, there's a 68% chance Democrats will sweep and retake both houses of Congress (i.e., a blue wave).

BREAKING: Democrats surge in odds of sweeping both the House & Senate, with just 10 days until the midterm elections. 66% chance. https://t.co/0VsfxSpQSA

Based on what history shows, a split Congress isn't inherently bad for Wall Street. Given the ideological differences between Democrats and Republicans, it virtually removes the passage of major tax and spending legislation. A blue wave would likely make personal and corporate income tax law predictable through the end of President Donald Trump's term in January 2029. Investors love when things are predictable.

But a blue wave also holds risks for a historically expensive stock market.

Nothing has been more important to the Dow's, S&P 500's, and Nasdaq Composite's four-year rally than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and the ongoing AI build-out. Empowering software and systems with the tools to make autonomous, split-second decisions is a multitrillion-dollar opportunity.

Under a unified Republican government, AI has flourished with minimal regulation. However, several Democrats have called for stricter regulations concerning AI data centers and the rollout/testing of AI solutions, including large language models.

Keep in mind that if Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, it doesn't automatically mean anything changes for America's leading AI companies. Short of a two-thirds vote by the House and the Senate, President Trump still holds veto power over Congress.

JUST IN: Trump declares he will “veto everything” if Democrats gain control of Congress in the midterms.

Nevertheless, putting AI's shortcomings in the spotlight would be potentially terrible news for a pricey stock market that can ill afford any slowdown in the AI infrastructure build-out.

The other risk to the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite from a blue wave concerns debt-ceiling negotiations.

The debt ceiling is estimated to be reached in the first half of 2027. It's considerably easier to raise the debt ceiling under a unified Republican or Democratic government than it is with a split Congress. The ideological stalemate between America's two political parties could lead to a lengthy government shutdown in 2027.

Historically, government shutdowns haven't led to significant stock market downturns. But they have, on occasion, adversely affected U.S. gross domestic product, which can negatively impact corporate earnings.

#3119. Meet the Spectacular Vanguard ETF With 44.6% of Its Portfolio Parked in Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, and Microsoft

The Morningstar U.S. Total Market index is made up of all 3,476 companies listed on American stock exchanges. But then there is the Morningstar U.S. Mega Cap Growth index, which exclusively holds America's 52 most valuable growth companies, and they account for almost half the value of the entire U.S. Total Market Index.

That's right -- those 52 companies are worth almost as much as the other 3,424 listed companies combined. Perhaps that isn't a surprise given the four largest members in the Mega Cap Growth index are Nvidia (NVDA +1.50%), Alphabet (GOOGL +1.99%)(GOOG +1.91%), Apple (AAPL -1.39%), and Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%), which have a combined market capitalization of $17.6 trillion.

The Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF (MGK +0.44%) is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that mimics the Large Cap Growth index by holding the same stocks. Here's how adding it to a diversified portfolio can supercharge an investor's long-term returns.

Given the substantial value of the four largest members of the Mega Cap Growth index (and by extension, the Vanguard ETF), they represent an eye-popping 44.6% of the value of its portfolio.

Data source: Vanguard. Portfolio weightings are accurate as of Sept. 30, 2026, and are subject to change.

The four companies operate very different businesses, but they are powering the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution in their own unique way.

AI stocks are currently pulling back after posting blistering gains over the last few years. But Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, and Microsoft are still sitting on a median return of 195% since the AI boom started gathering momentum in January 2023, when OpenAI's ChatGPT application crossed 100 million users for the first time. Therefore, these stocks have been a major source of upside for the Vanguard ETF.

This Vanguard ETF also holds a number of other AI titans including Meta Platforms, Broadcom, Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, and Palantir Technologies. But it does offer some diversification through positions in payment giants Visa and Mastercard, industrial powerhouse Boeing, and consumer products company Monster Energy, to name just a few of its non-technology holdings.

The Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF has delivered a compound annual return of 13.8% since it was established in 2007, beating the S&P 500 index which gained an average of 10.9% per year over the same period. However, given its highly concentrated portfolio of just 52 stocks, investors probably shouldn't bet the farm on this fund alone.

Adding this ETF to a diversified portfolio of other funds and individual stocks might be a better strategy, because it can help minimize any potential downside risks. Technology companies are currently spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data center infrastructure each year, and concerns are mounting about a potential slowdown. If that happens, there could be further downside ahead for most of the stocks at the top of the Vanguard ETF.

Investors who put $20,000 into an S&P 500 index fund in 2007 would have $142,800 today. But had they split the $20,000 by placing $10,000 in the S&P 500 and the other $10,000 in the Vanguard ETF, they would have $188,000 today instead. At the same time, they would have smoothed out some of the volatility associated with having significant exposure to the tech industry.

In summary, this Vanguard ETF could be a great long-term investment, but diversification might be the key to yielding the best results.

#3118. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

#3117. W&T Offshore: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 30, 2026, W&T Offshore (WTI -6.91%) reported production of 38,200 barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) per day, exceeding the high end of its guidance by 4% without drilling new wells. The company continues to extract cash from mature Gulf of Mexico assets by funding cheap well repairs instead of expensive offshore drilling. That disciplined approach keeps debt low and builds cash for future property purchases. Three things management said stand out.

W&T avoids the massive capital expenditures that sink traditional offshore drillers. Instead, the company spent just over $3 million on seven workover projects and one recompletion, yielding an additional 2,000 BOE per day.

Cash on hand reached over $190 million while net debt fell 20% to $160 million, dropping leverage below 0.9 times trailing adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). Rather than funding speculative development wells, management plans to deploy that cash into acquiring producing Gulf properties.

Lease operating expenses (LOE), the ongoing costs to maintain producing wells and offshore platforms, came in at $77 million for the third quarter. Prior structural cost cuts helped buffer operating margins against commodity price swings.

Favorable Gulf energy prices give W&T room to accelerate maintenance into late 2026. That sets up higher production heading into early 2027.

On the portfolio side, management is evaluating shallow-water asset sales while maintaining low leverage and strict capital discipline across its legacy footprint.

#3116. UBS Just Initiated Coverage of Viking Therapeutics With a Buy Rating and a $94 Target. Here's the Bull Case.

Viking Therapeutics (VKTX +1.30%) received a new buy rating from UBS on Oct. 14, with analyst Joon Lee assigning the stock a 12-month price target of $94. With Viking shares trading around $26.75, that target suggests potential upside of approximately 250%.

UBS believes Viking's experimental weight loss treatment, VK2735, could deliver substantially greater weight loss than today's leading medications. The firm pointed to clinical data showing the drug could produce roughly twice the weight loss of semaglutide and 1.5 times that of tirzepatide.

Those are encouraging projections, although they aren't based on head-to-head clinical trials. Still, Viking's candidate has produced some impressive results, and the company is now conducting late-stage studies involving thousands of patients.

VK2735 works by activating two hormones that regulate appetite and blood sugar: GLP-1 and GIP. It's the same general approach used by Eli Lilly's (LLY -1.09%) blockbuster obesity medication Zepbound, generically known as tirzepatide. Novo Nordisk's (NVO +1.05%) Wegovy (aka semaglutide), meanwhile, targets GLP-1 alone.

Viking's injectable treatment produced average weight reductions of up to 14.7% after just 13 weekly doses in its phase 2 Venture trial. Patients were still losing weight when the study ended, suggesting that longer treatment periods could produce greater reductions. More recent clinical trial results have strengthened that argument.

In September, Viking reported results from a separate study involving approximately 180 adults with obesity. Patients receiving weekly VK2735 injections lost roughly 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. An exploratory group that continued to receive weekly treatments achieved an average weight reduction of 21.7% after 33 weeks.

To put that in perspective, for someone weighing 250 pounds, a 21.7% reduction would represent approximately 54 pounds. Make no mistake: These results are promising, but differences in trial design, patient populations, and treatment duration make direct comparisons with approved obesity drugs unreliable.

The trial results published in September also demonstrated that patients might not need to continue their weekly injections indefinitely. After an initial 21-week treatment period, some participants switched to less frequent injections for another 12 weeks.

Patients receiving injections every other week maintained up to 97% of their previous weight loss. Those receiving monthly injections maintained up to 90%.

Viking isn't relying exclusively on injections. On Oct. 14, the company announced that it had initiated its Phase 3 Sunrise clinical program for an oral version of VK2735. The program includes two studies. One will evaluate adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, while the other will focus on patients with type 2 diabetes. Both will evaluate once-daily treatment regimens over 68 weeks.

Earlier phase 2 results showed that patients taking oral VK2735 lost up to 12.2% of their body weight after 13 weeks. Up to 80% of treated participants lost at least 10% of their body weight, compared with just 5% receiving placebo.

Viking is still a clinical-stage biotechnology company -- in other words, it does not have any approved commercial products on the market. It will also need plenty of cash to continue moving forward with its research and development. As of Sept. 30, Viking held approximately $960 million in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, up from $502 million at the end of June. That increase was the result of a September financing effort that raised approximately $575 million through stock and convertible debt offerings, generating roughly $548 million in net proceeds.

With multiple phase 3 trials underway, Viking's development costs remain quite high. However, its September financing significantly reduced near-term funding concerns. The company still faces the possibility of future share dilution, though, particularly if its clinical development or commercialization efforts prove more expensive than anticipated.

Competition is another concern. Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk already have established weight loss franchises, significant manufacturing capabilities, and substantial resources for developing new treatments. And the promising early results for Viking's candidates don't guarantee regulatory approval.

UBS' $94 12-month price target for Viking is aggressive, but there are several factors supporting that bullish outlook. The biotech's injectable treatment candidate has produced substantial weight loss in trial participants, its maintenance study suggests that less frequent dosing could be a viable course for weight maintenance, and its oral formulation has advanced into phase 3 trials. The company also fully controls its lead drug rather than sharing ownership with a larger pharmaceutical partner.

The biggest question is whether Viking will be able to reproduce its earlier clinical results in larger, longer studies while maintaining an acceptable safety profile. If it can, VK2735 could become a serious competitor in the weight loss drug market, potentially attracting commercial partnerships or even acquisition interest for the company.

If you're willing to accept significant clinical and financial risk, Viking stock offers considerable upside potential. But UBS' $94 price target remains an analyst estimate, not a guarantee of where the stock is headed.

#3115. CME vs. SoFi Technologies: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Investors often choose between established industry giants and disruptive newcomers. CME Group (CME -0.16%) and SoFi Technologies (SOFI +3.49%) represent two very different paths within the financial landscape for those looking ahead to 2027.

CME operates massive exchanges for futures and options, thriving on market volatility and institutional volume. SoFi is a digital-first bank aiming to be a one-stop shop for young, high-earning consumers. This comparison examines their business models, growth trajectories, and financial health to help you decide which one fits your goals.

CME Group operates the world's most prominent derivatives marketplace, handling contracts for interest rates, equities, and commodities. Its clients include global financial institutions, central banks, and professional traders. The company also maintains a joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT +4.00%) to explore prediction markets.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, representing growth of roughly 6.4% over the prior year. This consistent expansion translated into net income of about $4 billion. The company maintained a high net margin of approximately 62% during this period.

As of CME's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.1. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was approximately 1. In fiscal 2025, CME generated approximately $4.2 billion in free cash flow. Free cash flow is the cash a company generates after subtracting capital expenditures from its operating cash flow.

SoFi Technologies serves members through an integrated app that provides banking, lending, and investment services. Through its Galileo and Technisys platforms, the company provides infrastructure to other banks and fintech stocks. This segment creates a diversified revenue stream beyond consumer lending. It also works with Mastercard (MA +2.26%) to facilitate modern payment solutions for its members.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $4.8 billion, representing growth of roughly 28.8% from the previous year. The business generated net income of nearly $481.3 million. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 10.1%.

As of SoFi's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2. The current ratio was approximately 0.2. In fiscal 2025, the company reported negative free cash flow of close to $4 billion.

CME Group faces competition from other major exchanges like Intercontinental Exchange (ICE +0.21%), Cboe Global Markets (CBOE +2.36%), and Nasdaq (NDAQ +1.40%). Its business is highly sensitive to global trading volumes, which can fluctuate based on geopolitical stability or economic shifts. Additionally, the company must manage significant cybersecurity risks and the potential for infrastructure failures, as seen in a 2025 data center incident.

SoFi Technologies is highly dependent on macroeconomic conditions and interest rate movements, which affect loan demand. As a bank holding company, it navigates complex regulatory environments that could impact its lending capacity. SoFi also faces credit and fraud risks in its digital asset offerings and potential reputational damage from legal challenges regarding talent acquisition.

SoFi Technologies carries a significantly lower price-to-sales multiple, while CME Group offers a lower forward earnings multiple despite its much higher net margin.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The forward P/E relates the stock price to future earnings estimates for the coming year. The P/S ratio compares the market value of the company to its sales over the past 12 months.

SoFi Technologies is posting significantly higher revenue growth, but the company is also earlier in its life cycle, so I would expect (at least, I would hope) that it would be doing so. However, CME Group's high net margin absolutely dwarfs SoFi's. CME also pays a modest dividend, and SoFi does not.

Over the past five years, CME Group shares have outperformed SoFi stock, although neither has matched the S&P 500's return.

Past performance is no guarantee of future results, but for investors, those results are disappointing. The point of buying individual stocks is to outperform the market. Why take the risk of a single stock when you could buy a large basket of some of the biggest companies in the U.S.?

Regardless, between CME and SoFi, I would be more inclined to invest in the former. The derivatives specialist's high net margin is attractive, and I like companies that reward shareholders with dividends.

#3114. 3 Bank Stocks With Buyback Plans of at Least $30 Billion Worth a Look

JPMorgan Chase (JPM +1.25%), Bank of America (BAC +0.27%), and Citigroup (C +1.75%) are putting billions behind their share buyback programs, with each bank authorizing at least $30 billion in repurchases.

All three banks released third-quarter results in mid-October, offering updates on their finances and their future plans. Which ones have actually followed through on these share repurchase agreements, shrinking their share count and giving investors more bang for their investment buck?

In June 2026, JPMorgan's board authorized a new $50 billion common stock repurchase program, effective July 1. And during the third quarter, JPMorgan repurchased around $1 billion in common stock but recorded only $664 million in net repurchases. In other words, that gross amount used only about 2% of the new authorization.

And not surprisingly, the impact on the share count was modest. The company ended September with 2.656 billion common shares outstanding, compared with 2.722 billion a year earlier. That means its share count declined just 2.4% year over year.

Management has emphasized that repurchases must compete with other uses of capital, including investments in the business, lending opportunities, and the maintenance of a strong balance sheet. The bank also faces risks around weaker credit quality and investment banking activity.

On top of that, at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 13 times, its valuation also leaves less room for disappointment than its peers'.

Bank of America has had a $40 billion common stock repurchase authorization in place since Aug. 1, 2025. By June 30, 2026, the bank had around $17 billion remaining under the authorization after repurchasing $13.2 billion in the first half of the year. Then, during the third quarter, it repurchased another $6 billion of common stock.

That brings the program's total repurchases to $29 billion, leaving $11 billion available. Put differently, it has used roughly 73% of the authorization in about 14 months and at its current pace, that remaining amount could be used relatively quickly.

The impact has already been meaningful. Bank of America ended September with 6.923 billion common shares outstanding, down 5.5% year over year from 7.329 billion.

That said, the bank faces risks around interest rates and regulatory issues. But at a forward P/E of 9.8 times, its valuation could look reasonable, especially given its aggressive buybacks.

Citigroup began a $30 billion multi-year common stock repurchase program in the second quarter of 2026. In that quarter alone, it repurchased $4 billion in common stock, leaving around $26 billion under authorization by June 30. That means Citi used about 13% of its authorization in a single quarter.

Then, in the third quarter, Citi reported returning $4.1 billion to common shareholders through a combination of common stock repurchases and dividends. As a result, the share count declined notably. The bank ended September with 1.655 billion common shares outstanding, down 7.5% from 1.789 billion a year earlier.

Of course, Citi also faces risks. Its ongoing transformation involves operational and regulatory work, and any setbacks could delay its profitability targets. Plus, its credit card business is under pressure.

And with the stock trading at a forward P/E ratio of just 9.4 times, valuation is less demanding than the other banks.

Ultimately, the best buyback opportunity comes down to which bank can deliver the most shareholder value. JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citigroup all have massive buyback programs. Among the three, Citi's share count has declined the most despite having the smallest buyback program.

Bank of America comes in second, while having a larger program. And JPMorgan has the largest buyback program among the three, but is the least eager to spend. At current paces, Bank of America has under two quarters left; the others have longer.

JPMorgan could suit investors looking for the most upside from buybacks, despite its buyback activity being slow. Bank of America could be the balanced pick, pairing aggressive buybacks with a reasonable valuation. At the other end, Citigroup could be the high-risk, high-reward choice, given its transformation.

#3113. The Trump Administration Is Wreaking Havoc on the Electoral System Before the Midterms

Polls are looking pretty bleak for Republicans—and the Trump administration’s various attempts to interfere with the elections haven’t been too successful either.

In recent weeks, the Department of Justice, helmed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, a proponent of conspiracy theories about widespread noncitizen voting in the 2020 election, has pulled out all the stops to sow doubt in voters’ minds about the security and validity of the electoral process.

To do this, the DOJ has spent the last year demanding unredacted voter rolls, issuing executive orders to wrest control of elections from states, raiding election offices, proposing new laws to disenfranchise millions of citizens, and claiming that noncitizens were voting en masse across the country. (Incidents of verified noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare, as multiple bipartisan investigations have shown.)

There have also been escalating threats by the DOJ against election officials. On Thursday, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states warning them that they would pursue criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days. Earlier that week, a federal judge had admonished the Trump administration for making similar threats around criminal prosecution against election officials in a different case.

“They're trying to create chaos and distrust in the system,” says Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at UCLA Law’s Safeguarding Democracy Project. “They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.”

“This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,” a spokesperson for the DOJ tells WIRED, pointing out that the previous administration’s Justice department sued Alabama and Virginia ahead of the 2024 election, claiming the DOJ was at the time trying “to stop them from removing suspected noncitizens from their voter rolls.”

Experts say that while the DOJ’s current legal efforts, including escalating fights in Alaska and California over candidates and voter rolls, are faltering, they’re also designed to lay the groundwork to question the results of this week’s vote.

“We have to expect absolutely, if the election doesn't go the way the president wants, that we will see the administration’s attempt to sow doubts in the election and maybe even challenge those results, but I'm also not worried about it,” David Becker, a former DOJ lawyer and the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, tells WIRED.

“They have failed at everything they've tried to do. Our systems have held firm. Our institutions have held firm.”

34 federal district courts have ruled against Trump since he took office in 2025 blocking access to voter rolls and preventing executive orders being implemented, according to analysis from the Brennan Center.

Former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division Justin Levitt thinks that a lot of the actions taken by the Trump administration are about a show of force and optics more than anything else. “What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing. They are trying to communicate that they're in charge, and I think it's not working,” says Levitt, now a law professor at Loyola Marymount University. “But it is really important to remember that the federal government isn't in charge of the election process. State and local officials are.”

WIRED has laid out the details of the DOJ’s legal efforts in California, Nevada, Washington, and Alaska below, which have all been met with disdain from local and state officials.

California is officially a hotbed of election controversy. In October, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking a court order against California to compel them to sequester mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 voters, claiming that these voters were noncitizens. On Wednesday, a federal judge in a strong-worded order rejected the request.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” US District Judge David Carter wrote in his order filed late on Wednesday.

Almost immediately, the DOJ filed an appeal and a federal court quickly denied it.

The judge pointed out that similar claims from the administration about noncitizens on voter rolls hadn’t held up to scrutiny, and he had “further questions of credibility” about how they arrived at that number in the first place.

Last week, a federal judge also ruled that the DOJ had to turn over its list of around 20,000 names to the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, so that the group could analyze the dataset. On Saturday, the group submitted a legal filing stating that an analysis of the list found that over 40 percent of the names weren’t even in the state’s current voter files. In response, the DOJ has suggested that the publication of their analysis violated the terms of the lists released to them, and is urging a federal judge to consider whether contempt charges might be applicable here.

“The DOJ has clearly written rules that prevent it from engaging in any investigative activity close to an election—rules that private attorney Todd Blanche cited when representing his client, Donald Trump, in September 2024,” Becker says. “But the DOJ continues to violate its own policies.”

To cap it all off, the DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas to California’s local election officials last week, indicating that despite repeated court losses it has no intention of backing down.

In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit designed to block certification of the election result in Alaska’s Senate race if Democrat candidate Mary Peltola wins.

The reason for the lawsuit is the presence of a spoiler candidate on the ballot with a similar name as the incumbent Republican candidate Daniel Sullivan. The DOJ’s lawsuit was filed despite the Alaska Supreme Court ruling in the summer that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr could remain on the ballot as no laws had been broken.

A New York Times investigation last week alleged that Democrat-aligned operatives were involved in getting a spoiler candidate on the ballot, though Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement in the effort to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the ballot. Asked about whether the common practice of putting spoiler candidates on the ballot was illegal, Todd Blanche said “it certainly should be.” On Truth Social, Trump said Peltola “should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.”

“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau last week. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”

On Thursday, Alaska Governor Michael Dunleavy ordered an investigation to determine whether state criminal or civil charges could be pursued against Peltola. In an interview with NewsNation, Dunleavy said that he could not commit to certifying victory for Peltola if that investigation was still ongoing.

“Dunleavy’s threat to overrule the will of Alaskan voters exemplifies what Alaskans hate about partisan politics and shows why he’s the least popular governor in the country,” a Peltola campaign spokeswoman tells WIRED. “Mary won’t be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted—and she’s going to win this race by focusing on solutions to Sullivan’s price hiking policies and putting Alaska first.”

On Friday, the DOJ held a press conference in Anchorage and said that, in addition to their lawsuit seeking to block the certification of the election result if Peltola wins, they were also launching their own investigation to determine if federal civil or criminal charges could be applicable in this case. "We are aware of … the sprawling conspiracy to prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate,” said US Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman.

On Sunday, a federal judge threw out the DOJ’s lawsuit, ruling that their request likely violated Alaskans' right to a secret ballot. Hours later, the DOJ asked a federal appeals court to overturn the ruling.

In July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed that they had identified over 270,000 noncitizen voters in just four states: California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. But that bold assertion soon started to unravel.

DHS officials had also claimed that there were 15,903 noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls, but then later conceded in a meeting with Nevada officials that they didn’t have evidence. The number of suspected noncitizens on voter rolls then dropped down to 185, but there was no evidence to support that claim either.

“As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens,” Nevada’s Deputy Attorney General Greg Ott wrote in a letter to DHS. “You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise.”

“The Department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED about the situation. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

Ott added in the letter that while Nevada takes allegations of noncitizen voting seriously, “it also has a strong interest in preventing the wrongful disenfranchisement of voters” and is “committed to preventing the chilling effect on the right to vote from taking actions based on unfounded and unverifiable allegations of noncitizen voting.”

Last week, the DOJ claimed that federal data appeared to show that 400 noncitizens were registered to vote in the state of Washington and demanded that officials isolate those ballots, describing them as “the tip of the iceberg.”

They received another withering letter in return: “The timing of your letter is profoundly disappointing,” wrote Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs. “If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was a month ago.” Hobbs added that their decision to publicly raise their concerns so close to the election was “not a sign of good faith to ensure a free, fair, and accurate election.”

Hobbs added that the DOJ had failed to provide individualized proof that any of the people on the list were ineligible to vote, and didn’t offer any information about how they arrived at the lists of names or what sources were used. “Given the Department of Justice’s recent acts of election interference in California, Alaska, and now in Washington, it would be particularly inappropriate for Washington to simply assume the Department’s unsupported allegations here are credible.”

While not a filing by the Justice department, the Potter County Republican party has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from certifying the vote unless all Texas ballots are counted by hand.

The GOP’s basis for demanding a manual audit include purported threats from artificial intelligence’s ability to supposedly hack into virtually any voting machine undetected, a claim presented without evidence, and the presence of voting machine parts manufactured in China. Levitt, the former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, described the lawsuit as “nuts.”

“That would be the technical term,” Levitt said. “I wish that they had filed the thing in Comic Sans on the back of a Burger King placemat, because I think that would help people evaluate how serious it is.”

#3111. Intel Stock Cratered 28%, Opening a Massive Buying Opportunity for Investors Looking for a Stock That Could Nearly Double

Shares of Intel (INTC -2.82%) have been in phenomenal form on the stock market since the beginning of 2025, rising by 225% as of this writing, but Chipzilla's investors received a huge shock after the release of its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29.

Intel stock plunged more than 28% the following day. Investors were spooked by the company's guidance, which was affected by the poor performance of its personal computer (PC) business. However, a closer look at Intel's numbers and guidance suggests that the stock is only taking a breather.

Let's look at the reasons why this semiconductor stock could overcome this setback and soar once again.

Intel's Q4 revenue increased 21% year over year to $16.5 billion. Even better, its non-GAAP earnings per share jumped by an incredible 126% from the year-ago period to $0.52. Wall Street would have settled for $0.40 in adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $16.5 billion, suggesting that Intel's bottom-line performance was well ahead of expectations.

However, the company's guidance led investors to press the panic button. The company expects revenue of $15-$16 billion in the current quarter, along with adjusted earnings per share of $0.25. Analysts were anticipating $0.43 in earnings per share on $17.1 billion in revenue. So, it is easy to see why Intel stock was hammered badly following its results.

The primary reason behind Intel's poor outlook is the PC business. The company's client computing and physical artificial intelligence (AI) business segment saw revenue drop 5% from the year-ago period to $8.1 billion. Intel management noted on the earnings call that the pace of the PC market slowdown has accelerated over the past couple of months, driven by high component costs that are weighing on IT budgets.

Intel noted that it expects "the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize." This statement indicates that Intel's client computing business faces sustained pressure, especially given its expectation that the PC market will shrink by 10% in 2027. However, Intel's data center business is more than making up for the decline in PCs.

Its data center and AI (DCAI) segment revenue jumped 78% year over year to $7.3 billion, driven by solid demand for its server central processing units (CPUs) that handle inference and agentic AI workloads in data centers. Importantly, Intel's server CPUs are gaining popularity among customers, with Oracle deciding to deploy its next-generation Diamond Rapids platform to power its cloud infrastructure.

At the same time, Intel's custom AI processor business is also gaining solid traction. The company noted that this is its "fastest growing business segment, tripling over the last 3 years and poised to triple again over the next few years." As such, there is a strong chance that the robust performance of the DCAI business will enable Intel to offset the weakness of the PC segment until the latter stabilizes.

Market research firm IDC expects the PC market to start growing again from 2028, so the pain Intel is facing in this segment may not last beyond next year. Additionally, Intel notes that it expects stronger demand from data center customers and that the market for data center chips will remain tight on supply in both 2027 and 2028.

This should help Intel deliver strong earnings growth on the back of favorable pricing. In fact, the company's earnings are expected to jump once again in the current quarter despite the challenging PC environment. The midpoint of its Q4 revenue guidance implies a 13% jump from the year-ago period, along with an impressive 67% increase in earnings per share.

So, Intel continues to clock impressive earnings growth even though it isn't firing on all cylinders. Once the PC market starts recovering from 2028, I won't be surprised to see Intel's growth accelerating further.

If you're looking to construct a million-dollar portfolio and want to buy a top growth stock trading at an attractive valuation right now, Intel seems like an ideal candidate. That's because Intel trades at an attractive 31 times forward earnings, which isn't very expensive considering that the iShares Semiconductor ETF, which tracks the semiconductor sector, has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 46.

Moreover, analysts expect Intel's earnings growth to continue at a solid pace.

INTC EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Even better, the long-term earnings-per-share growth estimates for Intel are a handsome 75%.

INTC EPS LT Growth Estimates data by YCharts

As such, there is a strong likelihood that this AI stock will regain its mojo. Let's say Intel's earnings per share reach $3.14 in 2028 (based on YCharts estimates), and it trades at 40 times earnings; its stock price could jump to $126. That's 90% higher than Intel's price right now, suggesting that this beaten-down chipmaker could almost double in just over two years.

So, the recent slide in Intel seems like a golden opportunity for investors to buy a top stock that could make them significantly richer.

#3110. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3109. Titan: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Titan (TWI +2.37%) discussed a definitive agreement to divest its ITM steel undercarriage business and refocus on core wheel and tire manufacturing. The transaction lets leadership pay down debt while directing capital toward higher-margin growth initiatives and selective acquisitions. Three takeaways from management's comments stand out.

Management agreed to sell ITM to lower debt levels and fund core wheel and tire operations. Removing non-core business lines sharpens strategic focus. And it's a clear step toward building long-term balance sheet strength.

Equipment buyers have delayed purchases during market downturns, but dealer inventory remains depleted. That matters because when agricultural demand rebounds, lean channel inventory means fresh orders flow to factory floors almost immediately.

Titan is expanding its footprint by acquiring initial minority stakes with built-in buyout options. Partnering with regional leaders lets management enter key growth markets like Brazil without overextending capital reserves upfront.

Agricultural demand remains subdued, but stabilizing crop prices and low channel inventory suggest fundamental conditions are bottoming out. In the meantime, management is leveraging its global manufacturing scale while watching input cost inflation.

Balance sheet deleveraging from the ITM sale will provide flexibility to pursue high-return investments as market demand resumes. And closing the planned divestiture sets up core growth heading into 2027.
