#3108. As Fed Holds Steady, Are 7.5% Mortgage Rates Still Possible?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The Fed voted to hold rates steady, but mortgage rates still have room to grow.

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve announced that central bankers would leave the federal funds rate unchanged. Since this was in line with market expectations, mortgage rates shouldn’t have much of a reaction — yet.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage slid 10 basis points to 7.17% APR in the week ending Oct. 28, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Central bankers have twin goals when setting monetary policy: Getting inflation as close to 2% as possible, and maintaining maximum employment. When inflation gets too high, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which causes consumer borrowing rates (like mortgage rates) to rise as well. When unemployment gets too high, they can lower the federal funds rate to make it cheaper for businesses to access credit and hire more employees.

Since the latest jobs report showed that employment was relatively steady last month, that leaves inflation as the hot topic.

Despite Fed Chair Kevin Warsh holding true to his signature tight-lipped style in the weeks leading up to the meeting — and despite September’s preliminary inflation numbers running high so far — futures traders were largely confident that the Fed would keep the federal funds rate as is this week after last month’s hike.

Not necessarily. Mortgage rates could be completely different tomorrow.

In fact, we’ll probably see rates shift in response to the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, or PCE, which is set to be released on Thursday, Oct. 29. This is the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. Central bankers didn’t have this data during voting, which may be one reason they decided against adjusting the federal funds rate again quite yet.

If this week’s PCE data shows inflation rising, mortgage rates will probably go up over the next few weeks as lenders look to protect their investment against a weakening dollar. Rising inflation also bolsters the case for a rate hike at the central bankers’ next meeting; according to the futures traders behind CME FedWatch, there’s a very good chance that the Fed will announce an increase on Dec. 9.

And there is reason to think that PCE will show growing inflation. September’s monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures changes in prices of everyday goods and services, was released on Oct. 14 and showed annual inflation rising to 3.7%.

Of course, mortgage rates respond to all sorts of things. Oil prices, the bond market, global and national events — any number of hard-to-predict happenings could swing rates in the coming days and weeks. But if market analysts dig their heels into the idea of a December rate hike from the Fed, you should probably prepare for higher mortgage rates in November.

So far, 30-year mortgage rates are averaging 7.3% for October, compared with September’s average of 6.98%. On this trajectory, it’s conceivable that we could see rates hit 7.5% this year — a monthly average we haven’t seen since October 2023.

If and when the Fed does raise the federal funds rate again, it will be meant as a temporary treatment for overheated inflation.

Think of it as bitter medicine: It might be tough to swallow, but getting inflation under control actually paves the way for lower rates down the line. Moderating inflation could also lead to lower prices on essential goods that have been eating away at the prospective home buyer’s wallet, freeing up more cash for your monthly mortgage payment.

#3106. My Top 3 AI Stock Picks for November

2026 is coming to a close, but that doesn't mean investors should ignore the remaining months. In fact, November averages the highest S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%) monthly returns of any month. Now, whether this will hold in 2026 is still a mystery, but I believe there are several attractive stocks that investors should consider buying at today's levels.

At the top of my shopping list are Nvidia (NVDA +1.60%), Micron (MU -1.28%), and Broadcom (AVGO +1.06%). All three of these companies have deep roots in the AI build-out, and each looks like a smart buy right now.

All three of these stocks are central pieces of the AI build-out.

Nvidia makes the world's leading AI computing units. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) have become the industry standard for AI computing, and every other computing unit is compared to their price and performance. Nvidia has been the top AI investment since the AI build-out kicked off in 2023, yet 2026 hasn't been its best year, at least from a stock perspective. Nvidia has delivered incredible growth, with it reporting a 106% growth rate last quarter. The future is also bright, because Nvidia informed investors that 2027's revenue growth will be about 70%. Those are strong future projections and make Nvidia a smart stock to invest in now.

Broadcom is an Nvidia challenger. While Nvidia's GPUs excel in just about any situation, Broadcom is taking a different approach to AI computing. It's working directly with AI hyperscalers to design computing units tailored to their workloads. This allows its custom AI chips to outperform Nvidia GPUs in these scenarios and drives down usage costs.

While not every application can use a custom AI chip, a growing number of them can, and Broadcom expects to deliver monster growth over the next few years. For 2026, it expects AI semiconductor revenue to be about $58 billion. That figure will double to $115 billion in 2027, and $230 billion in 2028. That's huge growth in the next few years, and shareholders should see massive gains in the near future.

Both Broadcom's and Nvidia's computing units require memory chips inside them to function properly, and one of the biggest manufacturers of those is Micron. The memory chip industry came under scrutiny in 2026, as it didn't have enough supply to meet demand. It's not going to get any better, as Micron's CEO noted that market conditions will likely get tighter in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026.

While that's not great news for its clients, it's great news for Micron, and as a result, its investors. Micron will likely continue to experience huge revenue and earnings growth over the next few years as the AI build-out stays intense. Even after the AI build-out is wrapped up, Micron has now started to get its clients to sign supply agreements that will decrease the severity of any market downturns. This is great for Micron's future and will likely lead to strong performance.

But just how good of a return can investors expect?

Micron has already entered fiscal year 2027, so I'll value the stock using its forward earnings.

MU PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts. P/E = price-to-earnings.

At just 5.5 times forward earnings, Micron is a dirt cheap stock and primed to soar. If it hits expectations and rises to 15 times trailing earnings, that would indicate about a triple for the stock.

Nvidia and Broadcom aren't as cheap as Micron, but they're still very attractive. When next year's earnings estimates are used, Nvidia trades for just 13.5 times next year's earnings, while Broadcom is at 18.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

That means not a lot of 2027's growth has been priced into these two stocks, which means there could be a huge end-of-year rally for them.

As a result, November is shaping up to be a great month to buy these three AI stocks.

JetBlue's seat selection policy is based on the type of fare, so include the selection fee when comparing prices.

Airline miles, hotel points, travel insurance

JetBlue Airways charges more for seat selection than any other major U.S. airline, according to a NerdWallet analysis, so it pays to know when you can pick a seat for free.

The airline offers several seat options, including standard economy seats, extra-legroom seats and lie-flat Mint suites. But whether you can select a seat for free depends on the type of seat and fare you book, as well as whether you have Mosaic elite status.

Here’s what to know about JetBlue seat selection, including the different seat types, how much seat selection costs and when you can choose a seat for free.

JetBlue offers several onboard experiences, ranging from standard economy to lie-flat business-class seats.

JetBlue’s standard economy product is called Main, and there are three types of seats in this cabin.

Main: Economy seats throughout the Main cabin. These seats may be complimentary, depending on the fare type chosen.

Main Preferred: Economy seats located closer to the front of the cabin. They cost extra.

Extra Legroom: Seats with additional legroom that are located over the wing, in front of the Main Preferred seats. These seats also cost extra.

All Main cabin passengers receive complimentary snacks, drinks and Wi-Fi. Each seat also offers an entertainment screen with live television and movies.

EvenMore is JetBlue’s premium economy experience, and the seats are located in front of the Main cabin. These seats offer up to 38 inches of legroom and include priority boarding, priority security (at select airports) and dedicated overhead bin space.

Travelers receive three complimentary alcoholic drinks, unlimited nonalcoholic drinks and snacks, along with free Wi-Fi and a seatback entertainment screen with movies and live TV.

BlueFirst is JetBlue’s new domestic first class, which is expected to start flying on Dec. 8, 2026, on non-Mint aircraft and routes.

Adding a domestic first class product allows JetBlue to better compete for travelers who prefer to fly first class within the U.S., a market currently served by American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

JetBlue’s premium business class experience is called Mint, and it is available on select domestic and international routes.

The front row of the cabin also includes Mint Studios, which offer even more space than a standard Mint Suite. Mint Studios also have a large 22-inch television screen, a mirrored vanity, additional storage and a guest seat that can accommodate another Mint passenger during flight.

If a Mint Studio seat is available, it will be displayed on the airplane seat map.

The Mint travel experience also includes a dedicated check-in desk, lounge access (except with Mint Base fares), priority boarding, priority baggage and two checked bags (one with Mint Base fare).

» Learn more: JetBlue boarding groups explained

JetBlue offers three fare categories: Base, Standard and Flex. The table below shows how the categories compare in terms of flexibility.

Base fares are the most affordable but the least flexible.

Main Base fares do not include complimentary seat selection, but travelers can purchase a seat at any time. Those with an EvenMore Base fare can select a seat for free, but only at check-in. If a seat isn’t chosen, JetBlue will assign one automatically before departure. (BlueFirst Base fares include free seat selection only within 24 hours of departure.)

Comparatively, Standard and Flex fares include complimentary seat selection. This also applies to Mint, except for the new Mint Base fare, which charges for advance seat selection; complimentary seat selection is included only with Mint or Mint Flex tickets. Passengers who want to select a Mint Studio will need to pay extra, and the cost of the seat varies. In an October 2026 sample search for a flight from New York to Paris, a Mint Studio upgrade cost an additional $299 on top of the Mint fare.

Seat selection fees vary among airlines. To get an idea of what passengers can expect to pay, NerdWallet analyzed seat selection fees across major U.S. airlines and found that JetBlue had the highest average one-way seat selection fee at $73.

» Learn more: Airlines with the best (and worst) fees in 2026

JetBlue’s elite status is called Mosaic, and there are four tiers, ranging from Mosaic 1 to Mosaic 4. Mosaic members receive complimentary access to certain upgraded seats, with the benefits depending on their status level.

All Mosaic members, plus JetBlue Premier Card holders who book with their card, can get complimentary space-available upgrades to BlueFirst for themselves and one companion. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares aren't eligible.

Main Base fares are excluded from complimentary seat selection benefits, regardless of Mosaic status.

All Mosaic members receive complimentary access to Main Preferred seating, but EvenMore benefits vary by status level. Mosaic 1 members can select EvenMore seats for free starting 36 hours before departure for themselves and up to two companions, while Mosaic 2 and above can select them at booking. Mosaic 3 and 4 members can extend this benefit to up to four companions.

Mosaic 3 and 4 members receive Premium Upgrade Certificates, and starting Feb. 1, 2027, Mosaic 2 members can choose one through Perks You Pick. Mosaic 4 members earn 2 additional certificates for every 100 Tiles earned beyond the Mosaic 4 threshold. Certificates can be used to upgrade eligible Main or EvenMore fares to Mint or BlueFirst (once it starts flying).

» Learn more: JetBlue Mint: your guide to flying business class

You can select a seat during the booking process, or after, through JetBlue’s website or mobile app. During booking, you’ll first choose your fare type (Base, Standard or Flex), which determines whether complimentary seat selection is included.

After you’ve selected the flight, you’ll see a seat map displayed with the available seats and any applicable fees. For example, passengers who purchase a Main fare can choose eligible Main seats for free but will see prices for upgraded seats.

If you purchase a Main Base fare, all advance seat selections will include an additional fee. Mint passengers can select an available Mint Suite at no additional cost or pay extra for an available Mint Studio.

» Learn more: How to navigate costly airline seat selection fees

#3104. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

#3103. Buy, Sell, or Hold Alphabet Stock After Its $505 Billion Meltdown?

Alphabet (GOOG +1.80%) (GOOGL +2.16%) fell 12.6% last Thursday, bringing its market cap down $505 billion in a single session.

Alphabet now has a negative year-to-date return and is down 30.5% from its all-time high.

Here's why investors are reacting so negatively to Alphabet's third-quarter results, and if the sell-off is a buying opportunity for the communication services stock.

At first glance, Alphabet's results were excellent. Revenue jumped 25% year-over-year to $128 billion, giving Alphabet a half-trillion annual run rate. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, and operating income shot up a staggering 30%.

What investors didn't like, however, was that capital expenditures (capex) skyrocketed 114% to $51.36 billion, pushing Alphabet's free cash flow (FCF) in the quarter down to a negative $9.07 billion. In the third quarter of 2025, Alphabet's FCF was $24.46 billion. The cash burn will get worse before it gets better. On its Q3 earnings call, Alphabet said it expects full-year 2026 capex to be $195 to $205 billion and capex to increase significantly in 2027.

Alphabet turning FCF-negative has impacts on its capital return program and balance sheet. In the first three quarters of 2025, Alphabet spent $39.81 billion on stock purchases. Through Sept. 30, 2026, year-to-date buybacks have been $0. As of Dec. 31, 2025, Alphabet had $46.55 billion in long-term debt. As of Sept. 30, 2026, its long-term debt jumped to $125.5 billion -- which is a red flag, considering interest rates are rising and will make the cost of taking on additional debt even more expensive.

Alphabet has been taking on debt and issuing stock to fund its artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. During the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Alphabet issued 12 million shares of Class A stock and 24 million shares of Class C stock for a combined net proceeds of $12.4 billion, with $27.6 billion remaining for future issuance.

So in the span of just one year, Alphabet has gone from managing its AI ramp-up with FCF while still reducing its share count throughout buybacks to turning FCF negative, taking on debt, and diluting shareholders.

The leverage and lack of FCF put significant pressure on Alphabet to prove to investors that it is getting a good return on its spending. And to be fair, there are already many positive signs -- including excellent Gemini traction, positive updates with self-driving car company Waymo, and a boom in Google Cloud. But part of the surge in Google Cloud revenue is due to one-time chip sales, as Alphabet includes sales of its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) chips under its Google Cloud revenue.

Google Search revenue was up 12% year-over-year, and YouTube ads revenue increased 9.2% -- which isn't bad but, it's a slowdown compared to Q3 2025 when Google Search revenue increased 14.5% and, YouTube ads jumped 15% year-over-year.

Alphabet is at a crossroads. Investors who don't believe in the payoff of its record capex may choose to sell the stock. Others who are skeptical but want to see how things play out may simply want to hold. I think Alphabet is misunderstood and a high conviction buy.

Operationally, Alphabet is at the top of its game -- with 32% operating margins in its latest quarter. On the earnings call, Alphabet said that around 65% of capex is in technology infrastructure like servers and networking equipment, which generally have useful lives of six years, and the remaining 35% is for data centers with useful lives ranging from seven to 40 years. Meaning that those investments aren't contributing to Alphabet's near-term results, but they will benefit the company over the long term.

Of all the hyperscalers, Alphabet is arguably the best positioned to invest aggressively in AI because it controls almost every layer of the AI ecosystem. It partners with Broadcom to manufacture TPUs, which have proven excellent for AI training and inference. As mentioned, Alphabet isn't just using TPUs in-house, but is now also selling them to third parties, which is contributing to Google Cloud revenue. In April, Anthropic expanded its partnership with Google and Broadcom for multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity. That same month, Broadcom and Google entered into a long-term TPU agreement through 2031.

In addition to its TPU boost, Google Cloud is now taking market share from Amazon and Microsoft in the cloud computing industry. Alphabet also has Gemini, powered by Google DeepMind, which is a legitimate heavyweight in frontier models alongside Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's ChatGPT, and xAI's Grok, owned by Space Exploration Technologies.

And to top it all off, Alphabet has consumer and enterprise apps in Gemini, Google Search, Android, and YouTube, and is a massive investor in physical AI through Waymo.

Alphabet's results look bad now because it's in the midst of a historic AI spending build-out, but it's not just throwing money at ideas and hoping it sticks. Rather, it has multiple levers to pull to monetize AI.

For that reason, I think Alphabet stands out as arguably one of the best AI stocks for patient long-term investors to buy now. But I could also see the sell-off worsening before it gets better, given Alphabet's accelerated cash burn.

TL;DR: Average mortgage interest rates jumped today.

If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.32% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 22 basis points higher than yesterday and 24 basis points higher than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This comes after the Federal Reserve announced central bankers’ decision to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday. While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, the federal funds rate is one factor that moves them. Last month, when markets began pricing in a possible federal funds rate increase, mortgage rates spiked.

The next Fed meeting isn’t until December, so any rate movement in the next week will likely stem from other factors, like the upcoming jobs report. For more on that, read on.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Traders expected that the Fed would vote to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday, so that wasn’t much of a factor for mortgage lenders as they set rates.

In his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that September’s rate increase is “starting to work some” toward moving inflation down to the Fed's 2% goal, but that central bankers don't have any firm conclusions yet. He also acknowledged that the Fed’s monetary policy actions hadn’t achieved price stability yet, but that they’re “working on it.”

This hints that if inflation data continues to trend upward, central bankers might raise the federal funds rate again at their December 8-9 meeting.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, dropped this morning — a day too late for central bankers to consider it in their decision-making process.

The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on November 25.

Next week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out Friday, Nov.6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build an even stronger case for the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again in December, because it would suggest that the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.82% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3101. United Parcel Service's Earnings Declined in Q3. Is the Dividend Still Safe?

Logistics giant United Parcel Service (UPS +1.62%) pays an attractive dividend that yields around 6.1%. That's far higher than the S&P 500 average of just 1.1% right now. Many investors, however, may be worried that its payout may not be sustainable given the current economic challenges and the company's underwhelming financials.

Last week, UPS released its latest earnings numbers for the third quarter, and its bottom line declined on a year-over-year basis. Does this mean its dividend isn't safe?

For the three-month period ending Sept. 30, UPS reported consolidated revenue of $22.9 billion, which rose by nearly 7% year over year. But of key concern for investors is the bottom line, where the shipping company's diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $1.37, down from $1.55 in the prior-year period. UPS did, however, incur $130 million in after-tax costs related to its transformation strategy as well as $182 million in goodwill impairment. On an adjusted basis, its EPS was $1.69.

Currently, the company's quarterly dividend is $1.64, which suggests that the payout may be barely sustainable given its most recent numbers.

Another way to evaluate the dividend is by looking at free cash flow, which is how much money the company is bringing in after factoring in its capital expenditures. At $4.2 billion over the past nine months, that averages out to $1.4 billion on a quarterly basis -- right around how much it pays in dividends.

Once again, there's a buffer there, but a fairly slim one.

A dividend cut doesn't look to be around the corner for UPS, but given the challenging economic conditions due to rising oil prices and higher inflation, it's possible that UPS' numbers deteriorate in future quarters. Cutting the dividend may be a necessary move in the near term to improve its bottom line, and that's why I wouldn't rely on its payout. When a company is in the midst of a transition and incurring charges related to it, the dividend it pays can be a sensitive area for management. While it doesn't want to disrupt it, the recurring payout can prove to be burdensome.

This year, UPS stock has risen by 9%, but I wouldn't rush to buy it given that its numbers don't look all that great, at a time when economic conditions may not be getting better down the road. While it can still be a good long-term investment, I think there are better dividend stocks available for investors.

#3098. ​The End Of Software Archaeology: Why The Old Rules Of System Modernization No Longer Apply

Kostiantyn Gitko is the CEO of Devox Software, specializing in AI-native transformation and scaling complex systems for global enterprises.

​I never would have thought that my childhood dream of becoming an archaeologist would have so much in common with what I do today. Even at age five, I was fascinated by the idea that a dusty, bearded archaeologist armed with a pickax and a shovel could look at an empty field and somehow know that an entire ancient city might lie beneath it. I was ready to walk miles through the desert for that kind of adventure. Today, I have a beard, and I run an IT company.

In programming, I found that same sense of discovery in legacy-heavy codebases. In large systems, the real cost of legacy often comes from more than the old code itself.

The longer a system has been around, the more unwritten decisions pile up around its older modules: why someone chose a particular approach in the first place or what trade-offs were made to meet a deadline. Beyond that, over the years, developers made assumptions about what the system could and couldn’t do. Those assumptions made sense at the time, but many are no longer valid given today’s technology.

​Unfortunately, that uncertainty creates problems that surface precisely when a company becomes successful, sometimes forcing it to pause marketing campaigns because its systems can’t keep up with demand. And the problem may have little to do with code quality. The code itself may have been perfectly good for its time; the real issue may lie in the legacy architecture, something I’ve seen firsthand many times.​

Just as archaeologists examine artifacts in the context of the layers around them, we need to understand legacy systems in the context of how they’ve evolved over time. A 1998 system is rarely a “1998 system”: It may contain a 1998 core, a compliance rule added in 2007, a workaround introduced after a 2014 incident, a 2019 API and a 2026 AI integration. A strange-looking rule may trace back to a regulation from years earlier. Fundamentally, those layers also preserve the business’s history.​

Interestingly, when it comes to modernization risk, age can be a red herring. A system can run reliably for 15 years while the business gradually adapts its processes to work around the system’s limitations. For instance, two modules may never call one another directly and still be tightly coupled through a shared table, or a three-year-old patch that tied five systems together turns out to be the dangerous one. That’s the trap.​

​So where do we start digging? For decades, legacy modernization meant mapping the system by hand: following calls from module to module to find out what a click sets in motion and where the data ends up. There was a lot to unearth. Field studies before AI found that developers spent 58% to 70% of their time trying to understand existing code and roughly 5% changing it. First dig, then map.​​

But now, with artificial intelligence, we can start with a map and dig into the areas we still don’t fully understand. In practice, AI usually builds on existing code-analysis tools that show which systems read and modify shared data, but the intelligent layer brings it all together into something closer to a map of the system. A well-engineered, secure AI setup can work through mountains of data and uncover hidden microconnections that algorithmic non-AI tools can miss because they only see what they’re built to find.​​

Together, these sources help produce a much more detailed dependency graph compared to traditional tools. An AI-enhanced dependency graph works like a street map of the system. It shows what relies on what and how far the impact of a change may spread, which also reveals where the architecture is vulnerable. A process tree takes this a step further, adding business context by showing how a component fits into day-to-day operations.​

Ultimately, AI can help make legacy systems less of a black box by answering questions like:

• What do we need to modernize first, and what can we leave alone? Do we need to invest in testing or anything else before we start?

• How much faster can we ship new features once we know what depends on what?

• Where will the system likely start to struggle as we grow?

• What depends on this component, and what else could break if we change it?

• How much time and money can we save by catching problems before we start?

If several critical processes depend on one component, start there, and, if it is needed, decouple it. Otherwise, you could spend millions rebuilding the system—and bring all its old problems with new technology. On the flip side, not every legacy system needs a rewrite. If the core works reliably, AI can help teams understand it, and modernization can add what’s missing. Keeping it may make better business sense.

Perhaps most importantly, AI can help senior engineers see where to dig and where to tread carefully. Where the code, runtime behavior and documentation don’t line up, they know to take a closer look. AI’s ability to analyze code and reconstruct its logic makes it possible to turn years of undocumented code into usable, careful documentation.​

Finally, don’t put the map away after the initial analysis. My team keeps this map in sync with the code and the way the system actually runs, so we always have an up-to-date picture of how the technology supports the business.​​

​Even the most experienced archaeologist can only uncover so much with a shovel. New technologies like ground-penetrating radar have extended that reach, helping researchers identify patterns and investigate areas they might otherwise overlook. AI offers a similar opportunity in enterprise IT.​

Fascinatingly (and yes, I confess I still geek out over archaeology news), AI has already transformed actual archaeology, too: Robotic systems now process radar data to build 3D subsurface models without digging a single trench. What we are seeing in enterprise IT today is a remarkably similar story, with AI giving us new ways to understand even the most complex legacy systems.​​

#3097. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3094. The Compliance Challenge Has Become An Engineering Problem. AI Can Help You Solve It

Danny Fields, Chief Technology and Customer Operations Officer Avalara, an agentic AI leader in global tax and compliance.

​When I talk to technology leaders about global trade compliance, I tend to get one of two responses. Either their business has already faced disruption—shipments held at customs, a refund claim that cascaded through the financials, a market entry delayed by months because the regulatory environment shifted—and they’ve been handed a mandate to make sure it doesn’t happen again. Or they haven’t, and the mandate has arrived anyway.

Either way, the message is the same: Compliance is no longer a problem that finance teams can manage through spreadsheets and experience. It’s now an engineering problem that can be solved with AI.

The volume, velocity and interconnectedness of global regulatory change has crossed a threshold where human experience alone can no longer keep pace. Tariff schedules update. HS classification rules shift. There were more than 417,000 taxability updates across the U.S. and Canada alone in 2025, according to the Avalara Tax Changes 2026 Midyear Update.

Then add in the transactions themselves subject to those changes. Over five days of Cyber Week last year, we processed 1.14 billion API calls, representing $187 billion in tax transactions and peaking at 9,124 transactions per second. The moment a compliance decision needs to be made faster than a person can make it, at a scale no team can match, across a level of complexity no spreadsheet can model, is when you’ve crossed from a compliance problem into a systems architecture problem.

The pace of change is what makes this so urgent. This year alone, companies have had to navigate legal challenges to tariff policies, fluctuating duties across major trade corridors and renewed threats of retaliatory tariffs across global markets, all while managing geopolitical uncertainty that has fundamentally changed how boards think about international growth. According to our recent data, 83% of business leaders said their cross-border operations are more complex than they were just 12 months ago.

What concerns me from a systems perspective isn’t the pace of change itself, but what happens downstream when systems can’t keep up. Every regulatory update ripples through thousands of transactions simultaneously. Any delay in implementing that change creates compliance exposure that cascades: shipment holds, customs penalties, disruptions that travel up the supply chain and into the P&L. It’s essentially a data latency problem.

Consider what this means in practice for classification alone. The World Customs Organization updates Harmonized System (HS) codes on a five-year cycle, but country-specific tariff rates tied to those codes can change multiple times a year, and in the current environment, they are.

An AI system trained on a comprehensive classification database and updated continuously can absorb a regulatory change and propagate it across an entire product catalog in minutes. A human team cannot. AI-based classification systems now draw on databases of millions of real-world product classifications. At this scale and pace of change, I believe AI is the only viable architecture for the problem.

In fact, nearly 40% of businesses we surveyed said they’ve delayed expansion specifically because of regulatory uncertainty. Companies that should be growing aren’t because their systems weren’t built to handle the pace. When compliance becomes a growth constraint, that’s the moment technology leaders have to step up.

The old model assumes a regulatory environment that is stable enough to configure once and revisit quarterly. It’s not. The companies getting this right are building systems designed from the ground up for constant change. That means a few things in practice:

• Real-Time Regulatory Ingestion: Your compliance systems need to consume regulatory changes as they happen, not after a quarterly review cycle. This requires API-connected content pipelines that surface rate changes, classification updates and policy shifts at the moment they’re published, not after they’ve created exposure.

• Agentic Compliance Workflows: This is where I think the most interesting engineering work is happening right now. Rather than building systems to alert human reviewers of compliance changes, the more powerful architecture would be one where AI agents identify the change, assess the impact across transaction data and implement required adjustments—with human review of edge cases.

• Transparency And Traceability By Design: Audit readiness is often an afterthought in system design, bolted on after the fact. The better approach is to build traceability into the core data model so every compliance decision has a logged chain of evidence: what changed, when it changed, what transactions it affected and what the system did in response.

According to our data, nearly half of U.S. businesses are already using AI as a core component of their cross-border risk management. But there’s a significant laggard population, with 13% of organizations not yet using AI for compliance at all. That gap is going to widen. The companies investing now in adaptive infrastructure are building a structural advantage, while others are accumulating a compliance debt that will eventually come due.

For a long time, compliance has been treated as finance’s problem. The tools were built for tax professionals and the processes were designed around human expertise, not system architecture. But that meant that when regulatory volatility spiked, as it unmistakably has, the systems weren’t ready.

Today, however, compliance needs the expertise of technology leaders, not to replace tax expertise, but to engineer the infrastructure that makes tax expertise scalable. A tax professional who understands customs classification can’t manually review 10,000 SKUs every time a tariff schedule changes. But a well-architected system with AI-assisted classification, real-time rate feeds and agent-driven change management can. That combination creates compliance certainty at velocity.

More than half of global respondents in Avalara’s research said that tariffs and changing duties have created the greatest operational burden in recent times for their businesses. The path forward is building systems that turn complexity into a managed, data-driven process, treating AI as production infrastructure. By turning complexity into a managed, data-driven process, organizations can stay ahead of risk, maintain consistent compliance and position themselves to grow confidently across borders. The time to build it is now.

#3093. The Biggest Crypto Hack in History Just Happened. Here's What the $6.3 Billion Breach Means for the Crypto Market.

Batten down the hatches, because trouble is here. Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, said on the evening of Oct. 29 that hackers had stolen about $6.3 billion from its coffers. That means it just experienced the biggest crypto hack in history, and perhaps even the biggest heist in history, period.

The market's response has been predictably sour. Bitcoin (BTC -0.28%) lost 5.6% within 24 hours of the hack being announced, while BNB (BNB -1.75%), the native coin of the Binance-linked BNB Chain, fell 6.2%.

The damage to coin prices may not be over. So what comes next for the crypto market?

In terms of the immediate market outlook, the direct losses from the hack already appear covered.

Binance had a rainy-day fund worth around $1 billion before this, and its management also says it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own capital to restore any affected customer balances, so it's reasonable to expect that all affected users will likely be made whole.

Another critical piece of context is that crypto hacks and theft are, unfortunately, as old as the asset class itself, and actually very common.

In 2011, hackers stole approximately 25,000 BTC from the Mt. Gox exchange, which at the time was the biggest. More than $3.3 billion was lost to hacks, exploits, and scams in 2025, and more than $8.7 billion has been lost in 2026 so far, including the Binance hack.

In light of 2025's toll and the advent of advanced artificial intelligence systems that streamline both cyber intrusion and cyber defense, the industry's responsiveness to these threats is improving rapidly. Tether froze more than $1.5 billion of its USDT stablecoin within an hour of the Binance hack being detected, and Circle Internet Group also froze $800 million of its USD Coin tied to the theft in the same period. This means the hackers couldn't exfiltrate the funds represented by those stablecoins for laundering and retention.

The major blockchains themselves continued to work as intended throughout the hack and afterward. While the attackers used a feature from a 2025 Ethereum (ETH +1.09%) upgrade to help empty certain Binance wallets, the trick only worked because they had first broken into Binance's own systems. So the blockchains themselves weren't breached.

The Binance hack is one more piece of evidence that the crypto market is on the front lines of the global cybersecurity crisis that's being fueled (and also mitigated) by AI. More serious breaches are inevitable and imminent.

The crypto industry will now, in all probability, accelerate its ongoing shift toward prioritizing cybersecurity investments to harden blockchains, wallet applications, decentralized finance (DeFi) projects, and centralized exchanges. Generally speaking, the biggest chains like Ethereum and Bitcoin had already striven to meet high standards of cybersecurity practices before this latest incident, and their hardening efforts will likely intensify and subsequently serve as models for smaller players to emulate. That does not mean that investors can relax just yet, as widespread theft could still affect them if their coins are not stored securely.

For most people, the simplest approach that provides the very highest level of security is to hold their crypto via a spot exchange-traded fund (ETF), which delegates the safe custody of the coins to a deep-pocketed asset manager that handles cybersecurity on their behalf. For example, the iShares Bitcoin Trust, the market's largest spot Bitcoin ETF, relies on its custodian, Coinbase Global, which keeps the keys in cold storage (offline), in accounts segregated from the custodian's own assets.

If you'd rather hold your coins more directly, use a large U.S.-regulated crypto exchange that discloses its custody practices. Coinbase, for instance, says that it aims to hold no more than 2% of its custodied assets in hot (online) wallets. Its crypto isn't government-insured, though, so even holding your crypto on an exchange isn't risk-free.

What is especially risky right now is self-custodying your coins, especially if you're not highly technical. Common wallet applications are likely to get hacked, and depending on how you store your cryptocurrency, it may then be possible to drain investors' funds.

The crypto market will likely recover from the dip caused by the Binance hack over time, as it has historically done after major hacks in the past.

But when it comes to which coins will recover the fastest and perhaps grow the most, I bet it'll be the projects most serious about cybersecurity leading the pack.

Alex Carchidi has positions in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and iShares Bitcoin Trust. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin, Ethereum, and iShares Bitcoin Trust. The Motley Fool recommends BNB and Coinbase Global. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3089. The Real Problem With Your CX AI Strategy Isn't Automation—It's The Mix

Niranjan Virjayaragavan is the Chief Technology Officer at Five9, an open cloud platform for customer experience.

Most organizations will tell you their customer experience (CX) AI strategy is working, and the numbers back them up.​​

A Gartner survey of service and support leaders found AI spending is up 38% while overall service budgets grew just 2%, a level of commitment that would have sounded implausible three years ago. But that measurement covers only half the question. It shows how aggressively organizations are investing in AI and almost nothing about how well AI and humans work the same queue together, which is the part many organizations haven’t engineered for at all. ​

That’s the real problem hiding underneath years of AI adoption headlines. The industry keeps asking how to automate more, when an equally consequential question is how to get the right mix of human and AI in interactions that need both.

Automation and collaboration aren’t the same investment; optimizing hard for one doesn’t get you the other for free. An organization can hit every automation target and still hand customers off to confused, underinformed agents every day, which is another way of saying the industry is measuring half the problem.

The pace of automation explains why the mix got overlooked. Gartner projects that by 2029, 80% of common customer service interactions will be handled by agentic AI, a shift most industries would take decades to absorb, compressed into a few years by real business pressure. Ninety-one percent of customer service leaders report pressure from senior leadership to implement AI, making automation more of an executive mandate than a strategic choice.

Mandates produce scoreboards, and the AI scoreboard in CX has almost always been “how much did we automate?” It’s an easy number to report up: interactions deflected, cost per contact down and headcount reallocated. What it doesn’t capture is what happens when AI can’t fully resolve alone, where the human half of the mix matters most. A virtual agent that hits an impressive containment number by refusing to escalate isn’t succeeding; it’s just deferring the cost.

Scores go up quarterly while quietly making the job harder for whoever’s left handling what AI couldn’t resolve. If the easy interactions get faster and the leftover ones get more complex and emotionally charged, an organization measuring only the aggregate has no way of seeing what’s “AI success” and where CX is breaking down. The result: AI strategies that look excellent on the chosen scorecard and remain untested on the one that wasn’t.

That gap shows up in deployments that automated first and designed the mix second. Three failure points account for most of it.​

First, context doesn’t survive the handoff. AI knows what the customer said, why they called and what it already tried, but the human agent who picks up next often knows none of that. In my company’s 2026 survey, 34% of leaders said context or data gets lost when a conversation switches channels. A transcript records what was said, not what’s already resolved, which is why a caller has to verify their identity with the AI and the human agent—a duplicate created by the architecture. It’s the most visible failure because the customer feels it directly, undoing whatever goodwill the automation built.

Second is escalation logic that was never defined. Many organizations can’t say when AI should hand off or keep working a problem. Our report found 37% of business leaders experience challenges such as agents lacking visibility into the prior AI interaction even after a transfer, so the agent starts partially blind by design, not by accident. Without an explicit rule, escalation happens inconsistently: sometimes too early, when AI could have resolved things itself, and sometimes too late, after a frustrated customer has already tried repeatedly to reach a human.​​

Third is a supervisor who can’t see the whole queue as one. Metrigy reports 66% of companies either run on a single-server hosted platform managed by a third-party or on-premises infrastructure rather than cloud-native platforms, a reasonable proxy for how many still lack a real-time, unified view spanning human and AI-handled interactions. Most supervisors are stitching together two separate systems mentally, letting problems go unnoticed until a customer complains.

Agents feel that gap first, long before it shows up in a dashboard. A 2026 NYU Tandon and Cornell Tech study found the strongest predictors of a stress spike were long calls with unresolved problems and calls requiring repeated explanations, a fair description of the hardest, least-prepared-for interactions from the inside.

This isn’t a model problem; it’s a design problem. The shift that matters is to stop treating escalation as a single handoff where AI exits and a human starts cold. Design instead for AI that stays present for the full interaction, with humans stepping in where needed. I’ve found that five principles make that work:

1. Context That Travels: What the customer asked, what’s verified and what AI already tried should follow the interaction so no one needs to repeat themselves.

2. Routing By Interaction Type: The human-to-AI ratio shouldn’t be uniform. A password reset and a billing dispute with an upset customer call for different mixes, so set the ratio deliberately for each.

3. Confidence-Based Escalation: Let real-time confidence determine how many attempts AI makes before a person joins, with explicit, auditable thresholds; then, tighten them for high-stakes or regulated issues.

4. AI That Never Fully Steps Aside: While the human handles the judgment call, AI should keep working in the background, pulling records and drafting notes, then picking the thread back up when the human’s part is done.

5. One View Of The Queue: Supervisors should see quality and outcomes across human and AI-handled interactions together.

To find where your mix is breaking, use the data you already have. Pull 50 escalated interactions and count how often customers repeated themselves. Compare containment rates with repeat contacts, since high containment alongside high repeat contact likely means AI is deferring cost, not resolving issues.

The contact centers that are successful won’t be the ones with the highest automation numbers. They’ll be the ones that build seamless coexistence of agentic and human-supported experiences—the difference customers notice and agents feel every time they pick up the phone.​

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3087. What Healthcare’s AI Readiness Gap Reveals About The Next Phase Of Adoption

Mark Thomas, Chief Technology Officer, MRO.

​AI is becoming more embedded in healthcare every day. As health systems explore ways to apply AI across a growing range of functions, the right foundation becomes more important.​

This is especially critical in healthcare quality. Quality operations rely on clinical context, accurate data and careful interpretation. If AI is being used to abstract clinical data, support quality reporting or measure performance, it needs to meet a high bar for accuracy, transparency and accountability.​

To understand how healthcare organizations are approaching AI adoption in quality, my company recently surveyed hospital and health system quality leaders about their current use of AI in quality operations. The results point to a gap between AI enthusiasm and organizational readiness. Nearly nine in 10 respondents (88%) are “interested in using AI in healthcare quality operations,” yet only 23% consider their organizations “very ready to adopt it.”​ This finding is consistent with a 2025 survey from Nordic and Modern Healthcare, which reported a large disconnect between healthcare executives’ confidence in their organization’s AI readiness and how prepared those organizations actually were.

It’s clear that while interest in AI is widespread, many organizations still need to put the policies, processes and infrastructure in place to create the foundation AI needs for success.

Our survey found that a quarter of respondents have already implemented AI in quality operations, and another 30% are piloting, testing or evaluating AI solutions.​

Quality leaders are most interested in using AI to help solve practical problems. The top motivation for using AI in quality was enhancing efficiency, cited by 57% of respondents. Deloitte’s latest global survey of healthcare executives points to the same priority: Operational efficiency ranked as AI’s most valuable use case in 2026. As for what specific quality functions respondents were most interested in supporting with AI, our survey found that the areas of greatest interest were quality or performance improvement, data analysis, data validation and quality assurance and clinical data abstraction.​

Many of these uses require significant clinical judgment. Consider clinical data abstraction, for example. AI can efficiently identify inconsistencies across large volumes of data, saving time and reducing manual effort. But flagging inconsistencies is only part of the job. Clinical data is highly nuanced and requires interpretation before it can be abstracted, making human expertise an important part of the process. Exploring AI for these types of tasks requires careful consideration of where AI can add value, where human judgment remains essential and how the two can work together effectively.​

That balance matters most as organizations consider expanding AI beyond pilots into broader quality operations. Respondents identified compliance concerns, trust in AI accuracy, costs and fragmented systems as their biggest barriers to AI adoption in quality.​

The survey also points to a gap in AI governance. Only a third of respondents said their organizations have formal, documented AI governance policies. A 2025 report from the Healthcare Financial Management Association and Eliciting Insights found a similar gap, noting that while most health systems used AI internally, just 18% had “a mature governance structure and fully formed AI strategy.” As adoption moves beyond experimentation, governance will become increasingly important to ensure organizations have a consistent approach to evaluating AI opportunities, managing risk, defining appropriate uses and monitoring performance.​

These challenges highlight the need for a thoughtful approach to AI adoption supported by the right infrastructure, processes and oversight.

Addressing the barriers to AI adoption starts with building the governance, people, systems and processes needed to use AI responsibly. Hospital and health system leaders can strengthen their readiness by focusing on a few key priorities.​

Organizations need clear policies for evaluating AI tools, approving use cases, managing data, monitoring performance and assigning accountability—but most organizations we surveyed don’t yet have these formal, documented policies in place. Quality, clinical, compliance and technology leaders should all have a role in developing these policies. Policies should also establish how organizations will protect data, manage vendor relationships and meet compliance requirements.

Human expertise is essential when AI is applied to work that requires clinical or quality judgment. AI can surface relevant information and suggest potential answers, but human experts should review that information and make the final determination. For example, at my company, we’ve built this directly into abstractors’ workflow: Every suggestion includes its source evidence, and a clinical expert must review and approve it before it counts.

Data integration and interoperability are major barriers to scaling AI solutions. Breaking down data silos and centralizing clinical data management through one enterprise platform gives AI access to the volume and consistency of data it needs to identify patterns and produce more useful outputs.

Our survey found that 83% of respondents use or are considering third-party AI solutions, whether on their own or in combination with internally developed solutions. When evaluating AI vendors, organizations should look for solutions that make outputs easy to understand and review, such as by showing supporting evidence and allowing users to accept, modify or reject an AI-generated result. Features like this bring greater visibility into AI decision-making and help build trust in its accuracy.

AI has massive potential to change how healthcare organizations manage quality. But because this work requires clinical context and judgment, organizations will need to be thoughtful about how they introduce and expand its use.​

The next phase of AI adoption will depend less on enthusiasm alone and more on organizational readiness. Healthcare organizations that establish clear governance, prioritize interoperability and maintain human oversight will be better positioned to move AI from isolated experiments into meaningful, scalable applications.​
