#3086. Beta Technologies Beat Archer and Joby to an FAA First. Here's Why I'd Still Rather Own Archer.

Not Joby Aviation, not Archer Aviation (ACHR +3.45%), but Beta Technologies (BETA +4.37%) gets bragging rights as the first electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) developer to secure Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) authorization to conduct demonstration flights with potential customers onboard.

That's a huge accomplishment. So why would I rather own Archer stock?

Beta Technologies is an aerospace company developing electric aircraft. Like Archer and Joby, Beta is building eVTOLs for commercial passenger services. Unlike the former two, however, which have electric air taxis at the heart of their ambitions, Beta is focusing on the nonpassenger transportation side of its business, like hauling cargo and medical supplies.

Beta is also building out a massive electric charging network across the U.S., which other eVTOL companies, like Archer, can use.

Admittedly, Beta hasn't received anywhere near as much attention as Archer and Joby, but that's been changing. On Oct. 21, the FAA announced it had granted Beta a first-of-its-kind airworthiness certificate for market surveys. With this certificate, Beta can now take prospective customers into the air -- that is, representatives from companies who might be interested in buying Beta's eVTOL.

This certificate doesn't allow Beta to take fare-paying passengers on air taxi rides (it still needs additional certificates to do that). But it does potentially open its business to buyers who might have hesitated to consider its aircraft without firsthand experience.

First, I don't want to diminish Beta's accomplishment. Obtaining this certificate is an exciting development for this company, and it's an accomplishment of which Archer is probably very envious. Indeed, in November 2024, in a commercialization update on X, Archer plainly listed something like it as the second step of its strategy: "Fly piloted market survey trips with Midnight carrying passengers on our first air taxi routes."

Still, if I had to choose between Beta and Archer today, I would lean toward the latter, largely because I think Archer's business model gives it more ways to profit directly from the (eventual) growth of passenger air taxi services.

For one, Beta does not want to operate an air taxi business. Instead, it wants to make money selling aircraft, batteries, charging equipment, and propulsion systems. While Archer also wants to sell aircraft, its focus is establishing a passenger service. This could, over the long run, become a much bigger opportunity. Indeed, in a 2021 report, analysts at Morgan Stanley estimated that passenger transportation from eVTOLs could become a roughly $3.7 trillion market by 2050. That would be an enormous opportunity for Archer, even if it takes decades to arrive.

To be fair, Beta can also benefit from that multitrillion-dollar opportunity by selling aircraft designed for passenger services. Still, given that Archer intends to manufacture aircraft and operate its own air taxi services, I think it has more ways to capitalize on that growth of passenger transportation.

But there's no reason why investors have to choose just one. Both Beta and Archer could find success in this nascent industry. For investors willing to tolerate the risks, owning a little of both could be a sensible way to bet on the future of eVTOLs. I still prefer Archer, but I wouldn't count Beta out.

Steven Porrello has positions in Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation. The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3084. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3080. Key-Person Risk: The Hidden Operating Dependency In Your Business

Anila is a fractional exec at opsbridge.io, helping scaling orgs restore ops discipline & clarity to improve margins & accelerate growth.

Every company I’ve worked with has a key person. Their name comes up whenever someone asks who knows how something works. Depending on the function, that person may be very senior or more junior; there’s no single title for them. It’s rarely about authority, but about what they know.

Most leaders call this a retention risk. They worry the person will leave, so they plan a raise, a new title, maybe even a retention bonus. Those aren’t bad ideas, but they miss the bigger issue. The problem was there long before anyone started worrying about retention. The company learned to run on one person’s memory, experience and judgment. That person probably didn’t choose this either; it just happened, one reasonable shortcut at a time.

So, the more useful question for leaders is, “Why does the business still need this one person for these things to work?”

Key-person risk stays hidden because, for a long time, it looks like strength. The person is fast, they’re right most of the time, customers ask for them by name, and when something is stuck, asking them is quicker than figuring out why or writing anything down. So, everyone keeps going to them, and every trip makes the next one more likely.

A couple of years in, you end up with a small group holding much of the real operating knowledge of the business, particularly the exceptions nobody else knows. Which customer gets special handling? Why does that billing concession exist? Which number in the report should you trust?

Almost none of it is written down because much of it was never really a formal decision. It was just a habit that worked...until the business grew around it.

The cost of this dependency rarely arrives as a crisis. More often, it becomes an invisible queue waiting for someone’s calendar. A question waits until they’re available. A customer issue sits until they can weigh in. Someone has most of the information but not the piece only they know. Eventually, that waiting becomes so normal that it stops looking like a delay and becomes the process. A process that should flow from one team to another now has a gate in the middle, though nobody intentionally designed it.

There is also another cost. The more people learn to check with the person who knows, the less opportunity they have to develop that judgment themselves. Asking becomes easier than learning. At that point, the organization isn’t just concentrating knowledge; it’s discouraging anyone else from building it, and that’s what makes this a leadership issue.​

Nobody designs this deliberately; it just evolves. As companies grow, especially at pace, shortcuts are useful. Asking the person who knows is faster than stopping to redesign a process. Letting one person handle an unusual customer exception is easier than writing down why it exists.

Each decision makes sense on its own, but the accumulated system doesn’t. Growth adds more customers, people, products and exceptions, but the knowledge underneath the business doesn’t always grow with it.

Here’s a simple way to see how exposed you are. I call it the two-week test:

• First, write down the 10 or 15 things your company cannot afford to get wrong: customer commitments, the release process, a large renewal, pricing, forecasting or whatever applies to your business.

• Next to each, put the name of the person it actually depends on. Not the name on the org chart or the person who technically owns the process. Put down the person you would really call if something went wrong.

• Then ask: “If this person were unreachable for two weeks, what would stop and what would keep running but quietly get worse?”

A few names will probably appear again and again. You may also find rows where nobody is quite sure whose name to put down. Both tell you something: repeated names show you where dependency has concentrated, and empty rows show you where ownership exists largely by assumption.

Now, look at why each person’s name is there. Do they have information nobody else has? Are they the person everyone trusts to have the answer? Do they hold a customer or supplier relationship that hasn’t been built beyond them? Or does the normal process work until something unusual happens, and then everybody calls them? Those are different dependencies and they require different fixes.

Once companies identify key-person risk, the instinct is often to document everything that person does. That helps, but it only gets you so far. Process documents describe a normal day, but what often makes the key person valuable is what they do on an abnormal one: when to bend the rule, when to escalate, what they check first and which apparently urgent issue can actually wait. That’s judgment, and judgment is harder to put into a flowchart.

Start with the last few times something went sideways and that person was called in. What did they notice? What did they ask? What did they decide, and why? Then put someone else alongside them the next time those decisions come up. The goal isn’t simply to transfer information; it’s to build the judgment to use it.

And sometimes, the answer isn’t another person at all. If somebody has become a permanent gate in a process, ask whether the gate still needs to exist, or whether what they know belongs in the process itself. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of time solving key-person risk by creating a second key person.

The two-week test isn’t really a list of people you can’t afford to lose. It’s a map of where your business still depends on what one or two people know to run it the way you expect. Run the test and look at the names, then look past them.

#3077. Marvell Technology vs. SK Hynix: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is driving massive demand for data center infrastructure, making it difficult for investors to choose the best winners. Deciding between Marvell Technology (MRVL -6.66%) and SK hynix (SKHY +2.32%) requires a closer look.

Marvell provides the networking and custom silicon brains that allow data to move efficiently, while SK Hynix supplies the high-speed memory required for heavy AI processing. Both companies occupy critical spots in the tech stack, but their financial profiles and market valuations vary significantly, creating two distinct paths for long-term investors.

Marvell Technology provides critical data-infrastructure chips for the AI, cloud, and automotive markets. The company designs specialized solutions for networking and accelerated compute, making it a prominent player among semiconductor stocks. Customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business, as a major distributor accounted for roughly 37% of revenue and one direct customer represented nearly 14% of revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

On a trailing-12-month (TTM) basis, revenue reached nearly $9.4 billion in the July fiscal quarter, representing an increase of approximately 30% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income of roughly $2.6 billion, which equals a net margin of close to 28%.

As of its July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, showing that total debt is low relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at about 3.1x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets.

TTM free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was roughly $1.7 billion. However, stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

SK Hynix is a global leader in memory semiconductors, producing the DRAM and NAND Flash products that serve as the foundation for AI-era computing. The business serves a global customer base, providing high-bandwidth memory chips that power the world's most advanced data centers. It competes in a high-stakes market where technological leadership directly dictates market share.

TTM revenue reached nearly $122 billion as of the June quarter, roughly a 114% increase over the year-ago period. Net income for the period was roughly $104 billion. This performance highlights the intense demand for high-performance memory components used in server environments.

As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1x. Its current ratio is close to 2.6x, suggesting the company maintains sufficient liquidity to meet its immediate financial obligations.

TTM free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached $59 billion, providing ample capital for the business to reinvest in new manufacturing technology.

Marvell Technology faces significant revenue concentration, as its top 10 customers accounted for roughly 82% of net revenue in the latest fiscal year. The company also faces geopolitical risks and export restrictions related to China that could disrupt its supply chain or demand. Additionally, it faces competition from hyperscale cloud providers that may design their own silicon internally rather than buy from external vendors.

SK Hynix operates in the highly cyclical memory market, where component prices can fluctuate wildly based on global supply and demand. It competes against large rivals like Micron Technology and Intel in a race to produce faster components for the AI era. The company also relies on complex global supply chains that are vulnerable to regional political instability or manufacturing disruptions.

SK Hynix appears much cheaper than Marvell based on both earnings and sales multiples, suggesting the market is pricing in more future growth for Marvell.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Both companies operate in a cyclical industry that occasionally experiences weak periods of growth. But I would buy Marvell stock over SK Hynix right now. Both stocks can outperform the market in 2027, but looking beyond next year, Marvell operates in a less cyclical segment of the semiconductor industry, providing greater visibility into long-term growth and shareholder returns.

Marvell just held its Investor Day in October, where management outlined a path for its custom chip business to reach $12 billion in revenue by fiscal 2029. This would be more than triple its custom revenue expected in fiscal 2028. This implies a strong growth ramp, as Marvell is shipping to all four U.S. hyperscalers.

Marvell has also issued a long-term target to reach $30 in earnings per share by fiscal 2031. So management expects growth in highly specialized AI products to drive healthy margins. This makes Marvell's current $202 share price, as of Oct. 30, look relatively inexpensive -- a forward earnings multiple of about 7x on the fiscal 2031 target.

If SK Hynix could sustain its current growth trajectory, it would be the better buy. The problem is that there is less long-term visibility into selling prices for its products, which are notorious for large swings driven by demand and supply. Competition has a lot to do with those swings, as memory and storage technology is largely a commodity, with little differentiation among SK Hynix and its competitors.

Marvell's revenue has historically been more predictable year-to-year than SK Hynix. With Marvell trading at a cheap valuation relative to its long-term potential, I would buy the stock right now.

#3076. How Federal Deregulation Isn't Making AI Compliance Easier—Just Harder To Navigate

David Talby, PhD, MBA, CEO at John Snow Labs. Solving real-world problems in healthcare, life sciences and related fields with AI.

​In the US, conversations about AI regulation in 2026 have focused largely on deregulation. The White House has challenged state-level restrictions, federal agencies have withdrawn AI guidance and policymakers have proposed reducing certain technology requirements. But for companies actually deploying AI, that’s only part of the story.

The library of global AI-related laws, regulations, standards and frameworks grew from around 250 instruments in March to 619 in September. More than 200 come from US states alone. For technology leaders, it’s not about whether Washington is regulating more or less. It’s what rules apply to the AI systems we operate, and how we can prove those systems comply.

Federal policy has shifted. In December 2025, Executive Order 14365 directed the Justice Department to challenge state AI laws the administration considers inconsistent with federal policy. Federal agencies have also withdrawn guidance concerning AI in areas such as employment and credit. But withdrawing guidance doesn’t repeal the underlying statutes, and state legislatures continue to act.

​For companies operating nationwide, a state law rarely stays neatly contained within the state’s borders. Texas and California, for example, both brought major AI legislation into effect in 2026. Colorado replaced its original AI Act with a new automated decision-making law. Several states have also enacted requirements governing conversational AI.

Companies could theoretically maintain different AI behavior for every jurisdiction. In practice, many will find it simpler to engineer systems around the strictest requirements that affect a meaningful share of their users. That makes state legislation important even without federal preemption. A requirement adopted by several large markets can effectively influence product design nationwide.

The most consequential regulatory change is not simply the number of laws but what some of them require AI systems to do. Consider conversational AI—Oregon has enacted requirements for AI companion operators to maintain protocols for detecting suicidal ideation or self-harm and providing crisis resources. Colorado has adopted similar requirements for conversational AI services.

For engineering teams, that creates a concrete question: Does the system respond correctly when a user expresses suicidal intent? Answering it requires testing multiple direct, indirect and adversarial formulations, and then repeating those tests as models, prompts and surrounding applications change.

Healthcare provides another example. California requires certain AI-generated communications involving patient clinical information to disclose the use of generative AI and provide clear instructions for contacting a human healthcare provider. As such, compliance can’t simply live in a policy document. Teams need to verify that required disclosures and escalation paths actually appear in the product.

The same principle applies to discrimination. When AI contributes to consequential decisions involving employment, lending, healthcare or other sensitive areas, organizations increasingly need processes to identify risks, evaluate outcomes and respond when systems change.

This shift changes what AI governance programs need to accomplish. First, organizations must maintain inventory of applicable requirements organized by jurisdiction and use case.

Second, those requirements should be translated into concrete controls: disclosures, prohibited behaviors, escalation rules and documentation requirements.

Third, every AI system needs a repeatable risk assessment tied to those controls.

Fourth, teams need release testing that verifies required behavior before deployment.

Finally, they need production monitoring for drift, failures and incidents.

Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 can provide structure for this process. But a framework cannot determine every law that applies to a particular system or automatically translate those laws into test cases. That operational layer is becoming the difficult part.

A central committee can review a handful of AI systems manually. That approach becomes difficult to sustain when an organization operates dozens or hundreds of systems across jurisdictions and the applicable rules keep changing. The scalable model is a continuous loop that involves tracking requirements, mapping them to systems, translating them into controls, testing those controls and monitoring them in production.

At the federal level, there are meaningful deregulatory signals. But technology leaders should not mistake that for a shrinking compliance burden. For deployed AI, the rulebook is becoming larger, harder to keep up with and more operational. Increasingly, compliance will not be demonstrated by what an organization says its AI should do, but instead, by what the system actually does in production. ​

#3075. C3.ai: What's Behind the Stock's Surge in the Past 3 Months?

Shares of tech company C3.ai (AI -2.07%) finished the month of October at $11.85 -- far higher than the $9.18 they were at three months earlier, at the close of July. That's a near-30% rally over three months, and it would have been even higher had it not been for the recent sell-off in the tech sector. Over that time frame, it's even outperformed chip giant Nvidia, whose shares have risen by just 2%.

Why has C3.ai stock suddenly gotten so hot, and could its rally continue?

There hasn't been a big development for C3.ai in recent months that would explain its impressive rally. Even its most recent earnings numbers weren't impressive. At $52.4 million in revenue for the period ending July 31, the company's top line was down 25% compared to the previous year. And it still incurred a significant net loss of $92.8 million.

The company, which sells artificial intelligence (AI) applications, simply hasn't demonstrated strong demand for its products and services, at a time when demand should be red hot, as it has been for many other tech businesses.

Over the past five years, however, the stock is down a mammoth 74%, and C3.ai's recent rally may have more to do with investors loading up on the stock amid a low and hoping for a turnaround with its CEO Tom Siebel back at the helm. Siebel resigned a year ago due to health reasons, but ultimately ended up returning in May.

C3.ai has a market cap of $1.9 billion, and its valuation may seem low as it trades at around seven times its trailing revenue. But with choppy sales numbers and its bottom line well into the red, I don't see a reason to be bullish on the company's future, either in the short term or the long term.

Even under Siebel, the company faced challenges in growing its operations consistently, and a path to profitability was questionable. While the situation got worse after Siebel left the company, investors shouldn't assume that the path ahead will be a much better one.

There's growing competition in AI these days, and it may inevitably end up being more difficult for C3.ai to compete and grow its business without incurring losses. I'm not optimistic that the stock will go much higher, as it's still a fairly risky investment to own. Investors may be better off taking a wait-and-see approach.

#3074. We're Witnessing the Stock Market Do Something for Only the 3rd Time in 100 Years. History Says This Could Come Next

So far, 2026 has been a solid year for stock market investors, with the benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%) up around 11% year to date. This follows even bigger gains of 17.88% in 2025 and 25.02% in 2024. Optimism is largely being driven by generative artificial intelligence (AI), a technology trend that has seen many of America's biggest tech companies pour hundreds of billions into data center infrastructure.

However, there are a growing number of warning signs in the stock market (and economy as a whole) that suggest this boom might be on its last legs. Let's dig deeper to find out what could happen next.

Over the long term, the stock market will consistently go up, but it is far from a smooth ride. Periodic drawdowns are a normal way for financial markets to remain grounded in economic reality. And the period before a big crash is usually marked by abnormally high valuations as measured by metrics like the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio.

The CAPE ratio now stands at 40.1 compared to its historic average of 17.4. In fact, over the last 100 years, this number has only substantially peaked three times. The first was in late 1929, when it hit 33 shortly before a stock market crash ushered in the Great Depression. The second time was in late 1999, shortly before the dot-com bubble burst. Both peaks preceded huge multi-year declines in equity prices.

The situation today has the most similarities with the dot-com bubble. Both rallies were driven by a transformational new technology with growth concentrated in this specific sector. According to CME Group, information technology now represents 40% of the S&P 500's value, up from just under 7% in 1990. This extreme concentration means weakness in a relatively small number of companies could have a substantial negative impact on the performance of the entire index.

For clues about how this alarming situation may play out, investors should look at the example of South Korea. Like the US, this Asian nation has seen its stock market become totally dominated by the AI trade, with chipmakers like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix representing more than half of the benchmark Kospi Index's total capitalization.

The South Korean market is down by a whopping 37.1% from its June 22 peak of 9,114.55 as investors get pessimistic about the sustainability of the AI boom. Many fear that rising global interest rates will make capital more expensive and cause companies to be less willing to pour hundreds of billions into acquiring expensive data center equipment for AI.

The US market also isn't immune. On October 30, US markets shed more than $1 trillion in value, led by technology stocks like Intel, which dropped by 29% on concerns about disappointing earnings and heavy spending as it invests in expanding its manufacturing capacity. Alphabet also faced pressure, dropping by 12% in response to slower search growth as AI cannibalizes its traditional business. Investors fear that companies are spending more on AI than they will be able to get back.

The good news is that over the long haul, time in the market beats trying to time the market. And this is especially true today as increasingly aggressive fiscal and monetary policy is being used to prevent the huge multi-year crashes we saw during the great depression and the dot-com bubble. Investors should look at drawdowns as an opportunity to shop for quality stocks at a discount. And it makes sense to keep some cash available as the market's future becomes increasingly uncertain.

#3073. ​The Tool Sprawl Problem: Why Security Leaders Are Turning To Unified Platforms

Kevin Tian, Co-Founder and CEO at Doppel, an AI-native social engineering defense platform.

Cybersecurity didn’t become fragmented by accident. For years, organizations built their defenses one threat at a time. A new attack emerged, a vendor addressed it and another tool entered the stack. Email phishing, security awareness training, identity and more have each developed their own products, teams, metrics and workflows.

Historically, the cybersecurity model rewarded specialization. A brand protection product tracked takedowns. An email product tracked detections. A training product tracked participation rates. Each tool could demonstrate value within its boundary.

That model had its time and place, but it wasn’t built for complex, coordinated, multichannel attacks, particularly in social engineering. Today’s security environment is filled with tools that manage isolated pieces of the same campaign. Attackers, meanwhile, operate like businesses, coordinating tactics and channels toward a single objective. As one-off attacks give way to sustained campaigns, fragmented defenses can make it harder to identify and respond to coordinated attacks.

Security leaders are now confronting the cost of fragmentation as attackers become more coordinated and effective with AI.

In social engineering, AI has intensified several challenges associated with fragmented security models. Historically, a sophisticated multichannel campaign demanded considerable time and specialized talent. An attacker had to research the target, construct a credible persona, write convincing messages and coordinate interactions. Those economics limited how many campaigns an operator could run.

AI removes that constraint. Attackers can now generate localized lures, synthetic voices, credible personas and tailored scenarios at scale. They can adapt those campaigns in real time and repeat them across email, SMS, social media, voice and video. Techniques reserved for high-value targets can now be deployed against thousands at once.

AI has widened the gap between the speed of coordinated attacks and the ability of disconnected tools to identify them. Closing that gap requires security strategies built around how these attacks actually operate: across channels, identities, and interactions. ​As AI agents take on more workflows, that defense must protect both the human and agent layers.

A modern social engineering campaign may begin with a fake domain or social profile, move into SMS or email and culminate in a voice call or video meeting. Modern attacks focus on building credibility across channels and over time.

Traditional anti-phishing guidance tells people to verify a suspicious request out of band. But when an adversary controls multiple points of contact, the second channel can reinforce the first. A spoofed executive email looks more credible when it’s followed by a text message, a LinkedIn profile and a convincing phone call.

With the legacy siloed approach, each control sees only one fragment. The email system sees a message. The digital risk tool sees a domain. The awareness platform sees a training opportunity. The full campaign becomes visible only when signals are connected across the social engineering attack chain. By the time a human analyst assembles the pieces, the attacker may have succeeded.

These scenarios make integration worth evaluating, particularly where teams struggle to correlate signals across channels. The benefits depend on the quality of the integrations, the context shared and the organization’s existing controls.

Consolidation can reduce procurement and management overhead, but those benefits do not necessarily translate into better threat detection or response. Combining products under one contract or login may simplify procurement, but it doesn’t automatically improve security. If the capabilities operate independently, the organization has changed the packaging without changing the technology.

Consolidation​ is most useful when integration provides capabilities or efficiencies that standalone tools cannot readily provide. Signals should be connected through shared context, allowing security teams to identify relationships between threats and coordinate responses across disconnected controls.

A threat detected in an inbox should enrich threat intelligence, trigger infrastructure disruption, inform simulations and improve future detection. Intelligence gathered from impersonation campaigns should strengthen email and messaging controls before the same infrastructure reaches an employee or customer.

Over time, these feedback loops may improve detection and response, provided the information is reliable and used effectively. Visibility is only the starting point. The value of consolidation depends on whether it enables meaningful information-sharing, coordinated responses and feedback across security functions.​

Consolidation also requires consideration of how capabilities are integrated and managed. When organizations rely on a single vendor for multiple security functions, they need confidence the provider can deliver across them all without introducing new gaps or dependencies.

Security leaders considering consolidation should ask three key questions.

First, will the tools share context and reduce operational complexity? That means fewer disconnected workflows, portals, less manual correlation and less time managing vendors. The intent is to reduce routine coordination work and free analysts to focus on investigation and risk reduction.

Second, will intelligence move automatically across capabilities? The platform should connect insights, apply them across controls and coordinate action without waiting for an analyst to move information between systems.

Third, does the system cover the full attack lifecycle? Social engineering leaves evidence before an incident, during it and after it occurs. Infrastructure appears before a lure is delivered. Messages, calls and identity signals emerge during the campaign. The outcome should improve future detection, training and disruption.

As I have argued before, AI has changed the speed and economics of cyberattacks, but human nature remains an attractive target. It’s cheaper than ever for attackers to create convincing personas, localized messages, synthetic voices and coordinated campaigns at enormous scale. As AI agents take on more responsibility, attackers have a growing set of non-human targets to manipulate.

Social communication is no longer limited to human-to-human interaction. Organizations must consider human-to-agent, agent-to-human and agent-to-agent exchanges, including how AI systems can be manipulated through email, collaboration tools, voice interfaces and emerging protocols. Whether the interaction involves a person or an AI agent, the objective is the same: manipulate trust to drive an action. Protecting those interactions will require shared intelligence across inbound and outbound channels.

Tool sprawl is a symptom of defenses built around isolated pieces of a connected threat. Consolidation will work only when it connects the underlying intelligence and actions, not merely the vendors. As the attack surface expands from humans to agents, the need for coordinated defense will grow. As attacks become more coordinated, organizations may need to place greater emphasis on cross-channel visibility and response.​

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

#3071. VGT vs. QQQ: Which Tech ETF Is the Better Long-Term Buy?

The Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ +0.62%) is one of the most popular ways to invest in technology stocks, but there's a problem with that.

That's the one thing that matters when comparing it with the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT -0.19%). For investors specifically targeting long-term technology growth, I believe VGT is the better choice.

To be clear, the Invesco QQQ ETF is mostly a tech fund. But that's almost by coincidence. Specifically, the fund's objective is to track the Nasdaq-100, which comprises the 100 largest non-financial stocks traded on the Nasdaq. That's it. There's no specific targeting of size, sector, style, or anything else.

It looks like a tech fund because most of the major tech companies have chosen to list their stocks on that exchange. Currently, about 68% of the index is dedicated to tech. The other one-third includes consumer discretionary, telecom, healthcare, industrials, and minor additional allocations elsewhere. It includes Walmart, Costco Wholesale, Amgen, and PepsiCo, some very non-tech holdings.

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF is a pure tech fund. It tracks an index that holds more than 300 positions entirely devoted to tech. Plus, in true Vanguard-ian fashion, its 0.09% expense ratio is one of the lowest in this space and half that of the Invesco QQQ ETF.

If you want tech exposure in your portfolio, choose the tech ETF, not the fund that is mostly a tech ETF.

#3070. Marvell Just Bet $115 Billion On AI's 'Once In A Generation' Opportunity. Should You Buy The Stock?

Marvell (MRVL -7.00%) stock fell 13% on Thursday when word of a Lumentum (LITE -11.01%) takeover leaked, and the official terms, announced Monday, show what holders are paying. Marvell, which designs chips for data infrastructure, agreed to buy the optical-parts maker for about $115 billion in an all-stock deal, handing Lumentum's owners about a third of the combined company.

Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share, or about $1,132 a share, a premium of about 23.9% to the October 28 closing prices, the last trading day before deal speculation began. After closing, current Marvell holders will own about 67% of the combined company on a fully diluted basis, and Lumentum holders about 33%.So that's roughly a third of the ownership handed over. In the meantime, the deal is not expected to close until the first half of 2028, and it needs approval from both companies' shareholders and from regulators. Both boards approved it unanimously.

Lumentum makes lasers and optical components that link AI chips inside data centers. Its latest quarter, which ended on September 26, brought revenue up 136.5% to $1.26 billion, and it guided to roughly $350 million more next quarter, according to the Monday release.Marvell CEO Matt Murphy, who stays chairman and CEO, called the moment one that "comes along once in a generation," adding that the companies that move first "will set the standard for decades to come." The companies say the combination expands their addressable market to $550 billion. Three Lumentum directors, including CEO Michael Hurlston, will join Marvell's seven-member board.Meanwhile, Marvell's own targets are rising: It lifted its fiscal 2028 revenue outlook to $20 billion at its October 6 investor day and set a fiscal 2031 goal of $70 billion to $90 billion in revenue and earnings per share of $30 or more. Its fiscal 2026 diluted earnings per share was $3.07.Marvell also points to more than $1 billion a year in cost savings, but that is a target the companies see "line of sight" to, rather than a result.

The sell-off came on higher volume, totaling about 40.4 million shares, which was well above the three-month average of 21.6 million. Investors worried over integration risk specific to the deal, but also more broadly about the massive amounts of AI spending that's impacting cash flow across the sector, as exemplified by Intel (INTC -2.82%) stock's record plunge on Friday. Marvell shares are down about 3% in pre-market trading on Monday, suggesting that investors still aren't sure about the deal's potential.If you believe AI data-center spending has years to run, Marvell just bought a larger slice of it. But if you worry that spending will slow, you now own more of the part of AI that depends on it most, with a long wait and regulatory approval between you and the payoff.

Long-term investors, however, should find comfort in how much demand Marvell has already locked in. In August, it signed a deal to supply chips that sit alongside Google's AI processors, worth up to $120 billion in sales through fiscal 2033. Nvidia (NVDA +1.50%), the company at the center of the AI boom, invested $2 billion each in Marvell and Lumentum earlier this year. And despite the dilution, Marvell says the deal should add to its adjusted earnings per share in the first year after closing.There's also the price. Since talks were first reported, Marvell shares have tanked over 20% amid the broader chip sell-off. Still, Wall Street hasn't walked away, with Stifel and Piper Sandler both reaffirming bullish ratings during the sell-off, and management, meanwhile, is aiming for $70 billion to $90 billion in revenue and $30 or more in earnings per share by fiscal 2031, up from $3.07 in fiscal 2026. Those targets are ambitious and far from guaranteed. But for investors who can hold through a 2028 closing, today's sell-off means buying into Marvell's biggest AI bet at a lower price than before anyone knew about it.

Marvell's next scheduled earnings report is expected on November 26.

#3069. ​The Account Creation Paradox: How AI Agents Could Transform E-Commerce Registration

Craig DeWitt is the founder of Skyfire, a payment network for AI.

Every merchant leadership team I meet agrees on two things. The first is that customer relationships are the business. Accounts, loyalty, purchase history and permission to communicate are what separate a brand from a vending operation. The second is that the moment designed to create that relationship—account registration—is one of the most disliked steps in all of shopping.

Baymard Institute has tracked the reasons shoppers abandon carts for more than a decade, and being asked to create an account consistently ranks near the top of the list. Think about what that means. A customer has found the product, decided to buy and reached for their wallet. At the exact peak of their intent, we interrupt them with a form. The form asks them to invent a password they will forget, confirm an email address and volunteer personal details before they have received anything in return.

Some buyers simply leave. Many of the ones who stay protect themselves with a throwaway email and whatever birthday gets them through the screen. The customer relationship starts with friction.

Guest checkout became the industry’s compromise, and it is a strange one when you look at it directly. To save the sale, the merchant gives up the relationship. The customer gets convenience, the brand gets a transaction with no guaranteed future and the premise of direct commerce quietly leaks away one order at a time.

Merchants accepted this trade because the alternative was losing the order entirely, but we are leaving that world.

AI shopping agents are usually discussed as a checkout story: software that can search, compare and complete a purchase on a person’s behalf. The more interesting story is what they change about the beginning of the relationship. An agent acting for a customer can do the one thing we could never reasonably ask of the customer at the moment of purchase: handle the registration.

This is not a speculative audience, either. Salesforce measured $262 billion in global online sales influenced by AI and agents during the 2025 holiday season alone. The delegation habit is forming right now, at scale, and every delegated purchase raises a similar question: What happens to the relationship when the customer sends software in their place?

Picture the same purchase with a trusted agent involved. The customer delegates the errand. Their agent arrives at the storefront carrying proof that it represents a real, verified person, along with the permissions that person has chosen to extend. Creating the account takes the agent seconds and costs the customer nothing. The merchant receives something better than a filled-in form: a customer record that is accurate on day one and honest about what it is allowed to be used for.

For marketing teams, this arrives at a useful moment. The industry has spent years watching third-party signals degrade while regulators and platforms narrow what can be tracked. An account created by a verified agent is first-party data of the highest grade, explicitly permissioned and correct from the first interaction. The addressable relationship marketers have been trying to reconstruct through clean rooms and probabilistic matching simply shows up at the front door and introduces itself.

Merchants block automated traffic today for good reason. Radware found that total bot traffic on e-commerce sites passed human traffic for the first time in the 2024 holiday season, and its latest report puts malicious bots alone at 43% of traffic, within three points of human shoppers and fake registrations up sixfold. Fake account creation is already a fraud pattern merchants are trying to suppress. Any honest vision for autonomous registration has to start by acknowledging that an unverified agent asking to open an account looks exactly like the attack.

Building that proof layer is now industry work. Letting an agent cryptographically prove which operator sent it is moving through the IETF, and the major AI assistants already sign their traffic that way. The harder part—binding an agent’s action to a verified person’s specific intent—entered formal standards work in spring 2026 when the FIDO Alliance (the body behind passkeys) formed working groups on agentic authentication and commerce. Most standards are still drafts, and the work is strongest at payment and thinnest at registration. Who bears the loss on a fraudulent agent-created account is unsettled, but the sequencing holds. Agent identity has to come before agent commerce. Once verification is solved, registration stops being a form and becomes a handshake.

For marketing and growth leaders, preparing for this is less technical than it sounds. Start by walking your own registration flow and counting what it asks of a customer at their moment of highest intent. Every field you cannot justify is friction an agent will soon make unnecessary, and a competitor may drop it first.

Then decide what a verified, agent-created account should be entitled to on day one. If a customer arrives with proven identity and explicit permissions, do they start at the bottom of your loyalty program, or do they start recognized? The answer says a lot about whether your brand treats registration as a gate or as a welcome, and the merchants who treat permissioning as part of the product will be the ones agents and their owners prefer to transact with.

The paradox was never permanent. Merchants were right to insist on relationships, and customers were right to resent the way we asked for them. Agents help resolve the standoff by absorbing the clerical work that neither side ever wanted to do, and the relationship that emerges is stronger because nothing false was required to start it.

The most hated step in the customer journey just might disappear. What replaces it is the thing merchants wanted all along: a customer who is genuinely, verifiably there.​​

#3068. The Midterms Are Tomorrow. Here's What History Says Defense Stocks Do in the 6 Months After a Midterm -- and the 2 I'd Buy First

Midterm Election Day is tomorrow, and, as elections often do, the 2026 midterm is prompting plenty of speculation about potential effects on stocks. That scenario is heightened because if polls and prediction markets prove accurate, the Democrats are heading to a Congressional sweep, meaning that come January 2027, they'll control the House and the Senate.

Alone, that's not cause for alarm. After all, history confirms that stocks often perform well under divided governments, and the third year of the presidential cycle, that'd be 2027, is often the best for the S&P 500.

Defense stocks may fall after Election Day, but they could bounce back sooner than some investors think. Image source: Getty Images

Still, investors often fret about sector- and industry-level implications following shifts in congressional majorities. Of late, the aerospace and defense industry has been an epicenter of those worries. Amid increasing talk of a "blue wave," the iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA +2.07%), one of the largest exchange-traded funds (ETFs) tracking the industry, resides 18.4% below its 52-week high.

On the other hand, the history of defense stocks under Democrat-controlled Congresses isn't as dire as the industry's recent price action suggests. Navigating the expected 2027 political landscape, however, requires selective focus on defense equities. Hence, GE Aerospace (GE +3.91%) and RTX (RTX +0.15%) are two of the top names to consider.

Investors anticipating a blue wave/Democrat sweep on Tuesday have some recent history to lean on regarding the post-election outlook for defense stocks. Democrats held a trifecta -- House, Senate, and the presidency -- from Inauguration Day 2021 through the end of 2022. Over that time, the iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF gained 22.1%, handily outpacing the broader market. In fact, that run-up include impressive performance six months after Election Day.

Following the 2018 midterms in which Democrats gained control of the house, defense stocks and the broader pulled back, but by the end of May 2019, both the bellwether ETF and the S&P 500 posted gains.

Because as soon as the 2026 midterms wrap up, attention will turn to the 2028 presidential contest, neither party will want to be seen as taking an axe to defense spending. Not with the wars in Iran and Ukraine raging on. Prevailing wisdom indicates that if Democrats control both chambers of Congress, they may seek to delay or roll back spending on specific defense programs, such as the Golden Dome or certain fighter jets or tanks.

That implies potential vulnerability for shares of program-specific defense contractors, and the market is already reflecting as much. In part because of significant commercial aerospace exposure, GE Aerospace and RTX have some buffering against a possible Congressional move to rein in spending on select military products and programs.

RTX engines are found in 13,000 commercial aircraft worldwide, and the company is a leader in private business jet engines. Regarding GE Aerospace, if Boeing's recent production update proves accurate, the commercial aircraft aftermarket is expected to be robust in 2027, providing a compelling runway for the stock that isn't dependent on defense spending.

History can be instructive, but regardless of industry, market participants shouldn't be emotional about election results. Yes, that can be difficult, but one of the biggest mistakes some investors make is selling stocks based on election results.

That advice applies to defense stocks even if congressional majorities change hands. Several large defense contractors, including RTX, are sitting on massive order backlogs, some of which are at all-time highs.

In a political context, that's pertinent to investors mulling RTX in the near term, because significant portions of the defense industry's backlogs aren't tied to new programs. Rather, those orders pertain to the three "R's" of readiness, rearmament, and replenishment, which are front and center due to the war in Iran. Remembering that, in the U.S., it often feels as though it's an election year even when it's not, it must be acknowledged that the three R's are examples of rare bipartisanship. So the knee-jerk reactions to a blue wave may be creating buying opportunities in defense stocks.

#3067. Here's Why I Think Every Investor Needs to Invest in These "Miracle" Drugs

Sales and profits from GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy are already huge. They're only going to get bigger.

Eli Lilly's (LLY -1.09%) GLP-1 drug tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, dethroned Merck's (MRK -0.75%) cancer drug Keytruda last year to become the world's best-selling drug.

Novo Nordisk's (NVO +1.05%) sales of the GLP-1 drugs Wegovy and Ozempic pushed the drug manufacturer's market cap above the GDP of its home country, Denmark.

So, did investors who didn't buy these stocks years ago miss the boat?

Hardly. The numbers mentioned above are just the beginning. Morgan Stanley forecasts that the market for obesity miracle drugs will reach $190 billion by 2035, more than double its 2025 level. Right now, that growth is being driven by new oral treatments, expected to be adopted by consumers at a faster pace than injection-based delivery systems, and by expanded coverage from Medicare, the largest payer for healthcare services in the U.S.

But I think those predictions are far too small. Because medical researchers continue to find new and novel uses for the drugs, apart from obesity and weight loss. I believe these are truly miracle drugs that will cause a tectonic shift in the healthcare industry. It's definitely not too late to invest, as most of the growth in these drugs lies ahead, not in the past.

First, there are international markets, largely untapped so far (outside of Europe). Morgan Stanley estimates there are more than 1 billion people with obesity living outside the U.S. To date, adoption in foreign markets has been constrained by several factors, including affordability, needle aversion, and safety concerns -- all of which can be overcome. The investment bank's research mentions Brazil and China, in particular.

And then there are new use cases for GLP-1 drugs. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) says that the medicines also improve outcomes in people with cardiovascular, kidney, liver, arthritis, and sleep apnea disorders. Those improvements are mediated in part through anti-inflammatory and metabolic pathways.

And there will be more uses in the future, I predict, some of them astounding. For example, a recent study conducted on mice and funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has shown that the GLP-1 drug semaglutide (made by Novo Nordisk) extended lifespan in older, healthy mice by tempering the detrimental effects of aging.

Of course, researchers have long known that calorie restriction can have anti-aging benefits. And GLP-1 drugs are designed to suppress appetite, thereby reducing calorie intake. But the new study, conducted at the University of California, found that the drugs' effects on mice could be more than just a consequence of lower-calorie diets.

In fact, the new study in healthy older mice offers evidence that these drugs may slow physiological aging itself. According to the NIH press release: "Compared with a control group, mice treated with the drug showed improved muscle and cognitive function. Gene expression analysis showed that several hallmarks of natural aging, such as increased inflammation and reduced regenerative capacity, were reduced in treated animals."

I assume that semaglutide's anti-aging effects in the study could be replicated with tirzepatide. And that should be fantastic news for both Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly. Of course, the research remains a long way from establishing the same anti-aging results in humans. But if people believe it might, that will only encourage the adoption of the drugs.

Expanded use of GLP-1 drugs domestically and internationally for weight loss, expanded use cases for the drugs, and potentially more to come; there are many reasons to think GLP-1 drugs can revolutionize healthcare.

That's why I firmly believe that every investor should have some portion of their portfolio in this rapidly expanding market. It's worth looking at Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, and even Pfizer and Merck, which don't yet have a GLP-1 drug on the market but have several in development. That's where to start.

#3065. Why Integration Test Environments Are A Leadership Problem, Not An Engineering One

Nitesh Sinha is the Founder & CEO of Sacumen, a cybersecurity innovator.

​Picture a Thursday release review. The integration is built, and the code has passed review. But nothing can ship because nobody has been able to run it against the real product it connects to.

The engineers aren’t the problem—the environment is. Access hasn’t been approved, a license is missing or the only sandbox lacks the feature customers use.

I hear versions of this scenario from technology leaders across industries. It’s one of the most underestimated constraints in integration delivery, and it’s rarely treated as a leadership issue.​

Engineers can build and test an integration. But they usually can’t approve a vendor license, negotiate access to a partner environment, fund the infrastructure behind a realistic test environment or decide which products deserve dedicated coverage.

These are budget, contract and priority decisions that require leadership ownership. Without it, environment requests become queues, and queues become release delays.

The dependency also extends beyond engineering. QA needs environments for validation, product teams require them for acceptance testing, sales people need them for demos and the support staff have to have them for reproducing customer issues. When no one owns the dependency end to end, everyone feels the delay, but no one can fix it.​

An integration is only as trustworthy as the environment it was tested in. The team is testing against someone else’s product, so it doesn’t control that product’s authentication model, permission roles, data structures or release cycle.

The same integration can behave differently across product versions, editions and customer configurations. API behavior often differs from what the documentation promises. A demo tenant with 10 records says little about an instance holding 10 million.

This is where the gap between “the integration works” and “the integration works for customers” begins.​

A test lab gives teams controlled access to realistic product environments, so they can validate integrations against the behavior they’re expected to support. A lab isn’t unrestricted access to everything. Security controls, licensing terms and data-protection rules still apply. It also isn’t the only tool. Sandboxes suit routine checks, and mocks are the right choice for fast, isolated tests. The mistake is treating a passing mock as proof an integration will work somewhere it’s never run.

The lab exists for the high-risk cases, where product-specific behavior has to be proven before a customer finds the problem.​

Having access to an environment is only part of the problem. The environment also needs to contain enough realistic data to test the workflows the integration is expected to handle.

For example, a security integration may need realistic alerts, events, incidents, users, assets or activity logs before a team can properly validate ingestion, mappings, enrichment or outbound actions. Creating that data manually can become another bottleneck. A sandbox that’s accessible but empty isn’t ready for meaningful validation.

For sensitive use cases, synthetic data can provide realistic, schema-conformant behavior without exposing production data or customer information. The goal isn’t simply to give teams somewhere to run a test—it’s to give them an environment that’s ready to prove whether the integration will work in the conditions that matter.​

A lab isn’t a one-time purchase. It needs licenses, infrastructure, vendor relationships, access governance and upkeep as products release new versions. Left to chance, it goes stale, and a stale lab gives false confidence.

Those costs and trade-offs are leadership decisions, and so is the choice of how to provide it: build it in-house, share it with partners or rely on a trusted third party. Each can work, but none works without a named owner and a budget.​

AI can now generate an integration faster than many teams can find somewhere to test it. Faster code followed by the same wait at the end means the bottleneck has only moved downstream.

In cybersecurity, where integrations move data between products that organizations rely on for detection and response, a failure is a coverage gap. And a failure found by a customer cost far more than a delay found by a test.​

• Name one owner. Environment access sits between engineering, procurement, security and partner management, which is why it often belongs to no one. Choose one person with authority across all of them.

• Rank by customer dependence. Few companies can afford a realistic environment for every product they connect to. Start with the handful of customers who rely on it the most and accept lighter coverage for the rest.

• Write test access into contracts. Production access is usually negotiated. Test access, licensing and sandbox terms often aren’t, and they’re much harder to add after signing.

• Fund upkeep like building infrastructure. Environments go stale as products release new versions. Budget for refreshes and time-bound credentials, and track how long it takes to go from request to usable.

Integration isn’t done when the code is complete. It’s done when the business can trust it.

A simple place to start on Monday: Ask who owns your test environment. If the answer takes more than a few seconds, the problem is already on your desk.​

#3064. Chipotle Mexican Grill Is Down 15% and Growing. Here's Why It Has the Makings of a Monster Stock for the Next Decade.

Stocks change as investors incorporate information. But sometimes, it's due to short-term factors.

The key is to distinguish between growth companies with bright long-term prospects and those whose business prospects have been permanently altered.

Chipotle Mexican Grill's (CMG +3.34%) share price has dropped 15.5% in 2026, through Oct. 29. During this time, the S&P 500 Growth index gained 12.1%. Here's why investors should view this as an opportunity to pick up Chipotle shares.

There's no doubt that higher overall prices, including for basic items like energy and gas, have hurt consumer discretionary spending. That's squeezed people's wallets and caused them to eat out less. There have also been cost pressures affecting Chipotle Mexican Grill's profitability.

Still, management has taken steps to improve sales, particularly sluggish traffic, and profitability. Earlier this year, CEO Scott Boatwright announced his Recipe for Growth strategy, which includes five parts. This includes updating the menu to include more value and protein items.

Fortunately, the last two quarters have shown initial success. Chipotle's second-quarter same-store sales (comps) grew 2.2%. Importantly, higher customer traffic was a positive contributor for the second straight quarter, adding 1 percentage point for the period. An increase in spending, measured by the average check, made up the balance of the comps' growth. Management expects a low-single-digit percentage in the company's comps for this year.

Still, costs, including food, beverage, and packaging, along with labor, increased at a higher pace. That's why Chipotle's operating margin contracted 2.5 percentage points to 15.7%.

That's not too concerning to me since the company should recoup the costs over time with higher menu prices. That's particularly true since it has drawn customers, indicating people like its offerings.

In the meantime, Chipotle has plenty of expansion opportunities ahead. With sales moving in the right direction, that's encouraging.

The company had over 4,200 restaurants as of June 30. That's after opening 100 locations in June.

Management plans to add 350-370 restaurants this year. It's also expanding outside the United States, with that total including 10-15 international locations.

Chipotle's stock price drop has created a better valuation. The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio has dropped from 35 to 30 this year.

To give that historical context, the shares have a five-year median P/E ratio of 51. The shares trade at a richer valuation than the S&P 500's P/E multiple of 26. However, with Chipotle's sales growing and the company expanding, paying a premium to the overall market seems warranted.

With a better valuation and the company moving in the right direction, Chipotle's stock represents a big money-making opportunity in which investors can benefit from growing earnings and an expanded P/E ratio.
