#3061. 19 Ways To Set Boundaries For Autonomous AI Agents

Gopichand Mannava, Independent Researcher, Chief Data & AI Architect, State of Connecticut.

Even when AI agents perform reliably in testing, certain actions warrant human oversight. For example, consider a semantic-integrity gate: automatically verify that each record’s meaning matches its metadata—not just its schema—before ingestion. An invoice date can be valid yet mislabeled as a payment date. Quarantine that mismatch before the model or vector store sees it. The failure this prevents is subtle: an AI answer that is perfectly grounded in the wrong business meaning.

Technology leaders must establish clear boundaries around agent autonomy. The challenge is enforcing those limits through system architecture rather than relying on prompts or trust alone. To help, I asked members of the Software Architects Group, a community that I lead through Forbes Technology Council, to share which actions they would reserve for human approval and how they build those safeguards into their systems.

Never let an AI agent expand its own authority without human approval. The bigger risk is not one bad action—it’s an agent quietly gaining the ability to take many consequential ones. The architecture for bounded autonomy is fixed permission ceilings, policy-based escalation and cryptographic auditability. This way, AI can act fast without redefining its own limits. - Swati Deepak Kumar (Nema), Citigroup

I am working on governance architecture for a workflow in our platform, using GPT-6 Astra. So far, I’ve learned never to accept governance architecture without verifying it and to make sure all incorrect cases are addressed. Also, keep it simple. An AI agent’s solution is complex and accommodates use cases that are not correct. One can evaluate different designs, but always verify and approve. Make your own judgment calls and never accept AI suggestions at face value. - Siva Nookala, Decision Lens

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Don’t allow an AI agent to independently make a binding commercial commitment, even with a flawless testing record. Agreeing to terms, accepting liability or committing funds requires human accountability. Architecturally, I would enforce this through restricted permissions, approval gates at the transaction layer and immutable audit logs. The agent can negotiate, recommend and prepare the action, but only an authorized human can commit the organization. - Prajkta Waditwar, Box Inc

Don’t let an AI agent change any privilege or authorization given, nor update the way it acts without any human supervision. Also, never let it update the way it works with data beyond the original responsibility granted. - Gregorio Alejandro Patiño Zabala, Pragma

We never allow database migrations to be performed by an AI agent autonomously. Many operations are irreversible, and if done without a human knowing, they can lead to permanent data loss and an SLA breach. - Jeff An, Momentic

I would never let an AI agent change a supplier’s bank details without human approval. The FBI documents scams that redirect legitimate invoice payments. My design would require verification through a known contact and server-side approval tied to the exact new account. Any subsequent edit would invalidate that approval. A routine data update can decide where the next million dollars goes. - Nikhil Jathar, AvanSaber Technologies

Don’t let an AI agent irreversibly destroy data, such as dropping a production database, force-pushing over shared history, or deleting backups, because a thousand clean test runs can’t pay for one unrecoverable mistake. That boundary lives outside the agent’s judgment. Deny rules and pre-execution hooks block those commands before they run, and the agent never has production-write or backup-delete credentials. A person should grant that access separately for each task. - Srinivas Chippagiri, Salesforce Inc

I would never let an AI agent change a ledger entry. Similarly, I wouldn’t allow it to cancel or add charges to an accounting system. Only humans can and should make those kinds of decisions. - Timmi Ryerson, Smart Property Systems

My non-negotiable boundary is that an AI agent must never independently authorize irreversible, high-consequence actions. Across high-risk defense-grade assurance environments, testing proves capability, not authority. You must enforce this through policy-gated execution, least-privilege identities, human approval and immutable audit evidence. Why? Reliability earns trust; it never grants permission to act. - Rajjie Sarmey, FutureProof CXO™

Never let an AI agent finalize safety controls for a hazardous job. It can identify missed hazards and recommend controls, but it cannot authorize them. We enforce that boundary in the application, not a prompt: AI output remains a recommendation until a human reviews and confirms it. Even a model that performs reliably in testing can miss the one hazard that changes someone’s life forever. Human judgment is not an optional safeguard. - Julia Penfield, PH.D., VelocityEHS

Don’t let an AI agent update its own behavior from live production data, such as changing prompts, memory, or retrieval sources, without human review. Small silent shifts can compound into a very different system from the one we tested. In our architecture, changes go through a versioned release pipeline with regression tests and a named approver, so production always runs what we validated. - Venkatesh Sankaran, Saguna Consulting Services LLC

Changing the architecture is something I would not let an AI do without human oversight. Best, if such changes are happening through a platform like CALM, make sure that the architecture is reviewable, drifts are detectable, and active oversight (which might possibly involve) can be expressed. The change in architecture might cause scalability issues, security lapses, and, really, any kind of “unknown unknowns” that you are trying to prevent the system from falling into. - Peter Smulovics, Morgan Stanley

Avoid letting an AI agent handle anything a customer cannot undo: deleting records, issuing refunds, changing someone’s access. Testing only tells you how the agent behaves on cases you thought of. Enforcement belongs in the permissions, not the prompt. The agent gets credentials that cannot make those calls at all, and the approval step sits in the service, so a manipulated agent has nothing to act with. - Kriti Faujdar, Yelp

I would never let an AI agent expand its own permissions or delegate authority without human approval. Reliability in testing does not establish authority. Architecturally, agents cannot modify their own access policies. A separate authorization layer enforces permissions, requires human approval for privilege changes and records the decision. - Vibhor Kumar, EnterpriseDB

I’d never let an AI agent make irreversible production changes—like finalizing financial payouts or deleting customer records—without human sign-off. We enforce this with air-gapped execution: The AI can draft and stage transactions, but our downstream APIs require a signed approval token from a verified human before processing the event. - Mahendran Chinnaiah

Don’t let an AI agent post a financial adjustment to a customer account or the general ledger without human approval. In large transformations, I have seen one adjustment ripple through billing, reporting and reconciliation. The boundary sits outside the model: The agent proposes, while a separate workflow verifies the approver’s role, issues a one-time posting token, and logs the trail. - Govinda Rao Banothu, Cognizant Technology Solutions

I would never let an AI agent elevate its own production privileges without human approval. I would enforce this through an independent authorization service, least-privilege access, and time-limited permissions tied to approved requests. The agent could propose changes but could not approve them or bypass the gate. All actions would be logged. - Vikram Pande, HCLTech

The right way is always verification before action. It often delivers a larger reliability improvement than using a bigger model at one go. - Santanu Boral, Cognizant Technology Solutions

I would never allow an AI agent to redefine the original human intent without explicit human approval. It can adapt how it executes a task, but changing the objective, scope, or constraints requires a human decision. I’d enforce that boundary through controls outside the agent, with approval required for changes to its authorized mandate.- Arun Kumar Elengovan, Okta, Inc.

#3059. 3 Reasons to Buy Alphabet Stock Right Now

Alphabet (GOOG +1.80%) (GOOGL +2.16%) stock hit an all-time high earlier this year, but it's been downhill ever since. Shares are currently down 11% year-to-date, even as the S&P 500 has gained 10%. What's going on with Alphabet? Many investors are worried about the company's significant spending on artificial intelligence (AI), and the tech leader's latest earnings report has exacerbated these fears, leading to a post-earnings dip.

Despite these challenges, Alphabet remains a great stock to buy and hold for the long term. Here are three reasons why.

In the third quarter, Alphabet's revenue grew by 25% year over year to $127.6 billion. That came in below analyst estimates, and it is one of the reasons why the market's reaction to the company's quarterly update was negative. But it gets worse. Alphabet's net earnings per share dropped by 26% year over year to $2.12, while its free cash flow was a negative $9.1 billion, significantly worse than the (positive) free cash flow of $24.5 billion recorded in the prior-year quarter.

Alphabet is investing heavily, but the company's spending isn't yielding top-line growth in line with Wall Street's expectations, and earnings and free cash flow are declining rapidly. That's a bad combination. However, there was at least one bright spot for Alphabet: Its cloud computing segment, Google Cloud.

During the period, cloud sales came in at $30.7 billion, 103% higher than the year-ago period. It's worth highlighting just how much Alphabet's cloud sales have been accelerating in recent quarters.

Notice also that the jumps have gotten bigger since Q4 2025. Google Cloud is proving to be a major growth driver for Alphabet, and there is more to come. The company noted that Cloud backlog was $561 billion as of the end of the period, an increase of 262% year over year. The company expects to recognize 55% of that -- or about $309 billion -- over the next 24 months -- that's roughly eight quarters at an average of $38.6 billion per quarter.

This points to sustained demand for the company's cloud services, and by the looks of it, the company will continue to capitalize on it at least over the next few years. That's great news for investors.

Alphabet's AI business is booming. It is helping boost cloud sales growth, for instance. Alphabet noted that demand for enterprise AI solutions contributed meaningfully to the performance of its cloud computing business. Alphabet is also making progress elsewhere. For instance, the company highlighted that the Gemini app now has reached one billion users.

This grants the company significant monetization opportunities, which it will seek to exploit in the coming years. Further, Alphabet has started selling its custom AI chips, and according to management, this business is experiencing strong demand and meaningfully contributing to the top line.

Custom AI chips can sometimes be cost-efficient for corporations, and as AI infrastructure spending continues to grow, demand for these chips could rise. That gives Alphabet yet another meaningful growth avenue. The company's AI-related investments may be harming profits and free cash flow now, but they could pay for themselves several times over in the medium term.

That's why the post-earnings dip is not justified, in my view, and represents a great buying opportunity for long-term investors.

Beyond cloud and AI, Alphabet has plenty of opportunities. Its search business remains rock solid; it remains a leader in streaming thanks to YouTube; it has a promising autonomous-vehicle business with Waymo; and more. The company's outlook appears bright, and the stock looks fairly valued right now.

Alphabet is trading at 18x forward earnings, versus an average of 17x for communication services stocks. Alphabet is worth a much steeper premium given the company's prospects, and buying the company's shares at current levels could yield above-average returns over the next five years.

#3055. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3054. The Next Frontier Of Business Requires A Space Mindset

Shelli Brunswick is CEO & Founder of SB Global LLC and an international keynote speaker on tech used for the betterment of humanity.

​Leaders will shape the next era of innovation by creating opportunities for more people and organizations to contribute.

Artificial intelligence (AI), satellite services and digital infrastructure are expanding what organizations can accomplish. Turning that potential into lasting progress requires a broader strategic lens: understanding the systems that sustain innovation, developing the people who can put it to work and creating partnerships that move from ambition to execution.

Space makes these leadership challenges tangible. Every mission operates within an environment shaped by nations, institutions and companies. Scientific discovery depends on expertise and resources distributed across borders. Today’s decisions shape tomorrow’s opportunities.

These relationships came into focus when I convened The Space Mindset: Navigating Space Policy, Diplomacy and Global Leadership during the Science Summit at the United Nations General Assembly. Bringing together perspectives from diplomacy, governance, research and innovation revealed a leadership opportunity extending well beyond space.

The next frontier of growth lies in connecting technological ambition with resilient systems, human expertise and effective cooperation.

Every growth strategy rests on systems the organization does not fully control. Communications networks, cloud platforms, energy supplies and external data connect individual businesses to a wider environment.

Space makes this relationship visible. A satellite operator can achieve its mission objectives while contributing to congestion that complicates future operations for everyone. The European Space Agency’s (ESA) 2026 Space Environment Report describes growing collision risks as constellations expand and too many satellites remain in congested orbits after their operational lives end. Protecting shared systems preserves the capacity to innovate and grow.

Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, linked the reliability of space services to economic resilience. Former Ecuadorian President Rosalía Arteaga brought a generational perspective, asking leaders to consider people who cannot yet participate in today’s decisions.

Together, those perspectives suggest a more ambitious role for technology leadership: building systems that remain useful as dependence on them grows. For executives, this means evaluating expansion through two lenses: What value will the initiative create? What must remain reliable for that value to endure?

As a business leader, you should map out the dependencies supporting your most important customer outcomes. Examine reliance on providers, recovery options and the consequences of failure across connected services. Include maintenance, interoperability and plans for replacing or phasing out systems and services in investment decisions. Then identify where coordinated action can strengthen the environment: shared security practices, clearer interfaces or better communication among providers.

Resilience can become a source of confidence for customers and partners. Organizations that strengthen the surrounding systems create firmer foundations for their own growth.

The opportunity created by a technology expands when people can adapt it to their circumstances, solve problems with it and contribute improvements.

Access to a platform creates a starting point. Economic value develops through relevant applications, informed judgment and the ability to integrate new tools into real work.

Holla-Maini highlighted the difficulty of attracting investment in human capital compared with visible infrastructure. Bahrain Space Agency chief executive officer Mohamed Al-Aseeri described a complementary approach: combining education, specialized training and mission experience to build capabilities that can support future work.

Dr. Masami Onoda of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency explored international collaboration and capacity building through relationships that connect agencies, researchers and private-sector participants.

These examples show that expertise develops when people apply their knowledge to real problems and work alongside experienced practitioners.

The World Bank’s Digital Progress and Trends Report 2025 reinforces that wider view. It identifies connectivity, compute, context and competency as foundations for effective AI ecosystems, connecting infrastructure and computing power with relevant data and skills.

Leaders should prepare people to use technology effectively as part of every investment. They should budget for training and guided practice so they can adapt new tools to local needs, identify errors and question results. Extend that investment to customers, suppliers, and partners. Their expertise may reveal applications and market needs your organization would otherwise miss. Measure whether people can solve relevant problems, improve processes and respond effectively as conditions change. These outcomes demonstrate readiness more clearly than course completion.

Some of the most valuable opportunities emerge where different capabilities meet. A research institution may understand a scientific challenge. A business may know how to commercialize a solution. A government may create the conditions for adoption. Each contributes something the others need.

Professor Dr. Kai-Uwe Schrogl, a special advisor for political affairs at the ESA, described regional cooperation that enables countries to pool resources and pursue programs beyond their individual reach. Michal Brichta, director of the Innovation Department at Slovakia’s Ministry of Economy, emphasized understanding existing strengths and finding a distinctive contribution within the international landscape.

Leaders need to choose partners whose strengths complement your own and define the outcome you will pursue together. Cooperation requires clear working agreements. Partners need to know who makes which decisions, what information is shared and how to resolve competing priorities. They also need enough trust to discuss difficult issues openly as circumstances change. The Artemis Accords illustrate this approach through shared principles for civil space exploration, including transparency, interoperability and scientific data sharing.

For AI partnerships, the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s AI Risk Management Framework provides a relevant foundation by incorporating trustworthiness considerations into AI design, development, use and evaluation.

Before expanding the partnership, test those agreements against a realistic challenge, such as a service disruption or conflicting customer needs. Can partners share information, resolve disagreements and respond together? Effective cooperation increases what participants can accomplish together.

The strategic question for technology leaders is whether each investment strengthens the collective ability to innovate. Consider whose expertise it develops, which shared systems it strengthens and what new possibilities it opens through cooperation. These choices shape a shared future. When leaders build the conditions for others to succeed, they expand the possibilities for their organizations and for the generations of innovators who will follow.

The space mindset challenges us to see beyond current limits, act with purpose and build opportunities that others can carry forward.

#3052. If Moderna's CEO Is Right, the Stock's Rally Could Just Be Getting Started

Moderna (MRNA +0.89%) has been the hottest stock in the S&P 500 this year, and it hasn't been close. Up around 650%, the next-best-performing stock is Sandisk, with gains of about 380% thus far.

It's been an exceptional performance for Moderna, which struggled in recent years after its sales nosedived as demand for its COVID vaccine and pill dwindled.

Now, however, there's plenty of excitement around the business due to the cancer vaccine it's been working on with Merck. And if it can be as successful as Moderna's CEO believes it can be, then it may not be unrealistic to expect the healthcare stock to surge even higher in value.

Moderna and Merck have been working on a cancer vaccine for years, and the results are starting to pay off significantly. A recent late-stage trial demonstrated that the vaccine, intismeran, reduced the risk of death or recurrence in melanoma patients when paired with Keytruda, Merck's highly successful cancer drug, by an impressive 42%.

Investors are thrilled with the results and the money that intismeran may bring in for Moderna in the future. CEO Stéphane Bancel is excited about the possibility for the treatment to also go beyond just melanoma, stating that, "We believe it will work everywhere Keytruda works."

That would be monstrous, as Keytruda brought in $32 billion in revenue for Merck's business last year. A growth catalyst, meanwhile, is exactly what Moderna needs, as in the past three years its revenue has been declining sharply, totaling just $1.9 billion throughout all of 2025.

If intismeran proves to be the real deal for Moderna, unlocking all sorts of growth for the business, then it may not be hard to see a path for the stock to rise even higher, potentially doubling from where it is right now. Merck, whose business centers heavily around Keytruda, has a market cap of around $370 billion, while Moderna's valuation is far lighter, at less than $90 billion.

There are, however, sky-high expectations for the stock these days, in light of not only the encouraging trial results but also the CEO's comments and excitement. At the end of the day, intismeran isn't approved yet, and while there is potential for it to help with other illnesses, investors shouldn't assume that's a sure thing.

The healthcare company has a ton of potential, but massive gains at this stage are by no means a guarantee, especially given the company's underwhelming financial results. Investors should tread carefully.

David Jagielski, CPA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Merck and Moderna. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3047. How AI-Driven Loyalty Programs Drive Better Business Outcomes

As CTO of Engage People Inc. Len Covello helps companies differentiate loyalty programs to deliver a better experience for their customers.

AI enhances a loyalty program’s key features and helps guide customer decisions through an interactive experience. Customers not only see the number of points and rewards options but also get advice about how best to spend points, combine points with other deals or achieve a larger goal. They get a better experience, and the retailer sees stronger sales and conversion rates.

​AI in loyalty is still emerging, but it’s growing quickly. By 2030, AI is expected to handle 80% of customer interactions. Now is the time to learn how it is transforming customer loyalty and delivering real-time value to customers and brands.

Through all of its iterations, the purpose of a loyalty program is to increase customer retention, repeat sales and build brand recognition. With AI in play, loyalty programs are evolving beyond a tool for retention. The program can define customer intent, create personalized value, provide a real-time understanding of point and reward offerings, and trigger immediate action. With these benefits, AI connects a customer’s entire value ecosystem and creates a new value layer that hasn’t previously existed in loyalty.

​Traditional loyalty works through customer segmentation, and pushes tailored campaigns to those customer segments to engage with the customer. AI in loyalty can achieve a higher level of personalized customer engagement. The AI loyalty model is understand-recommend-decide-execute-learn. It is more than a conversational interface or chatbot; it provides real-time intelligence to customers and provides individualized recommendations based on their points and rewards availability. The program can suggest the best way to spend points to maximize financial value. This form of hyper-personalization encourages engagement and ultimately increases conversion rates.

​With these added features, the loyalty program can serve as a customer management tool. It effectively responds to customer complaints or questions and manages returns. Research from McKinsey found that AI-powered customer experience, which includes loyalty as part of the tool kit, can increase customer satisfaction by 15% to 20% while reducing the cost to serve customers by 20% to 30%. This benefit happens when brands builds the right data foundation with integrated models, advanced analytics, decision orchestration and delivery infrastructure—not a prepackaged chatbot.

The robust list of benefits stems from a high-quality interactive system that communicates directly with customers. Some people might imagine a chatbot, but the AI programming is capable of much more than a script-driven question-and-answer tool. It is a new type of loyalty interaction model that can answer complex financial questions and provide direction.

​For customers, the model will become a trusted guide that can offer thoughtful, accurate guidance about the financial value of loyalty points and how to best earn and spend points to maximize value. Customers can ask direct questions as well, to better understand their options. For example, a customer can ask for the stronger value: using points toward upcoming travel plans versus using the points to make a daily purchase, as well as how best to earn those points in specific categories to achieve that goal.

​This level of flexibility is the goal of the pay-with-points system: giving customers the opportunity to utilize points when and where is best for them. Now, the AI helps customers make those decisions with their financial well-being in mind. That feature builds a deeper loyalty connection to the brand, motivates action and increases sales and conversion. McKinsey found that a specific case of AI-driven personalization at a U.S. airline led to 210% improvement in targeting at-risk customers, 800% improvement in customer satisfaction and a 59% reduction in churn.

Data collection is one of the major benefits of a loyalty program. Brands use them to track behaviors and habits, gaining feedback on campaigns. While traditional programs measure membership growth and redemptions, AI shifts this model. It analyzes specific nuances to understand customer behavior and predict outcomes.

​The AI system uses more effective metrics to track these behaviors, including activity metrics and real business outcomes. The list of nuanced metrics in these categories is endless, and the AI will inherently analyze ultra-specific datasets. Some of the types of metrics on that list are the experiences that drive incremental revenue growth, the reward types that create behavior change and the reward offers that improve profitability for the brand.

Fraud protection in loyalty is vital against misuse. AI strengthens defenses by identifying unusual purchase patterns, account take-over attempts and abuse of promotions. Systems can also make recommendations to close loopholes to prevent future fraudulent activity.

​Fraudulent use of a loyalty program can lead to significant losses for a brand. Between 2016 and 2017, for example, American Express faced widespread reports of customers exploiting generous introductory bonus-point offers, prompting the company to freeze accounts, claw back rewards and tighten its terms. This is exactly the type of incident that AI in loyalty can prevent by creating a real-time risk and decisioning layer that prevents bad actors from taking advantage of the program.

​The future of loyalty has arrived, but it doesn’t look like more rewards or more options or more offers. AI is helping customers make better decisions in real time when spending points and extract the most value from the program. Pay-with-points has become an essential part of loyalty, and now, AI is optimizing the experience to transform loyalty into a value engine.

#3046. Centrus Spent $116 Million on a Supplier With Oil and Gas Customers. Here's the Nuclear Reason Why.

Rising power demands from data centers and zero-emissions targets make nuclear an ideal energy source because it can provide 24/7, reliable baseload power. Meanwhile, next-generation small modular nuclear reactors require special fuel, and Centrus Energy (LEU +1.16%) provides it.

With federal bans on Russian nuclear imports slated to go into effect in 2028, Centrus is working to establish an American-owned and operated uranium enrichment supply chain. To do so, the company is reestablishing commercial enrichment capacity in the U.S. as it aims to be a vital domestic supplier for traditional nuclear plants and advanced small modular reactors.

As part of its efforts, Centrus recently acquired an oil and gas supplier, but for very specific nuclear reasons.

Centrus Energy recently acquired Westerman Holdings for $116 million, funded with $95 million in cash and $21 million in stock. Westerman operates manufacturing facilities that produce equipment and systems for upstream and midstream oil and gas operations. It also fabricates uranium hexafluoride cylinders, centrifuge casings, and large-scale components that Centrus needs to expand its manufacturing abilities.

Westerman was already a key vendor for Centrus, and bringing this specialized manufacturing in-house will help Centrus mitigate supply chain bottlenecks and gain direct control over production timelines. In addition, vertically integrating this part of the supply chain can help Centrus lower manufacturing project costs and capture the margin internally.

Beyond nuclear components, Westerman manufactures surface equipment and storage systems for upstream and midstream oil, gas, and marine markets, helping diversify Centrus's earnings beyond nuclear fuel.

The acquisition is part of Centrus's primary objective to transform from a nuclear fuel broker to a producer of low-enriched uranium (LEU), which is the nuclear fuel used in traditional nuclear reactors, and high-assay, low-enriched uranium (HALEU), the nuclear fuel that powers many of the next-generation small modular reactors (SMRs).

Centrus has relied heavily on TENEX, a Russian state-owned entity, for its LEU. However, in 2023, Congress passed the "Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act," which blocks imports of natural uranium and LEU produced by Russian entities. Some have been granted waivers, but the waivers expire on Jan. 1, 2028, while the ban extends through 2040.

Centrus is investing billions of dollars in its Ohio and Tennessee facilities to build on its domestic enrichment capacity. The company is investing $560 million to produce thousands of AC100M centrifuges in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, while expanding its Piketon, Ohio centrifuge and enrichment plant to develop LEU and HALEU at scale.

The Westerman acquisition is part of Centrus's broader strategy to boost American-produced nuclear fuel. The move helps bring some processes in-house and de-risk Centrus's supply chain while also underscoring the capital intensity of Centrus's multi-year domestic build-out.

That said, Centrus is well-positioned to become the domestic nuclear fuel supplier for traditional and next-generation nuclear technology and is a picks-and-shovels play on America's nuclear future.

Courtney Carlsen has positions in Centrus Energy. The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3041. The Engineering Behind An AI-Native Software Development Life Cycle

Sergey Marchuk is CTO & Co-Founder at Oxagile, a software engineering company enhancing online video experiences with AI.

​Agents have lowered the cost of producing code, but writing code was never the whole job.

A production feature still needs someone to figure out what it should do, make architectural decisions, break the work down, test the result, review it and take responsibility when something goes wrong. Give an agent a vague Jira ticket and ask it to code, and you’ll still have to solve all of those problems. ​

In other words, even as implementation gets cheaper, ambiguity in the requirements, weak architectural decisions and gaps in verification can cost you more than before. ​

For example, as reported by Ars Technica, a recent study from Harvard University researchers found that introducing coding agents leads to a 30% increase in total lines of code generated, but that the time between a pull request being submitted and the code being merged into the codebase rose 49%. ​​

The distinction I find useful is between giving developers AI coding tools and building an engineering operating model around agents.

As the CTO of a software development and consulting company, I’m seeing the results firsthand. My team is still experimenting with what works, and I don’t think anyone can credibly claim yet that the industry has settled on one model, but I’m seeing several patterns becoming clear.

Requirements, architecture, decomposition, implementation, review, testing. AI didn’t break or reinvent the software development life cycle, but human effort is being redistributed inside it. ​

In my experience, writing code by hand becomes an exception in an AI-native SDLC. Instead, engineers spend more time on interfaces, constraints, architectural decisions and decomposition. My team breaks work into atomic tasks with their own completion criteria, small enough to finish inside a single clean agent context.

Code review, however, can consume more of the development process than it does in a conventional SDLC. Agents can handle routine checks for correctness, test coverage and conformance to the spec. Human review goes deeper on changes that are costly or hard to reverse, including security, architecture, public interfaces, data operations and business-critical logic. ​

In that sense, the human role moves up a level. People focus more on deciding what to build, expressing intent precisely, defining boundaries and invariants, setting acceptance criteria, reviewing generated work and identifying where human judgment is still needed.

Those responsibilities don’t necessarily map neatly to traditional roles. In a highly automated team, the same person may work across requirements, architecture, implementation and verification. That puts a higher premium on engineering expertise because effective AI-native work requires a broader understanding of how the software is built, tested and operated.

There is an uncomfortable property of the capable coding agents that I’ve worked with: Give it an underspecified task, and it may still give you a very convincing answer.

An engineer who knows the project will often notice when something sounds off and ask, “What did you mean here?” An agent may simply fill the gap itself and keep going, which makes ambiguity expensive.

On the AI-native projects my team works on, we start with a specification that captures functional requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria and what is explicitly out of scope. Before implementation, the spec is checked for gaps and contradictions and the answers go back into it. Otherwise, unanswered questions become assumptions in the code.

The specification has to carry enough context into the technical plan and implementation so that the agent isn’t left inventing missing requirements. The acceptance criteria defined in the spec are then used to verify the result.

An experienced developer carries far more project context than is written in the current ticket. They understand the architecture, the patterns the team follows and the shortcuts that caused trouble before. An AI agent doesn’t inherit any of that history.

By harness, I mean the project instructions, tools, permissions, checks and feedback loops that surround the model. On our projects, harness lives in the repository and captures architecture, conventions, anti-patterns and other context the agent needs. I recommend keeping the context modular and starting unrelated tasks with a clean context, so the agent isn’t carrying irrelevant history from one piece of work into the next.

That harness needs continuous maintenance as the project changes. Lessons from code review, continuous integration, observability and incidents feed back into the harness and tooling.

Engineering teams have plenty of rules that amount to “developers know not to do this.” That’s a weak control when an agent is doing the work.

Some of those rules can be enforced directly in the agent loop. Secrets are blocked before the file opens, destructive commands before they run and every tool call leaves an audit trail.

For decisions that can’t be encoded that way, I’ve found it’s important to have four review gates for requirements, architecture, decomposition and implementation. Each should be a concrete artifact and a named person responsible for sign-off, and the agent shouldn’t advance itself through the process.

There is a temptation to treat AI-native development as a shortcut around the practices software teams spent decades learning. My experience so far points in the opposite direction: Those practices become part of the environment the agent works against.

Tests are a good example. In our current setup, each unit of work comes with its own tests, written by the agent in the same session as the implementation. The harness runs them alongside static checks, while version control, CI/CD, observability, infrastructure as code and isolated environments make the agent’s changes easier to verify and trace.

But the question I’m more interested in is how much implementation we can delegate to AI without handing over engineering judgment with it.

That boundary is still moving. I expect our own answer to look different a year from now. Yet that, more than any individual AI tool, is where I believe the real work of becoming AI-native is happening. ​​

#3039. Here's How Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway Stock Did in Every S&P 500 Down Year Since 2000

Counting dividends, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.61%) has been down in six calendar years since 2000. Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +1.01%)(BRKB +1.22%) stock beat the index in all of them.

The record is from Berkshire's own annual letter, which has a table comparing the yearly change in its per-share market value to the S&P 500's return, including dividends.

In 2000, Berkshire's stock rose 26.6% but the index slid 9.1%. It added 6.5% in 2001 versus an 11.9% decline, and it dipped just 3.8% in 2002, as the index shed 22.1%. In 2008, the stock fell 31.8%, a little less than the index's 37% drop. And in 2018 and 2022, Berkshire climbed 2.8% and 4% but the index fell 4.4% and 18.1%.

So, Berkshire made money in four of those six years. On a simple average, the stock gained less than 1% a year over all six, while the index dropped around 17%.

Of course, the definition matters here. A down year in this case follows the table's S&P column, which counts dividends. Berkshire hasn't paid a dividend since 1967, so its column is just the change in the stock's market value.

On price alone, two more years would make the list. The index ended 2011 a fraction of a point down and dropped 0.7% in 2015. And Berkshire's shares slid both years, by 4.7% and 12.5%, so the streak arguably depends on where the line gets drawn.

Warren Buffett wrote about keeping Berkshire liquid for decades, and he stuck to it in 2008, the worst of those six years for the market. That year, Berkshire put $14.5 billion into high-yielding fixed-income securities from three companies, getting an equity stake in each deal as a bonus. To pay for them, Buffett trimmed some stock holdings he would've preferred to keep.

In his 2008 letter to shareholders, he said that he'd pledged to always run Berkshire "with more than ample cash."

"We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations," Buffett wrote.

But that pledge was about the company, not the share price. Berkshire's stock still lost 31.8% in 2008. And the calendar-year number hides the worst of it. In his 2017 letter, Buffett listed the stock's largest drops, including a 50.7% slide in the Class A shares between Sept. 19, 2008, and March 5, 2009.

He never said the stock was immune, either. In his 2014 letter, Buffett noted that Berkshire's shares had fallen around 50% from a peak three times since 1965.

"Someday, something close to this kind of drop will happen again, and no one knows when," he wrote.

I'd say the record's best run also owes something to where the stock started. According to the same 2017 letter, Berkshire's Class A shares slid 48.9% between June 1998 and March 2000, bottoming at $41,300. That was only about 9% over the $37,987 in book value per share Berkshire reported for the end of 1999 (book value is what's left after subtracting a company's liabilities from its assets).

Notably, Berkshire's edge was narrowest in 2008, at about 5 percentage points, the year the market's drop was largest. In the other five down years, the margin ranged from around 7 points in 2018 to about 36 points in 2000.

Berkshire's Class B shares closed at around $542 on Oct. 29, under 2% off their 52-week high of $549.96. With book value of around $348 per Class B share at the end of June, the stock trades at about 1.6 times book value -- well over the roughly 1.1 times book value it hit in March 2000.

The cash, of course, is still there. Greg Abel, Berkshire's CEO since January, described a "fortress-like balance sheet" in his first annual letter. And Berkshire had around $365 billion in cash and Treasury bills at the end of June, or about 31% of its market value at the Oct. 29 close. Some of that money is needed to back Berkshire's insurance business, Abel said.

Still, can investors count on Berkshire in the next down year? I think the record makes a decent case that the stock could hold up better than the index again. But it doesn't promise a gain, and the shares aren't starting from anywhere near their March 2000 valuation.

For me, that still makes Berkshire worth owning as a steadier part of a portfolio. I'd just expect its edge in the next down year to be narrower than it was in 2000.

Most are still rooting hard for him to succeed, and perhaps the lineup change mentioned above will get him on the right track over that stretch of games.

Lastly, I want to see Jordan Ott take additional steps toward being a solid NBA coach. The lineup moves above would be a step in that direction.

What are the top criticisms in the Bright Side comments? Rotation rigidity, a disconnected defense, and too much small ball. I think of other great coaches and how they will ride a hot hand, pull players lacking effort or missing assignments, and match up with size when needed. He has the opportunity to adapt here. #3033. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3032. Congratulations, Everyone Can Build (Allegedly). Now What?

Neda Nia drives Stibo Systems’ product vision, shaping strategy, innovation and growth to create measurable value for customers.

Andrew Chen, a general partner at the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, recently captured the shift in one sentence: “When anyone can build, the person who decides WHAT to build becomes the bottleneck.”

AI is dramatically reducing the time and technical effort required to turn an idea into a working product. Prototypes that once took months can now be built in days. Agents can write code, analyze customer feedback, test workflows and identify recurring problems.

But lower barriers to building do not guarantee better products. In fact, the opposite may be true. As Robby Stein, vice president of product at Google Search, recently wrote: “Because building is so easy with AI, it’s never been easier to build things nobody wants.”

Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi recently shared a revealing example in a Sequoia Capital interview. Building the core code for a connector took him two days, while getting a production-ready connector through the organization had been taking three quarters. The real bottlenecks were not limited to writing code. They included gathering customer feedback, writing the PRD, configuring external systems and testing. His conclusion was that capturing the benefits of AI required reengineering the entire process, not simply accelerating one step.

This changes product management too. The opportunity is not to produce the same artifacts faster. It is to redesign how customer context moves from discovery to decision to a working product. Speed may be easier to measure. Knowing whether you’re solving the right problem is much harder and ultimately much more valuable and something that product management can manage.

This is why I believe product management is becoming more important, not less.

For years, a significant part of product management involved coordinating execution. Product managers wrote requirements, managed dependencies, prioritized backlogs and helped engineering teams move work through the organization. Those responsibilities will not disappear, but AI will automate or accelerate many of them. The product manager’s value will increasingly come from something harder to automate: understanding context and exercising judgment.

What problem is worth solving? Which customer behavior actually matters? What trade-offs are acceptable? What does good look like in this specific environment?

These questions become even more important when we build agents.

Traditional software usually follows predefined rules. An agent operates with more autonomy and produces probabilistic results. It may complete the same task differently depending on the available data, instructions and context. Someone must define where that autonomy begins, where it ends and how the organization will determine whether the outcome is good enough.

Teresa Torres makes this connection practical in her excellent Product Talk guide, “AI Evals: A Hands-On Guide for Product Teams.”

Evals measure whether an AI product or workflow is performing as expected. But the difficult part is not simply measuring the output. It is deciding what should be measured in the first place. As Torres writes: “Correctness is context dependent. Don’t let a vendor define correctness for your product.”

An engineer can build the evaluation infrastructure. A model can even help score another model’s output. But neither can independently decide what “good” means for a particular customer, workflow or business.

Should an agent optimize for speed, accuracy or explainability? Which errors are inconvenient, and which could create material business risk? When should the agent ask for human approval? What customer behavior indicates that an answer was genuinely useful? These decisions require customer understanding, business context and judgment.

Torres also describes four common approaches to evals: golden datasets, code assertions, an LLM acting as a judge and customer feedback. Choosing among them is not only a technical decision. It depends on the nature of the problem, the consequences of failure and the outcome customers expect.

The next generation of strong product managers will not need to become machine-learning engineers. But they will need to become fluent in how AI products behave. They will need to understand agents, evals, traces and feedback loops well enough to work closely with engineering and data teams. More importantly, they will need to translate customer needs into clear measures of quality.

This creates a new product loop: Understand the customer. Define what good looks like. Build quickly. Evaluate the outcome. Learn from real behavior. Improve continuously.

AI can accelerate nearly every step in that loop. It cannot remove the need for someone to make sense of it.

The future product manager will spend less time moving work through a process and more time defining intent, establishing boundaries and judging outcomes. In an environment where almost anyone can build, knowing what deserves to be built, and whether it is actually good, becomes the real competitive advantage.

When execution was expensive, building was the constraint. As execution becomes cheaper, the constraint moves upstream to understanding the customer, choosing the right problem and defining what good looks like.

Congratulations, everyone can build. The advantage now belongs to those who know what is worth building and how to tell when it is good.​

#3031. Prediction: This Will Be Sandisk’s Stock Price After 1 Year

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are witnessing a bloodbath on the market due to various reasons, including hotter-than-expected inflation, higher interest rates, concerns about access to financing amid higher capital costs, and the aggressive spending on AI infrastructure by hyperscalers that's hurting their cash flow.

Shares of Sandisk (SNDK -1.87%) have been caught in the broader tech rout, and a strong earnings report from the company didn't help it arrest the slide. Let's take a closer look at Sandisk's results and check if its fortunes will turn around in the coming year.

Sandisk released fiscal 2027 first-quarter results (for the three months ended Oct. 2) on Oct. 29. The stock plunged over 13% the next day amid a broader sell-off in tech stocks. However, Sandisk's drop isn't justified when we take a closer look at its earnings and guidance.

Sandisk's revenue jumped by a whopping 378% year over year to $11.03 billion. Meanwhile, non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) increased from just $1.22 in the year-ago period to $49.51 in the previous quarter. The numbers comfortably exceeded Wall Street's expectations. Even better, Sandisk's guidance for the current quarter is better than what analysts were looking for.

The company expects $12.4 billion in revenue in the current quarter at the midpoint of its guidance range. It anticipates earnings per share of $56.00. Analysts were looking for $54.69 in earnings per share on revenue of $12.29 billion. Moreover, Sandisk's outlook clearly suggests that its red-hot growth is sustainable.

The company reported $3 billion in revenue and $6.20 in non-GAAP earnings per share in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. So, its top and bottom lines are poised for an exponential jump once again. It is worth noting that Sandisk's revenue increased at a much slower pace of 61% in the same quarter last year, while earnings increased by 5x year over year.

So, Sandisk's growth continues to accelerate, which explains why analysts anticipate its bottom line to jump by 220% in fiscal 2027 to $226.85. However, Sandisk's EPS growth in Q1 and the guidance for Q2 indicate that it could outpace analysts' expectations, and that could set the stock up for big gains over the coming year.

Sandisk's 12-month median price target of $2,167 implies 88% gains, which is quite healthy. However, the stunning earnings growth the company has been clocking indicates that it can do better than that.

I say this because of the stock's dirt cheap valuation. Sandisk trades at just 9 times earnings, well below the S&P 500 index's earnings multiple of 23. The S&P 500's average earnings are anticipated to increase by 33% this year. Sandisk, therefore, deserves to trade at a premium to the S&P 500.

Let's say the stock trades at even 15 times earnings at the end of fiscal 2027, which will end in early July next year, and it clocks $226.85 in EPS (in line with consensus expectations); its price could reach $3,403. That's nearly 3x Sandisk's price right now, indicating that it has the potential to become a multibagger given its red-hot growth and attractive valuation.

#3028. Reddit Stock Crashes Again. Is the Stock a Buy on the Dip or a Value Trap?

For the second straight quarter, shares of Reddit (RDDT +1.69%) got absolutely pummeled following its earnings report. The stock fell 21% in the session after its Q2 report, while it plunged 29% after releasing its Q3 results.

While the social media company continues to see rapid revenue growth and the stock is cheap, it's increasingly looking like a potential value trap.

Reddit has been seeing rapid revenue growth, and that continued in Q3, with revenue surging 53% year over year to $895 million. That handily topped the $878 million analyst consensus, as compiled by LSEG.

Ad revenue jumped 54% to $847 million, with other revenue, which includes data licensing, rose 35% to $48 million. U.S ad revenue climbed 51%, while international ad revenue jumped 68%. Growth was led by lower funnel performance revenue, like shopping apps and app installations, while upper funnel video revenue more than doubled.

The company continued to add new users to its platform, but the pace is slowing. Daily users increased 12% to 130.3 million, while weekly users grew by 16% to 515.2 million. However, the daily user number fell short of analyst expectations of 133.7 million users. Meanwhile, more valuable U.S. daily users fell 2% to 50.7 million and missed the 53.5 million analyst consensus.

User growth is one of the big reasons for the collapse in Reddit's stock price and Alphabet's Google search engine is one of the big reasons behind this. CEO Steve Huffman said Alphabet has "shifted in their relationship with the rest of the Internet," as AI Overviews and AI Mode push links down the search page and are driving less traffic to websites. He also believes that Reddit's "machine-translated" content is also being ranked lower." Reddit uses machine learning to translate posts into other languages.

Given this shift, Reddit saw an average decline of 1 million referrals per week in October. It said that if the trend continues, daily active users could drop by low double digits in Q4. In response, the company plans to require all users to create accounts to access its platform moving forward. Currently, around 80% of its revenue comes from logged-in users.

While traffic is becoming an issue, the company has been doing a nice job of monetizing its current user base. Global average revenue per user (ARPU) climbed 36% to $6.87, while U.S. ARPU surged 53% to $13.82. Reddit has been investing in machine learning and automated ad tools that are improving advertising campaigns and boosting ad performance.

Looking at profitability, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) soared from $166 million a year ago to $402 million. Earnings per share (EPS), meanwhile, surged 75% to $1.40, topping the $1.35 consensus.

Moving forward, the company forecast Q4 revenue to be between $1 billion to $1.03 billion, representing 38% growth. It projected adjusted EBITDA in a range of $480 million to $510 million, compared to adjusted EBITDA of $327 million a year ago.

Reddit is doing a great job of growing revenue, users, ARPU, and profits. However, the shifts with Google search present a real potential problem, and the rise of AI agents could only add to that. Google Search acts as Reddit's primary organic customer acquisition, and without it, its ability to bring in new users becomes more difficult over time. Meanwhile, when an AI agent takes content from Reddit, like a product recommendation, the user never visits the site, costing the company potential ad revenue.

RDDT PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

The entire internet landscape is evolving, and what the ultimate impact on web-based companies like Reddit is still largely unknown, but it likely isn't a positive. So while the stock looks extremely cheap with a forward P/E below 9.5 times 2027 analyst estimates given its current growth, it could well turn out to be a value trap.
